From April 2021, a new revenue recognition standard (新たな収益認識基準) applies to large companies (大企業) and listed companies (上場企業) in Japan.
Under the new standard, revenue recording criteria (計上基準) must be considered from the perspective of when a performance obligation (履行義務) is fulfilled.

Compliance involves highly specialized accounting judgments and policy setting, so companies that must apply the standard should decide after consultation and discussion with experts such as audit firms (監査法人), certified public accountants (公認会計士), and tax accountants (税理士).
Even beginner accounting and finance staff at large or listed companies should at least know the terminology and the existence of this revenue recognition standard.
A simple merchandising-company example starts on 1/1 with capital of 1 million yen and cash of 1 million yen. Journal entry: Debit 現預金 (cash) 1,000,000 / Credit 資本金 (capital) 1,000,000.

On 1/15 the company purchases goods with a cost of 1 million yen and pays in cash. The goods are designed to sell for 1.25 million yen, producing 250,000 yen of profit (粗利益率 / gross-profit rate of 20%). Journal entry: Debit 仕入 (purchases) 1,000,000 / Credit 現預金 (cash) 1,000,000.
On 3/10, goods whose cost was 600,000 yen are sold for 750,000 yen, again realizing the planned 20% gross-profit rate. Journal entry: Debit 現預金 (cash) 750,000 / Credit 売上高 (sales) 750,000.

At the 3/31 fiscal-year-end closing, remaining inventory has a cost of 400,000 yen. Under the periodic-inventory method this is recorded as: Debit 商品 (merchandise inventory) 400,000 / Credit 期末商品棚卸高 (ending merchandise inventory, which reduces 仕入高 / purchases) 400,000.

The sequence illustrates the periodic inventory system used in Japanese bookkeeping: all purchases are charged to 仕入 during the period; unsold goods are then deducted from purchases at year-end so that cost of goods sold equals purchases minus ending inventory.
Gross-profit design of 20% means selling price = cost ÷ 0.8 (i.e., cost × 1.25).
As of March 31, the Balance Sheet (B/S / 貸借対照表) and Profit and Loss statement (P/L / 損益計算書) are presented together to show the company's financial position and results.
Example figures: cash and deposits (現預金) of 1,000,000 yen on the B/S; merchandise (商品) of 400,000 yen on the B/S; cost of goods sold (売上原価) of 600,000 yen and sales (売上高) on the P/L.
Important accounting point: Unsold merchandise totaling 400,000 yen is recorded as inventory (在庫) and therefore appears as an asset on the Balance Sheet rather than being fully expensed.
Unsold goods remain on the Balance Sheet as assets until they are sold; only the cost of goods actually sold is recognized as an expense (売上原価) on the P/L.

The matching principle of revenues and expenses (費用収益対応の原則) requires that only the sold portion of goods is reflected in the income statement: sales revenue is matched with the corresponding cost of goods sold so that the profit margin is correctly shown. Unsold goods remain as inventory on the balance sheet rather than being expensed.

Illustrative matching example: sold goods produce sales of 750,000 yen and cost of goods sold of 600,000 yen (20% profit margin). The 400,000 yen cost of unsold inventory is recorded as inventory on the 3/31 fiscal year-end so that the revenue-expense correspondence is preserved.
Acquisition of a long-lived asset (パソコン / computer) is capitalized, not immediately expensed. On 4/1 a 400,000-yen computer purchased for cash is recorded: Debit 工具器具備品 400,000 / Credit 現預金 400,000.

Depreciation of the computer uses the straight-line method over a 4-year useful life, producing annual depreciation of 100,000 yen. At each 3/31 year-end the entry is: Debit 減価償却費 100,000 / Credit 工具器具備品 100,000. The same entry is repeated in subsequent years until the asset is fully depreciated.

When a company purchases an expensive asset that will be used over a long period, the amount paid is not recorded in full as an expense at the time of purchase. Instead, depreciation (減価償却) is applied over a set number of years.
Depreciation is the process of converting the expenditure incurred to acquire a fixed asset into expense over a long period, gradually transferring cost from the asset to expense.

Assets such as computers are not consumed in a short period; they are used over multiple years. Their cost is therefore allocated to expense over their useful life (耐用年数). In the example, a computer is depreciated over 4 years.

Illustrative example: a 160,000-yen fixed asset is depreciated at 40,000 yen per year. The remaining book value declines over time (e.g., 160,000 → 120,000 yen after the first year) while 40,000 yen is recognized as depreciation expense each year.
This treatment differs from inventory (goods purchased for resale), which is typically expensed when sold rather than allocated over multiple years.
減価償却 (depreciation) is one application of the 費用収益対応の原則 (matching principle of expenses and revenues).

固定資産 (fixed assets) are acquired to generate revenue over the long term rather than the short term; therefore their cost is not expensed immediately but is allocated as expense over a long period so that it corresponds to the revenues obtained.
The matching principle is an additional rule layered on top of 発生主義 (accrual basis / recognition when the expense occurs).

In general, expenses are recognized under the accrual principle; however, expenses that directly correspond to revenues (e.g., 売上原価 / cost of goods sold) and expenditures whose benefits last over a long period (e.g., 減価償却) are recognized so as to match the related revenues.
Revenue is recognized under 実現主義 (realization principle), for example 売上計上 (sales recognition).

A useful way to organize the two ideas is: (1) expenses are basically recognized on an accrual basis, and (2) those expenses that can be matched to specific revenues or that have long-term effects are additionally timed to the revenues they help generate.

The third major premise of accounting standards is the going concern assumption (継続企業の前提 / ゴーイングコンサーン): accounting treatments and financial statements rest on the implicit understanding that an enterprise will not go bankrupt immediately but will continue operating as a going concern.

The going concern assumption gives rise to period accounting—the practice of dividing a company’s life into reporting periods (typically one year) and measuring performance and financial position at fiscal year-end cutoffs. News reports of ‘this period’s results’ rely on this implicit cutoff.

Because the entity is assumed to continue, accrual accounting (発生主義) is possible: credit sales and credit purchases can be recorded as accounts receivable and accounts payable (assets and liabilities) rather than waiting for cash settlement.
The same premise supports the matching principle (費用収益対応の原則): costs that do not correspond to current-period revenue can be deferred as assets and charged in later periods.
Without the period-division premise there would be no need to allocate cash receipts and payments across assets and liabilities.

Depreciation (減価償却) also depends on going concern: the cost of a long-lived asset is allocated as expense over its useful life, and the remaining book value is assumed to retain value. If immediate liquidation were expected, the asset would have to be sold or written off rather than carried as a fixed asset.
The going concern assumption is therefore the foundational premise that underpins the entire structure of the other accounting principles (accrual, matching, depreciation, etc.).
In day-to-day practice, accounting and finance staff rarely examine the going concern assumption itself, yet knowing it as a core principle remains essential for accounting/finance professionals.
Daily journal entries (仕訳) and bookkeeping (記帳) are fundamental accounting tasks that occupy a large share of accounting work.
Bookkeeping (記帳) means creating journal entries (仕訳) in accordance with accounting rules.
Even a single journal entry is not simple; many factors must be considered when posting it.
Daily journal entries are typically entered using accounting software.
Accounting software is broadly classified into on-premise tools and cloud-based tools.
On-premise type: software that must be installed on each PC before it can be used.
Cloud type: software that does not require PC installation; bookkeeping can be done from anywhere by logging in with an internet connection and account information.
The market share of cloud-type accounting software is currently increasing.
Cloud-type software is recommended when newly introducing accounting software, or when aiming for flexible, efficient, low-cost introduction that also supports remote work.
On-premise type is relatively well suited to an always-in-office work style or when stronger security inside the office is required.
Account subject master settings (勘定科目のマスター設定) should be configured to match the business.

To post journal entries (仕訳), a company must set account titles (勘定科目) that fit its operations. Settings in accounting software such as account titles are called マスター (master data); become familiar with this term.
Basic/standard account titles are preconfigured in most accounting software, but companies should actively create new ones when the business model requires more flexible classification.

Example of customization: subscription (定額支払) fees for chat tools or cloud servers are often booked to the standard account 通信費 (communication expenses). Because 通信費 is also used for postage and stamps, many firms create distinct titles such as システム利用料 (system usage fees) or ライセンス利用料 (license usage fees) to keep expenses of different natures from being mixed.

Some accountants believe standard account titles must not be changed; this is incorrect. Setting titles that match the company’s business is what matters. Account titles are the accounting “words” that describe business activities, so choose terms that management and stakeholders can easily judge and read.
Pairs of account titles that are easy to confuse: システム利用料 vs 通信費; 地代家賃 vs 賃借料; 旅費交通費 vs 通勤手当; 福利厚生費 vs 通勤手当; 支払手数料 vs 販売手数料; 業務委託費 vs 支払報酬, etc.

Also configure 補助科目 (subsidiary / sub-accounts) under each account title to add finer detail. Example: breaking 売上高 (sales) down by customer/transaction partner improves the readability and analyzability of financial statements and produces better books.

There is no single correct way to set subsidiary accounts; it depends on the accounting software and the company’s accounting policy. In practice they are commonly determined according to typical conventions (the page cuts off before listing those conventions).

Points for setting subsidiary accounts (補助科目): For major balance-sheet accounts that have counterparties and frequent activity—such as accounts receivable (売掛金), accounts payable (買掛金), and unpaid expenses (未払金)—set a subsidiary account for each transaction partner (取引先).
For borrowings (借入金), set subsidiary accounts either by each loan contract or by each lender.
For withholdings/deposits (預り金), set subsidiary accounts separately for social insurance (社会保険), labor insurance (労働保険), and inhabitant tax (住民税).

For profit-and-loss (損益計算書) accounts, counterparties may be used, but setting subsidiary accounts according to the nature and content of revenues and expenses makes performance management and decision-making easier.

Most accounting software provide a ‘department’ (部門) dimension that is completely separate from subsidiary accounts; it is typically used for performance management by organizational unit or business line.

Consider introducing department codes only after the company has grown, businesses have diversified, or multiple large departments exist. Until then, the cost of administering departments often exceeds the benefit, so the timing of introduction is critical.
Departmental control of balance-sheet accounts requires advanced techniques; therefore begin by applying department information first to profit-and-loss accounts.
Bookkeeping (記帳) should be performed on a regular monthly cycle whose timing is dictated by the monthly-closing (月次決算) deadline.

Example of scheduling: if monthly closing must be completed by the 5th business day of the following month, bookkeeping should be finished by the 4th business day. Because invoices and receipts typically arrive at the start of the month, posting should occur between the 1st and 4th business days.

Bookkeeping (記帳業務) is often busiest at the beginning of the month; when it overlaps with other work, gather as much information as possible mid-month or at month-end and process some entries early as part of the schedule.
Accurate journal entries (仕訳) are produced by deciding each of the following items in turn according to the supporting documents and business facts.

Account title (勘定科目): Understanding what actually happened in the business is the most important step. Check invoices, contracts, receipts and other vouchers (証憑); interview sales or other departments when anything is unclear.
Subsidiary account (補助科目): Set a subsidiary for each account title to attach detailed information.
Department (部門): When departmental accounting is used, assign a department to each account title.
Journal-entry date (仕訳発生日): Normally the date the transaction occurred. Daily precision is preferable, but because books are often reviewed on a monthly basis the month must at least be correct.
Consumption-tax classification (消費税区分): The tax treatment differs by account title (details appear later in section 2-17).
Remarks (備考): Record internal information that cannot be conveyed by the account title or subsidiary; write it so that a third party can understand it.
出納業務 (suitou gyoumu) is the work of managing incoming payments (入金) and outgoing payments (出金). It is one of the most important fundamental operations in accounting and finance (経理財務).

Accounting and finance work includes daily management of money flow: issuing invoices for sold goods or services and confirming receipts, or receiving invoices from suppliers and making payments from cash or bank accounts.
Among cash-handling operations, invoice issuance (請求書発行業務) is especially important because it is how the incoming-payment side is grasped and managed.
In BtoB businesses (sales to companies, as opposed to BtoC sales to general consumers), invoice issuance for managing sales is the lifeline of cash flow (資金繰り) and the most basic operation.
When goods or services are sold, an invoice is issued to the buyer summarizing the sales content and payment terms.

Typical contents of an invoice: recipient (company name and person in charge), issuer, for each delivered item (delivery date, product name, amount), consumption tax amount, payment due date, and bank account for transfer.
A Japanese invoice (請求書) example from a back-office operations textbook shows the standard layout used in corporate billing between companies.

Issuer information typically includes company name (株式会社コンダクト), address (東京都世田谷区玉川三丁目20番2), telephone number, invoice date (請求日 2024-05-31), invoice number, and qualified invoice issuer registration number (登録番号 T2010901048837).
Recipient (bill-to) details include company name with 御中 honorific, postal address, department, and contact person (営業部 管理太朗 様).
The invoice subject or project name can be stated as 件名, here コーポレート導入コンサルティング (corporate implementation consulting).
Line items list service date, description, quantity (often 1式 meaning one set/package), unit price, and amount: 企画書作成 350,000 yen, 導入コンサルティング 680,000 yen, 保守サービス 160,000 yen.
Subtotal (小計) is the sum of line items before tax (1,190,000 yen); Japanese consumption tax (消費税) at 10% is shown separately (119,000 yen); grand total including tax is 1,309,000 yen.
Payment terms specify the due date (入金期日 2024-06-30) and bank transfer destination (振込先), commonly a major bank such as 三井住友銀行 with branch and account details.
A remarks (備考) section is used for supplementary conditions such as which party bears bank transfer fees (振込手数料の負担先).
Invoices (請求書) typically cannot be created by the accounting department alone; detailed information on delivered goods and services is provided by the sales department.
Price information, closing dates (締日), and payment due dates are set by sales through agreements with counterparties using contracts, estimates, and purchase orders at the time of the transaction.
The usual contact window with clients is sales, so sales and accounting must closely share information throughout the invoicing process.

Key collaboration steps: decide a schedule with sales for invoice issuance; determine by when and how invoice information will be received from sales; decide when invoices will be issued; mutually check created invoices for errors; after creation, issue invoices to clients and contact them (also decide whether sending/contact is done by accounting or sales).

Invoice issuance work is not finished when invoices are issued; actual incoming payment from the client must be confirmed, or the issued invoices become wasted. Do not let your guard down until funds are collected.

Perform payment (入金) checks according to each issued invoice's payment due date. In typical B2B transactions, due dates are often set at month-end. Example: for a current-month-close / next-month-end payment cycle, always perform the payment check after month-end has passed.
Invoice volume varies greatly by company size: large companies may issue 1,000 or more invoices per month, while small and medium enterprises may issue only a few per month or none in some months.
Invoices are a company's lifeline because they govern incoming payments and cash flow (資金繰り); therefore, avoiding mistakes is essential.

As organizational scale and transaction volume grow, creating invoices each time in Excel or Word increases errors; actively introduce an invoice management system as the key to operational efficiency.

Recent invoice (請求書) systems are often built into cloud-based accounting systems; trying them typically involves low introduction cost and little prior preparation. It is recommended to start by using the invoice function incorporated in accounting software.

Large companies and firms with many counterparties usually have independent systems. Invoice management is typically included in sales-management systems or in ERP (Enterprise Resources Planning) systems, which are core systems with many functions.

Japan’s Invoice system (インボイス制度) began in October 2023. An Invoice is also called a Qualified Invoice (適格請求書): an invoice that satisfies prescribed listing requirements. See also section 2-18 for details.

Even if the issuer is a registered Invoice business, issuing a document that fails the listing requirements prevents the recipient from claiming consumption-tax input-tax credit (仕入税額控除) and thereby inflicts a loss on the counterparty.
Therefore, every issued invoice must be checked against the Qualified Invoice listing requirements.

Qualified Invoice (適格請求書) listing requirements: (1) name or designation of the Qualified Invoice issuing business and its registration number; (2) transaction date; (3) description of the transaction (and an indication if the item is subject to the reduced tax rate); (4) consideration amount totaled separately by tax rate (tax-exclusive or tax-inclusive) together with the applicable tax rate; (5) consumption-tax amount etc. classified by tax rate; (6) name or designation of the business that receives the document.
The listed requirements are based on the National Tax Agency’s “Overview of the Qualified Invoice Preservation Method” (適格請求書保存方式の概要).

Sample invoice illustration on the page shows a November total of 131,200 yen, line items with amounts, tax-rate columns (including 8 %), and consumption tax of 8,000 yen, together with a reduced-rate indication.

Invoice issuance work includes making journal entries in the accounting books as an important task. Accounting entries for invoices and collections are divided into two stages: 発生 (accrual/occurrence) and 消込 (clearing/offsetting).
発生仕訳 (accrual journal entry): When issuing an invoice, record sales (売上高) and accounts receivable (売掛金).
消込仕訳 (clearing journal entry): When payment is confirmed, decrease accounts receivable (売掛金) and increase cash/deposits (現預金).

Example transaction: In April, 1 million yen of goods were sold to a customer. Invoice issued at the beginning of May; payment confirmed in the ordinary deposit account at the end of May. Terms: end-of-month closing, payment by end of the following month.
発生仕訳 on 4/30: Debit 売掛金 1,000,000 yen / Credit 売上高 1,000,000 yen.
消込仕訳 on 5/31: Debit 普通預金 1,000,000 yen / Credit 売掛金 1,000,000 yen.

In accounting ledgers, accounts receivable (売掛金) should be managed by setting subsidiary accounts (補助科目) for each customer within the accounts receivable account. This allows tracking of increases and decreases in accounts receivable not only in the invoice management system but also on the books themselves.

Per-customer subsidiary account setup for accounts receivable enables a double-check function between the accounting and sales departments, supporting more accurate and efficient cash collection management and, by extension, cash flow (資金繰り) management.

Common billing errors include double billing (二重請求), missed billing (請求漏れ), and amount mistakes (金額間違い). Solid invoice issuance management prevents these, but human error becomes more likely as the number of customers grows.

When accounting books display the occurrence and write-off (消込) trends of accounts receivable by customer, billing errors become easier to detect on the ledger side: double billing can cause the balance to double, while missed billing can cause the balance for that month to drop to zero.
Typical accounts receivable balance pattern when billing is correct: relatively stable monthly amounts (example: Company AAA showing 100, 90, 120, 95 across April–July).
A sudden spike in a customer’s accounts receivable balance (example: Company BBB jumping to 200 in June while other months are 30) warrants investigation for a special or unusual transaction.
A customer’s accounts receivable balance dropping to zero in a given month (example: Company AACCC showing 0 in May while other months are 50) should trigger a check for possible missed billing.
Invoice issuance (請求書発行) responsibility is not fixed: it may be performed by sales (営業) or by accounting (経理), and the assignment actually differs from company to company.

The source (primary) data for an invoice—item, price, payment terms, etc.—is decided by sales, while overall cash/money management belongs to accounting; therefore either department is capable of executing the issuance work.
Invoice issuance is an intermediate/cross-functional task that, inside the sales function, is often called “sales administration” (営業事務) or “sales management” (営業管理).
Which department actually issues invoices is largely determined by where the sales-management unit sits: inside the accounting department or inside the sales department.
A frequently observed split of the invoice cycle is: sales performs issuance while accounting/finance performs the subsequent cash-receipt (入金) check.

There is no generally “correct” answer to the efficiency question “which department should do which task.” The optimal split depends on each firm’s business flow, transaction volume, and the organizational design of sales versus accounting.
A critical perspective for any company is to examine its current role allocation and then design a company-specific, “should-be” division of labor rather than copying a generic model.
The first step in payment management (支払管理) is establishing rules (ルールの整備).
Companies conduct diverse business activities that generate many payment activities, not only in payment content but also in payment methods.
Payment methods are wide-ranging and include cash, bank transfers (口座振込), credit card payments, and reimbursements/advances (立替支払).
Because payment contents and methods vary widely, the requester, approver, and payment workflow (支払フロー) also differ from company to company.
When carrying out payment operations, start by understanding the overall picture of payment activities.
Although rules differ by company, summarizing them by payment method (for example) makes it easier to grasp the whole.
Example of company payment rules (会社の支払ルールの例) covering payment methods, contents, closing dates, and payment/debit timings for back-office operations.
Bank transfer (口座振込) is used for raw materials and merchandise purchases (原材料商品仕入), typically with month-end closing and payment by the end of the following month (月末締め翌月末払い).
Main operating expenses (主要経費の支払) follow the same bank-transfer schedule: month-end closing and payment by the end of the following month.
Employee reimbursed expenses (従業員の立替経費) are closed at the end of the current month and paid on the 10th of the following month, transferred together with salary (当月末締め翌月10日払い、給与支払と一緒に振込).
Various subscription services (各種サブスクリプションサービスの支払) use month-end closing with direct debit on the 25th of the following month (月末締め翌月25日引き落とし).
Rent (賃料) is typically debited on the 25th of the previous month (前月25日引落し).
Utilities (水道光熱費) are typically debited on the 10th of the following month (翌月10日引落し).
Small office supplies and similar minor items (少額の事務消耗品費等) as well as postage stamps and revenue stamps (切手印紙) are paid as needed / on an ad-hoc basis (都度).
Payments for services that cannot use bank transfer (それ以外の口座振込ができないサービスの支払) are handled via other methods such as direct debit with specified dates.
Among payment methods, bank transfer (口座振込) is the most important and is explained in detail.

Accounting receives many invoices (請求書) each month, often arriving at the beginning of the month. Invoices now arrive not only as paper documents but also by email or download from the vendor’s billing system; care must be taken to avoid missing any.

Upon receiving an invoice, first check its contents. In principle all items should be checked, with particular focus on: (1) whether payment content and due date match the contract or purchase order; (2) whether the due date fits the company’s transfer schedule; (3) whether the counterpart is an invoice-registered business (インボイス登録事業者) or a tax-exempt business (免税事業者); (4) if registered, whether the invoice satisfies invoice requirements (explained in section 2-12).

Ordering is performed by every department. If accounting cannot understand the order content, it should confirm or interview the relevant department. Leaving content ambiguous can result in paying invoices whose correctness is unknown and can harm the company’s cash flow.

After checking individual invoices, create a payment management table (支払管理表) that groups invoices by payment due date. This can be done in a spreadsheet (e.g., Excel) or with a dedicated payment management system. Cloud accounting systems often include this function, similar to invoice issuance systems.

When building a payment management table in a spreadsheet, include at least the items shown in the accompanying chart. The key point is to maintain a “status” column so that unpaid items can always be identified at a glance.
A payment management table (支払管理表) typically includes columns for management number (管理 No), counterparty/vendor (取引先), payment date (支払日), billed amount (請求金額), status (ステータス), and remarks (備考).
Example payment management table entries: (1) (株) ABC, payment date 2024/6/10, amount 400,000, status 支払済 (paid); (2) BDA (株), payment date 2024/6/30, amount 750,000, status 未処理 (unprocessed).
After preparing the payment management table, bank transfer processing is performed from the company's bank account.
Internet banking is commonly used to carry out transfer (振込) operations.

Internet banking offers two main transfer methods: 振込・振替 (individual transfers/remittances processed one payee at a time) and 総合振込 (bulk/comprehensive transfer that processes multiple payees together in one operation).
Staff should understand the respective merits and demerits of 振込・振替 versus 総合振込 when choosing how to execute payments.

In Japanese corporate back-office (accounting) operations, bank payments are commonly executed either as 振込・振替 (individual transfers/remittances, typically entered one-by-one in internet banking) or as 総合振込 (bulk/comprehensive transfers using a file such as Zengin format).
Merit of 振込・振替: even if the transfer destination is entered incorrectly, the bank’s system can often correct it internally, which tends to reduce operational mistakes.

Demerits of 振込・振替: each payment must be specified by manual input one by one, so the workload grows quickly as the number of vendors/counterparties increases; per-item transfer fees are relatively high.

Merits of 総合振込: transfer data exported from a payment-management system (全銀データ / Zengin-format files or CSV) can be imported, allowing large volumes of payments to be processed at once; transfer fees are cheaper than individual 振込.

Demerits of 総合振込: an erroneous transfer typically cannot be corrected until the next business day and the correction process is laborious; the company must maintain a payment master (payee bank details) and therefore needs a certain level of system literacy.
Related accounting practice: journal entries (仕訳) are posted in parallel with invoice receipt (請求書受領) and payment execution rather than as a completely separate later step.
Invoice payment processing, like invoice issuance, requires recording journal entries in the accounting books using a two-stage approach: occurrence (発生仕訳) and clearing/settlement (消込仕訳).
Occurrence journal (発生仕訳): When an invoice is received, debit Purchases/Expenses (仕入/経費) and credit Accounts Payable/Accrued Expenses (買掛金/未払金).
Clearing journal (消込仕訳): When payment is completed, debit Accounts Payable/Accrued Expenses (買掛金/未払金) to reduce the liability and credit Cash/Deposits (現預金) to decrease assets.
Example: Goods purchased in April for 800,000 yen; invoice received early May; paid by bank transfer at end of May. Terms: month-end close, payment by end of following month.
Occurrence entry dated 4/30: Debit Purchases (仕入高) 800,000 yen / Credit Accounts Payable (買掛金) 800,000 yen.
Clearing entry dated 5/31: Debit Accounts Payable (買掛金) 800,000 yen / Credit Ordinary Deposit (普通預金) 800,000 yen.
Similar to accounts receivable (売掛金), set up subsidiary accounts (補助科目) by vendor (取引先) within the accounts payable (買掛金) and unpaid amounts (未払金) ledger accounts, and manage them that way.
Confirm the balance trends of 買掛金 and 未払金 for each vendor while performing double-checks.
When making journal entries (仕訳) and choosing accounts, clearly understand and apply the distinction between 買掛金 and 未払金.
Common point of 買掛金 and 未払金: both are credit/trade debts (掛け債務), i.e. future payments arising from operating activities.
Key difference: whether the payment is for an expense directly tied to operating activities or sales (営業活動や売上に直接的に紐づく費用の支払か否か). This distinction is easy to confuse in practice.
買掛金 is used for future obligations tied to purchases (仕入高) and accounts that are included in manufacturing cost (製造原価).
未払金 is used for future obligations tied to selling, general and administrative expenses (販売費及び一般管理費), such as supplies expense (消耗品費).

A common worry among accounting staff is that they cannot verify whether invoices circulated from other departments are correct, whether large amounts should be paid, or which account titles to use for journal entries.
The most difficult and troubling aspect of invoice payment is that the final process—bank transfer—must always be performed by accounting.

Invoices arrive after goods or services have already been provided. In the business flow (negotiation → estimate → contract → order → delivery → invoice → payment), invoicing and payment are the last processes.

For more effective invoice operations, accounting should ideally grasp what is happening from the field’s negotiation and estimate-acquisition stage, not only at the final exit. Involvement from the entry point allows accounting to make judgments from the same perspective as the field.

In companies that have become overly siloed, only the final invoice payment is sent to accounting while the preceding processes remain completely unknown. This tendency appears more readily in companies that undervalue accounting and payment management.
Under fragmented systems, accounting does not deeply understand the payment contents, raising the risk of fraud such as kickbacks and embezzlement, which can even affect company management itself.

Invoice payment equals cash-flow management and should be regarded as the company’s lifeline. Mechanisms and structures that allow accounting and the field to share information openly and seamlessly are indispensable.
Accounting is therefore a department that unexpectedly requires strong communication skills.

Traditional bookkeeping textbooks describe using special paper vouchers when cash inflows/outflows occur and journal entries are made: 出金伝票 (payment voucher, printed in blue) for payment-related accounts, 入金伝票 (receipt voucher, printed in red) for receipt-related accounts, and 振替伝票 (transfer voucher) for accounts unrelated to cash in/out.

Veteran accounting/finance staff at long-established companies may still use these voucher terms and rules. In modern management that uses accounting software and IT-ized processes, the terms 出金伝票 and 入金伝票 are overwhelmingly rare; among companies founded in the last decade or so, usage is felt to be well under 1%.

Traditional Japanese accounting documents such as 出金伝票 (disbursement/payment slips), 入金伝票 (receipt/incoming payment slips), and 振替伝票 (transfer slips) are merely terms that describe debit-side or credit-side attributes for each individual row of data, rather than independent conceptual objects.

For performing modern accounting work, it is more effective to discuss operations using the larger systems concept of 「データの集合体 = データベース」 (a collection of data = a database) instead of legacy paper-slip terminology.
This shift in language and thinking is occurring because old expressions are being replaced as accounting environments change due to AI adoption and cloud tools.

In the accounting domain, as AI-ization and cloud-tool adoption advance and the operating environment changes significantly, traditional expressions fall out of use and ways of thinking that differ from the past become established in actual practice.

立替経費 (reimbursed / out-of-pocket expenses) are expenses temporarily paid from the personal pocket money of officers and employees (役職員) when the company cannot immediately pay from its bank account during business activities.

Typical reasons reimbursed expenses arise: sudden payments needed during field work; payees that accept only cash (no bank transfer or credit card); a policy of not holding petty cash (小口現金) so small payments are processed as personal reimbursements; transportation costs outside commuting-allowance coverage.
Reimbursed expenses have three operational traits that must be managed: they apply to all officers and employees; the payment is known only after the fact; they occur routinely and in large numbers.
Because of those traits, application mistakes, delayed submissions, and omitted claims occur regularly.
A company-wide application flow (申請フロー) with clearly defined rules must be created and consistently followed to control reimbursed-expense settlement and checking.

When establishing rules for 立替経費申請 (employee expense reimbursement applications), key decisions include: the application method (whether to use an expense settlement system), who approves applications, which expense types are eligible, application deadlines, settlement payment timing (e.g., whether to align with payroll transfers), and how long delayed applications will be tolerated.

A common problem with 立替経費 is delayed applications. Applications require attaching receipts and describing details, so busy employees often forget or postpone them. Delayed applications delay monthly book closing (月次決算の帳簿締め). This is especially critical during year-end closing when schedules are tight; extra attention is needed for reimbursements in the closing month.

To prevent missed applications, accounting should send company-wide announcements before typical deadlines (month-end or month-start) and individually communicate with employees who appear likely to delay, providing follow-up so applications are not overlooked.

Unlike invoice payments, 立替経費 cannot be checked at the moment of payment because the employee pays first. Applications always arrive after the fact, so content must be checked thoroughly. Checkpoints are similar to those for invoice payments, but evidence (エビデンス/証憑) is more varied (receipts, レシート, etc.), so reviews take more time. Ambiguous applications should be confirmed with the applicant promptly.
After checking reimbursed expense (立替経費) claims submitted by officers and employees, bank transfers are performed to settle them.
Two settlement methods exist for reimbursed expenses: combining the transfer with payroll (salary) payment, or making individual reimbursement transfers. Each method has merits and demerits.
If unsure which method to choose, settling reimbursed expenses together with payroll transfers poses no particular problem.

Merits of combining reimbursed-expense settlement with payroll transfer: transfer work is not duplicated (done together with salary payments); bank transfer fees are incurred only once, lowering cost.

Merits of individual reimbursement: settlement timing is not constrained by payroll cutoff or payment dates, giving greater flexibility to expense operations; it is easier to adjust the settlement schedule at financial closing (決算), which helps stabilize closing operations.
In reimbursed-expense settlement it is necessary to consider offsetting against any advance payments (仮払) already made to officers/employees.

Advance-payment processing (仮払処理) is used mainly for long-term or overseas business trips in which the amount the employee would have to advance is large and cannot be temporarily borne personally. Based on the trip application, the company pays an estimated amount in advance before the trip.

When expenses are settled after a trip for which an advance was paid, the settlement amount and the accounting journal entries must reflect the offset of the advance; mistakes in transfer amounts or journal entries must be avoided.
立替経費の会計処理は、申請・承認時と精算時に仕訳をするのが基本である。事前の仮払処理が発生する場合は、さらに仕訳が一手間増える。
仮払を含む立替精算の一連の仕訳例：10/3に海外出張の社員へ20万円の仮払を実施。11月初に10月分としてホテル代7万円＋航空券代15万円＝合計22万円の立替経費申請を承認し、11/25に差額2万円を追加精算した。
①仮払時（10/3仕訳）：【借方】仮払金 20万円 / 【貸方】普通預金 20万円
②経費申請時（10/31仕訳）：【借方】旅費交通費 22万円 / 【貸方】仮払金 20万円 および 未払金 2万円（申請・承認時点で費用計上し、仮払金を消し込むとともに不足分を未払金として認識する）
③経費精算時（11/25仕訳）：【借方】未払金 2万円 / 【貸方】普通預金 2万円（差額の追加支払い時に未払金を消し込む）
仮払金は事前に従業員へ渡した資金を資産として計上し、後の経費申請時に旅費交通費などの費用勘定へ振り替える。不足額は未払金経由で精算する。
Fixed assets (固定資産) are defined as assets used in business activities over a long period of time.
When a company purchases a fixed asset, it must first determine which account title (勘定科目) it falls under, because the asset is registered under that account name.

Main types of tangible and intangible fixed assets and typical examples: Buildings (建物) — offices, stores, factory buildings, and interior construction costs; Structures (構築物) — advertising signs, greening facilities/gardens, roads, bridges, and retaining-wall works; Machinery and equipment (機械装置) — complete manufacturing equipment; Vehicles and transportation equipment (車両運搬具) — company cars, transport trucks, and forklifts; Tools, furniture and fixtures (工具器具備品) — office furniture/fixtures, PCs, printers, molds, and medical equipment; Land (土地) — purchased land; Intangible fixed assets (無形固定資産) — internally used software and intellectual property rights.
Fixed assets are used over a long period, so under the matching principle of expenses and revenues they are allocated as expenses through depreciation (減価償却).
Accounting treatment of depreciation requires determining three items: acquisition cost (取得価額), useful life (耐用年数), and depreciation method (償却方法).

Acquisition cost is the amount spent to acquire a fixed asset and is the base amount used for depreciation. It generally includes not only the asset’s purchase price but also incidental costs directly related to acquisition (e.g., transportation fees and tariffs for manufacturing equipment). Invoices and estimates should be examined carefully to decide what to include.
Useful life is the number of years over which an asset is depreciated. There are two types: accounting useful life and tax useful life.

Accounting useful life is the economically usable period until the asset becomes economically obsolete—the period during which the asset can generate revenue. It is the most rational measure but is difficult to estimate.
Tax useful life is the period stipulated for each asset type under the Corporate Tax Law and set by Japan’s National Tax Agency; tax calculations must use this life.

In practice, estimating accounting useful life is very difficult. Even if an accounting life is set, tax calculations still require adjustment to the tax useful life. Therefore most companies simply use the tax useful life for both accounting and tax purposes.

The National Tax Agency (国税庁) website publishes a useful-life table (耐用年数表) for each category of fixed asset; accounting staff should form the habit of always looking it up rather than relying on memory.
Depreciation methods (償却方法) for fixed assets fall into two main types: the straight-line method (定額法) and the declining-balance method (定率法).
Under the straight-line method (定額法), the same depreciation amount is charged every year over the asset’s useful life (a flat line on a graph of amount versus years).

Under the declining-balance method (定率法), a larger depreciation expense is recorded in the early years and the amount declines over subsequent years (a downward-sloping curve on a graph of amount versus years).
Straight-line depreciation (定額法) formula: 定額法の減価償却費 = 取得価額 × 償却率, where 償却率 = 1 ÷ 耐用年数. The annual depreciation expense is constant and equals acquisition cost divided by useful life.
Depreciation rate (償却率) under the straight-line method is 1 divided by useful life in years. For a 5-year useful life the rate is 0.2.

Example of straight-line method: a ¥1,000,000 fixed asset with 5-year useful life is depreciated at ¥200,000 each year (1,000,000 × 0.2). Remaining book value declines as 1,000,000 → 800,000 → 600,000 → 400,000 → 200,000 while the annual charge stays 200,000 based on original cost.
Declining-balance depreciation (定率法) formula: 定率法の減価償却費 = 簿価 × 償却率, where 償却率 = (1 ÷ 耐用年数) × 200%. Depreciation is applied to the current book value, so the expense is larger in early years.
The declining-balance rate is twice the straight-line rate and is therefore also called the 200% declining-balance method (200%定率法).
Historically in Japan the declining-balance rate was 2.5 times the straight-line rate rather than 2 times.
The declining-balance depreciation method (定率法) was at one time referred to as the “250% declining-balance method” (250%定率法).

A critical feature of the declining-balance method is that the depreciation calculation itself changes as depreciation progresses: the rate is applied to ending book value rather than acquisition cost, so annual depreciation expense declines each year as book value falls.

If the same declining-balance rate were applied indefinitely, book value would never reach zero. Yet tax/accounting rules require that book value be reduced to zero by the end of the asset’s useful life (e.g., five years).

To resolve this contradiction, once a certain number of years have elapsed the method switches to “revised depreciation” (改定償却). The remaining book value is then depreciated at a new rate that brings it to zero over the remaining useful life.
After the switch, revised depreciation expense = book value at the revision date × revised depreciation rate.
The switch occurs when ordinary declining-balance depreciation expense falls below the “guaranteed depreciation amount” (償却保証額).
Guaranteed depreciation amount = acquisition cost × the statutory guarantee rate prescribed for each useful-life class.

Declining-balance depreciation (定率法) example for a 1,000,000 yen fixed asset with a 5-year useful life uses an initial depreciation rate of 0.4. Year 1: beginning book value 1,000,000, depreciation expense 400,000 (1,000,000 × 0.4), ending book value 600,000. Year 2: beginning 600,000, expense 240,000 (600,000 × 0.4), ending 360,000. Year 3: beginning 360,000, expense 144,000 (360,000 × 0.4), ending 216,000.

Under the Japanese declining-balance method, when remaining book value becomes relatively small a revised rate is applied (here 0.5). From the revised book value of 216,000: Year 4 depreciation 108,000; Year 5 depreciation 108,000, fully depreciating the remainder.

Depreciation method selection (償却方法の選択): Buildings and intangible fixed assets are required to use the straight-line method (定額法). For other depreciable assets the taxpayer may choose a method, but the statutory (default) method is declining-balance (定率法). Electing straight-line instead requires advance notification to the tax office.
In Japanese fixed-asset accounting, the allowable depreciation method (償却方法) depends on the asset category (固定資産の種類別の償却方法).
Buildings (建物) must be depreciated using the straight-line method (定額法).
Structures (構築物) may use either the straight-line method (定額法) or the declining-balance method (定率法).
Machinery and equipment (機械装置) may use either 定額法 or 定率法.
Vehicles (車両) may use either 定額法 or 定率法.
Tools, fixtures and fittings (工具器具備品) may use either 定額法 or 定率法.
Intangible fixed assets (無形固定資産) must be depreciated using the straight-line method (定額法).
When purchasing fixed assets, the key practical point is judging whether the purchased item qualifies as a fixed asset.
Pay attention specifically to amount-based criteria and to whether the expenditure is a repair cost rather than a capitalizable asset, and to the differences between those treatments.
Accounting treatment of an item as a fixed asset changes depending on whether its acquisition cost exceeds a certain (company- or tax-defined) amount threshold.
Understand first that fixed-asset classification and subsequent accounting (capitalization vs. expense) are driven by that amount criterion.
In Japanese accounting for small and medium-sized enterprises (中小企業), classification of an acquired item as a fixed asset (固定資産) versus an immediate expense depends on the amount per item (1件あたりの金額).
For SMEs, items under 100,000 yen are treated as expenses (費用処理), typically as consumable supplies (消耗品費など).

For SMEs, items of 100,000 yen or more but less than 300,000 yen may also be treated as expenses (消耗品費など), subject to an annual aggregate limit of 3 million yen; if the yearly total exceeds 3 million yen, expense treatment is not allowed and the items must be capitalized as fixed assets.
For SMEs, items of 300,000 yen or more must be recorded as fixed assets (固定資産計上) and subjected to depreciation (減価償却処理).
For large enterprises (大企業), items of 200,000 yen or more are recorded as fixed assets and depreciated.
The SME special rule allowing immediate expensing of 100,000–300,000 yen items is capped at a 3 million yen annual total; exceeding that cap forces capitalization even for items in that price range.

Accounting treatment of assets in the 100,000–200,000–300,000 yen range differs between small/medium enterprises and large enterprises in Japan, so each item’s processing method should be confirmed one by one until the rules become familiar.
The judgment amount is per item (1件あたり), not per purchase order. If one order covers two or more fixed assets, the amount test is applied separately to each item.
When spending on an existing fixed asset is replacement or repair rather than a new purchase, the accounting treatment depends on whether the outlay is a capital expenditure or a repair expense.

Capital expenditure (資本的支出) is spending recorded on the balance sheet (B/S); it is treated as an addition to the asset. Revenue expenditure (収益的支出) is spending recorded on the income statement (P/L) as a repair/maintenance cost (修繕費).
This distinction is especially important in manufacturing and other industries that carry large amounts of fixed assets.

Decision flow for capitalizing vs. expensing repairs/improvements: (1) If the cost of repair, improvement, etc. is under 200,000 yen per item, treat as revenue expenditure (修繕費). (2) If the work is clearly performed on a cycle of roughly three years or less, treat as revenue expenditure. (3) If the spending is clearly for ordinary maintenance or restoration to original condition, treat as revenue expenditure. (4) If the spending increases the asset’s value or extends its useful life, treat as capital expenditure. (5) Form-based safe harbor: if the amount is under 600,000 yen per item or not more than 10% of the prior year-end acquisition cost, it may be treated as repair expense.
Depreciation of fixed assets does not start at purchase or delivery; it starts on the date the asset is placed in service for business use (事業の用に供する日), i.e., the day actual operation/稼働 begins.

建設仮勘定 (construction in progress / CIP) is used while an acquired asset is delivered and even paid for but not yet fully operational—during test runs, trial operation, commissioning, and operator training. No depreciation is taken while the asset remains in 建設仮勘定.

When full operation starts, transfer the balance from 建設仮勘定 to the proper fixed-asset account (本勘定振替, e.g., 機械装置) and begin depreciation. This transfer-and-start sequence is essential practice for manufacturers that own substantial plant and equipment.
Example: 3 million yen manufacturing equipment delivered 4/10, then 3 months of trial run and adjustment; mass production starts 7/20. Fiscal year-end 12/31, 5-year useful life, straight-line method.
Journal at delivery (4/10): Dr. 建設仮勘定 3,000,000 / Cr. 未払金 3,000,000.
Journal at placed-in-service (7/20): Dr. 機械装置 3,000,000 / Cr. 建設仮勘定 3,000,000.
Year-end depreciation (12/31): Dr. 減価償却費 300,000 / Cr. 機械装置 300,000. Calculation: 3,000,000 ÷ 5 years × 6/12 (July–December).
When depreciation begins mid-year, first compute the full-year amount, then prorate by months actually in service (月割計算).
消費税 (consumption tax) is a tax on consumption behavior: it is levied on goods and services when consumers use or utilize them.
A distinctive feature of consumption tax is that the tax bearer and the taxpayer differ: the bearer (負担者) is the consumer, while the taxpayer (納税者) is the company or sole proprietor.

Consumers pay consumption tax in daily purchases (e.g., at stores), but the actual collection/payment method is that each company along the chain from raw materials to final goods or services remits tax on the additional value (付加価値) it has added—i.e., its profit portion.
Because of this incremental, value-added collection mechanism, consumption tax is also called 付加価値税 (VAT = Value Added Tax).
Japanese consumption tax (消費税) is explained via its principle calculation method (原則的な計算方法), which is a value-added tax collected along the supply chain rather than only at the final sale.
The conceptual image of consumption tax (消費税のイメージ) traces tax through production and distribution stages: processing factory (加工工場), sales store (販売店), and the end consumer (消費者).
Worked price example at 10% rate: a sale of 1,200 yen generates 120 yen of consumption tax; a later retail sale of 1,800 yen generates 180 yen of consumption tax.
The diagram illustrates that the tax burden is passed downstream and is ultimately borne by the consumer, while each business accounts for tax on the value it adds.
The surrounding book frames this as part of comprehensive back-office knowledge covering accounting (経理), HR (人事), legal (法務), general affairs (総務), management planning (経営企画), and DX.
Japanese consumption tax (消費税) payable is calculated in principle as: 消費税納税額 = ① − ②, where ① is output tax collected on sales (仮受消費税) and ② is input tax paid on purchases and expenses (仮払消費税).
仮受消費税 (karuke shōhizei) is the consumption tax received from customers on taxable sales (売上).
仮払消費税 (karibarai shōhizei) is the consumption tax prepaid to suppliers on taxable purchases and expenses (仕入/経費).
Consumption tax is a pass-through tax: the net amount remitted to the tax authority equals the tax on the company's own value-added (profit), not on the full sales amount.

Illustrative example of the sales–expense–profit relationship with 10% consumption tax: customer pays 1,100,000 yen (1,000,000 yen tax-excluded sales + 100,000 yen tax); the company pays the supplier 770,000 yen (700,000 yen tax-excluded purchases/expenses + 70,000 yen tax); the company therefore retains 330,000 yen, of which 300,000 yen is pretax profit and 30,000 yen is the net consumption tax payable (100,000 − 70,000).

The same arithmetic appears in three columns: tax-excluded amounts (本体), consumption-tax amounts, and tax-inclusive totals (税込), showing that the tax column nets to the tax on profit while cash flow nets to pretax profit plus net tax payable.

Consumption tax (消費税) payable by a business is the difference between consumption tax included in sales and prepaid consumption tax (仮払消費税) included in purchases and expenses. Example: sales of 1.1 million yen include 100,000 yen of consumption tax; purchases/expenses of 770,000 yen include 70,000 yen of prepaid consumption tax; the 30,000 yen difference is the amount of consumption tax to be paid.

As a rule, companies and sole proprietors are taxable businesses (課税事業者) that must calculate and pay consumption tax. An exception is the tax-exempt business (免税事業者), which is not required to pay consumption tax.

The condition for becoming a tax-exempt business is that sales in the fiscal period two years prior are 10 million yen or less. Consumption-tax status is judged on the basis of that earlier period’s results. When the threshold is met, both the consumption tax collected on sales and the prepaid consumption tax on purchases remain with the business and need not be remitted to the tax office.
A company in its first two years of existence has no sales two periods earlier, so it automatically qualifies as a tax-exempt business.
Even when the exemption criteria are satisfied, a business may voluntarily register as a taxable business by filing a notification with the tax office.
An alternative calculation method is the simplified taxation system (簡易課税制度). Its eligibility requirement is that sales two fiscal periods prior are 50 million yen or less.

Under simplified taxation the tax payable equals consumption tax collected on sales multiplied by (1 − deemed purchase ratio). Actual consumption tax on purchases need not be calculated or deducted; an industry-specific deemed purchase ratio (みなし仕入率) is applied instead, which reduces the practical administrative burden.

In Japan's consumption tax (消費税) system, businesses may elect the simplified taxation method (簡易課税) which applies a deemed purchase rate (みなし仕入率) by business classification (事業区分) instead of calculating actual input tax.
Type 1 business (第1種事業, wholesale / 卸売業) has a deemed purchase rate of 90%.
Type 2 business (第2種事業) covers retail (小売業) and agriculture/forestry/fishery limited to transfers of food and beverages (飲食料品の譲渡に係る事業).

Type 3 business (第3種事業) covers agriculture/forestry/fishery excluding food transfers, mining (鉱業), construction (建設業), manufacturing (製造業), electricity (電気業), gas (ガス業), heat supply (熱供給業), and water supply (水道業).
Type 4 business (第4種事業) is residual: businesses other than Types 1, 2, 3, 5, and 6.
Type 5 business (第5種事業) covers transportation and communications (運輸通信業), finance and insurance (金融業および保険業), and services excluding restaurants (サービス業で飲食店業に該当するものを除く).
Type 6 business (第6種事業, real estate / 不動産業) has a deemed purchase rate of 40%.
Choice between simplified taxation (簡易課税) and principle/actual taxation (原則課税) is free; taxpayers should run simulations of both methods because the resulting tax payable can differ substantially.

Election of simplified taxation requires filing the Notification of Election of the Simplified Consumption Tax System (消費税簡易課税制度選択届出書) with the tax office before the start of the relevant business year; simulations must therefore be completed in advance.
Consumption tax (消費税) has two accounting treatments in Japan: 税込経理方式 (tax-inclusive accounting method) and 税抜経理方式 (tax-exclusive accounting method).
The methods differ in whether each account (勘定科目) such as sales is shown tax-inclusive or tax-exclusive, and in how the consumption tax payable is processed.
税込経理方式: each account is recorded at the tax-included amount; the consumption tax payable is recorded as 租税公課 (taxes and public dues/charges).
税抜経理方式: each account is recorded at the tax-excluded amount; the consumption tax payable is not recorded on the income statement (損益計算書).
租税公課 is the expense account used to record tax-related costs.

Illustrative comparison (same economic result, different presentation): tax-inclusive may show sales 1,100,000 yen, related cost 770,000 yen, 租税公課 30,000 yen, profit 300,000 yen; tax-exclusive may show sales 1,000,000 yen, related cost 700,000 yen, no tax line on the P&L, profit 300,000 yen.

In Japanese consumption tax (消費税) accounting, the key point is that final profit does not change regardless of method, because consumption tax is a tax consumers should bear and intermediate companies do not bear; thus corporate profit calculations produce profit figures unaffected by consumption tax amounts.
For consumption-tax taxable businesses (課税事業者), the overwhelming majority of companies use tax-excluded accounting (税抜経理), so that processing method should be learned.

Tax-exempt businesses (免税事業者) with sales of 10 million yen or less, and simplified-taxation businesses (簡易課税事業者) with sales of 50 million yen or less, may use tax-included accounting (税込経理方式); in those cases recorded amounts of sales and expenses change, so caution is required.

Each transaction is classified for consumption tax as one of: 課税取引 (taxable transactions), 非課税取引 (non-taxable transactions), 免税取引 (tax-exempt transactions), or 不課税取引 (out-of-scope / non-applicable transactions).
課税取引 (taxable transactions): transactions taxed in the ordinary way; example: almost all domestic transactions.
非課税取引 (non-taxable transactions): transactions individually designated non-taxable due to special circumstances; examples: land sales (土地の売買), interest, and rent on residential housing (居住用住宅の賃料).
免税取引 (tax-exempt transactions): transactions because they are consumed overseas; example: overseas export sales (海外輸出売上).

不課税取引 (out-of-scope transactions): transactions that do not meet consumption-tax requirements (not conducted as a business, not consideration/対価 transactions, etc.); examples: gifts (贈与) and transactions conducted overseas.
When making journal entries (仕訳), every transaction must be classified according to consumption tax (消費税) categories; this classification is required for all transactions and journal entries.
Judging whether each specific transaction is subject to consumption tax is often difficult and is a well-known pain point in accounting practice (経理泣かせの実務).
When unsure about consumption-tax treatment, consult a tax advisor (顧問税理士) or refer to information published by accounting firms on their websites and blogs.
As of June 2024, Japan’s standard consumption tax rate is 10%.
A reduced rate of 8% applies to food and beverages (excluding newspapers, alcoholic beverages, and eating out/外食) in order to lighten the burden on consumers.

In practice, when processing receipts from supermarkets, convenience stores, and department stores that sell food, check items marked with the 8% reduced tax rate and enter that rate in the corresponding journal entries.

The Japanese Invoice System (インボイス制度 / Qualified Invoice System) began in October 2023. It requires issuance of invoices meeting specified recording requirements (called インボイス) so that the receiving trading partner can claim consumption-tax input tax credit (仕入税額控除).

Before the Invoice System, accounting staff mainly judged whether a transaction was taxable from invoices or receipts; detailed recording requirements were not required. After introduction, they must also verify whether each invoice satisfies Invoice System requirements.

Payments that fail Invoice System requirements cannot receive input tax credit, producing extra consumption-tax payment and therefore a dual burden of higher tax and extra administrative work. The change is treated as a major reform; companies have been occupied with compliance since implementation.

It is important to quantify the financial loss the system may cause. In the illustrative calculation, a firm previously deducted 70,000 yen of input tax and paid a net 30,000 yen of consumption tax. After the Invoice System, any portion of that 70,000 yen arising from non-compliant invoices is disallowed, increasing the tax payable and reducing profit.

Japan's Invoice System (インボイス制度) changes consumption-tax (消費税) treatment of sales, purchases/expenses, and profit; after introduction, input tax deduction (仕入税額控除) is allowed only when a Qualified Invoice (適格請求書, インボイス) is obtained.
Key rule: インボイス制度導入後は適格請求書 (インボイス) でないと、仕入税額控除ができない (after the Invoice System starts, input-tax credit cannot be claimed without a qualified invoice).

Illustrative flow: sales (売上高) of 1,000,000 yen plus 100,000 yen consumption tax versus purchases/expenses, with the input-tax credit affecting net profit; the tax relationship among 売上・経費・利益 therefore depends on whether the supplier issues a qualified invoice.
The surrounding book covers the full back-office stack (経理・人事・法務・総務・経営企画・DX) so the invoice-tax interaction is presented as a core accounting/compliance topic.

Japan's invoice (インボイス) system creates a structural problem: purchases from tax-exempt businesses (免税事業者) that cannot issue qualified invoices effectively become a price increase for the buyer, generating pressure to discontinue those transactions.

Companies that were previously tax-exempt—because taxable sales two periods earlier were 10 million yen or less, or because they were within two years of establishment and thus did not have to pay consumption tax—face client pressure to stop dealing with them unless they newly register as taxable businesses (課税事業者) able to issue invoices.
This forced conversion of former tax-exempt operators into invoice-issuing taxable businesses is identified as one of the major social issues surrounding introduction of the invoice system.
Because the invoice system imposes both consumption-tax burden and administrative burden on all companies and sole proprietors, time-limited relief measures were introduced.

Two important, easily confused relief measures both involve the figure “20%” but differ completely in target and content: (1) transitional measures for input tax credit (仕入税額控除の経過措置) and (2) the 20% special exception for former tax-exempt businesses (過去の免税事業者に対する2割特例).
Japan's Invoice System (インボイス制度) imposes compliance burdens, especially around input tax credits (仕入税額控除) when dealing with tax-exempt businesses (免税事業者).
Transitional measures (経過措置) allow a certain percentage of input tax credit on purchases/expenses from tax-exempt businesses for 6 years after the Invoice System's introduction.
Period 1 (Oct 2023–Sep 2026, 3 years): 80% deduction applies, equivalent to a 20% (2割) burden on the taxpayer.
Period 2 (Oct 2026–Sep 2029, 3 years): 50% deduction applies, equivalent to a 50% (5割) burden.
The 2割特例 (20% special exception) applies to businesses that were previously tax-exempt and became taxable as qualified invoice-issuing businesses (適格請求書発行事業者).
Under the 2割特例, consumption tax payable can be reduced to 20% of (taxable sales × consumption tax rate) for what would have been the tax-exempt period.
Taxpayers may choose the more advantageous amount between [taxable sales × consumption tax rate × 20%] and the amount calculated under the standard/principle taxation method.
These measures, including the 2割特例, function as special exceptions (特例) to reduce the practical operational burden of Invoice System compliance.

Two practical special provisions of Japan's qualified invoice (インボイス) system reduce invoice-procedure burden, not only tax amounts: (1) the small-amount exception for taxable purchases under 10,000 yen and (2) exemption from the duty to issue return invoices (返還インボイス).

Small-amount exception (1万円未満の課税仕入れについての少額特例): For taxable purchases under 10,000 yen, input tax credit (仕入税額控除) is allowed without retaining a qualified invoice (適格請求書) and without checking description requirements. Eligible businesses are taxable businesses whose taxable sales in the base period (基準期間) are 100 million yen or less. The application period is October 2023 through September 2029.

Return-invoice issuance exemption (返還インボイスの交付義務免除): When a discount or return is made on sales under 10,000 yen, the obligation to issue a return invoice is waived. This applies to all taxable businesses and has no specially defined application period.

Japanese consumption tax (消費税) practice is especially hard for accounting staff because classifications are numerous, confirmation is time-consuming and cumbersome, and mistakes therefore become frequent.
After the Invoice System (インボイス制度) began, consumption-tax treatment must be judged along four independent axes, producing a very large number of possible combinations.
Axis 1 – taxable-transaction determination: 課税取引 (taxable), 非課税取引 (non-taxable), 免税取引 (tax-exempt), 不課税取引 (out-of-scope / non-taxable).
Axis 2 – tax-rate determination: standard rate 10 % (通常税率), reduced rate 8 % (軽減税率), and the old 8 % rate that still applies to certain lease contracts concluded before October 2019.
Axis 3 – invoice-qualification determination: 適格請求書 (qualified invoice) versus 非適格請求書 (non-qualified invoice).

Axis 4 – input-tax-credit method determination: 課税売上対応の仕入 (purchases corresponding to taxable sales), 非課税売上対応の仕入 (purchases corresponding to non-taxable sales), and 共通対応の仕入 (common / mixed-use purchases).
Each of the four judgments is itself difficult; without quite deep knowledge of consumption-tax rules an accounting person can easily make an error.
The combination of four axes plus the inherent complexity of each axis is why consumption-tax classification remains one of the most error-prone areas of back-office work.
The Japanese Invoice System (インボイス制度) is widely regarded as a notorious system that imposes a large practical burden (実務負担) on accounting and tax operations.

Future developments in consumption-tax (消費税) practice after introduction of the Invoice System are a major focus of attention for tax specialists, accounting and finance staff, and anyone who performs accounting work.
Practitioners hope that subsequent legal amendments will not make the already complex consumption-tax rules even more complicated and mysterious (複雑怪奇).

The surrounding book treats back-office operations comprehensively, covering accounting (経理), human resources (人事), legal affairs (法務), general affairs (総務), management planning (経営企画) and digital transformation (DX).
月次決算 (monthly closing) means closing the books on a fixed schedule every month in order to grasp the performance of that period.

The main purpose of 月次決算 is to quickly grasp performance and financial condition on a monthly basis amid daily-changing management conditions, and to use that information for management decision-making.
A secondary purpose is to report the most recent management situation to external stakeholders when disclosure is required (for example when seeking financing).
Reported contents of 月次決算 include: performance results and analysis centered on the income statement (損益計算書), covering the whole company plus by business and by department.
Also reported: cash-flow / funding situation, via preparation and reporting of a 資金繰り表 (cash-flow / funding table).
Also reported: a forecast of how performance will land over the next several months.

Among small and medium-sized enterprises (中小企業), relatively few actually perform monthly closing. The legal obligation is only annual closing, so conducting 月次決算 implies a higher accounting-and-finance capability than annual closing alone.
A practical next step in implementing 月次決算 is to identify the necessary tasks and to build a schedule for them.
To properly execute monthly closing (月次決算), identify and design each required accounting task and build a schedule so the entire process finishes within the deadline.
When multiple people on the accounting/finance team share the work, also decide role assignments in advance.

Example monthly closing schedule (月次決算のスケジュールの例) assigns tasks across early business days (e.g., 2nd and 3rd business days), including invoice issuance (請求書発行), invoice receipt (請求書受領), expense reimbursement (立替経費精算), depreciation calculation (減価償却計算), payroll calculation (給与計算), balance check (残高チェック), and financial analysis (財務分析).
There is no single fixed method for financial analysis (財務分析); companies conduct it from various perspectives suited to their own situation.
Main perspectives for financial analysis include comparative analysis (対比分析): year-over-year same-month comparison (前年同月対比), month-over-month comparison (前月対比), and budget comparison (予算対比).
Ratio analysis (比率分析) commonly examines gross profit margin (粗利率), operating profit margin (営業利益率), and ordinary profit margin (経常利益率).

Financial analysis also includes comparison against target performance indicators (KPI), such as equipment utilization rate analysis (設備稼働率分析), productivity analysis per person (1人あたり生産性分析), selling-price analysis (売価), and quantity analysis (数量分析).
年度決算では、月次決算に加えてさらに詳細な実務が発生する。
年度決算で意識すべき処理は「決算整理仕訳」と「決算書と税務申告書の作成」に大別される。
決算整理仕訳に関する具体的実務には、預金口座の残高確認が含まれる。
決算整理仕訳に関する具体的実務には、実地棚卸と棚卸資産の計上が含まれる。
決算整理仕訳に関する具体的実務には、減価償却費の計上が含まれる。
決算整理仕訳に関する具体的実務には、未払債務の計上が含まれる。
決算整理仕訳に関する具体的実務には、借入金の残高チェックが含まれる。
決算整理仕訳に関する具体的実務には、引当金の計上が含まれる。
決算整理仕訳に関する具体的実務には、経過勘定処理が含まれる。
決算整理仕訳に関する具体的実務には、消費税のチェックが含まれる。
決算書と税務申告書の作成には、決算書の作成が含まれる。
決算書と税務申告書の作成には、法人税申告書の作成が含まれる。
Japanese year-end closing (年度決算) must in principle be completed within 2 months of the settlement date (決算日); if an extension application has been filed with the tax office, the deadline is 3 months.
Within that period, tax returns must be filed with the tax office, prefecture, and municipalities, and taxes must be paid.
Tax return filing requires prior approval of the financial statements (決算書) at a shareholders' meeting (株主総会), so the meeting itself must also be held within 2 months of the settlement date.
Non-public stock companies that have a board of directors must send the shareholders' meeting convocation notice at least 1 week in advance, among other preparatory rules.

Shareholders' meeting practical work belongs to legal/general affairs (法務・総務); accounting/finance (経理財務) must therefore agree in advance on schedule and role division. Small and medium enterprises may use simplified methods such as written resolutions (書面決議).
The larger the company, the more year-end practical work arises, so related teams should visualize tasks and turn them into a schedule (the same approach as for monthly closing).

Legal schedule example for a March year-end company: 3/31 settlement date; 4/19 submit calculation documents and annexed detailed statements to the auditor(s); 5/16 place calculation documents for inspection (generally 2 weeks before the ordinary shareholders' meeting, or 1 week if there is no board of directors); 5/20 auditor(s) submit audit report to directors; board of directors then approves; 5/22 send ordinary shareholders' meeting convocation notice (1 week before the meeting); 5/30 ordinary shareholders' meeting (commonly held within 2 months because corporate tax filing is due within 2 months); 5/31 corporate tax etc. filing (within 2 months from the day after the settlement date); financial-statement public notice (決算公告) without delay after the shareholders' meeting ends.

Companies that hold cash registers, safes, or manage petty cash must physically count cash as of the fiscal year-end (決算日末).
For store/retail businesses that already perform daily cash-on-hand checks, year-end counting can be done as an extension of those same procedures.
Key controls for cash physical count (現金実査):
- Prepare a written cash inspection/count sheet (現金実査表).
- Identify and record differences versus the books or cash journal (帳簿・現金出納表).
- Accounting staff should participate rather than leaving the count entirely to on-site personnel.
- Simultaneously review how safes and registers are managed.
A denomination-based cash inspection sheet (金種別現金実査表) typically records: company name; counts of each bill denomination (10,000 / 5,000 / 2,000 / 1,000 yen) and coin denomination (500 / 100 / 50 / 10 / 5 / 1 yen, plus rolls/packs); a counted total; the cash-journal balance; and any difference between counted cash and the books.
Physical inventory (実地棚卸) uses an inventory asset list (棚卸資産リスト) with columns such as item number (品目No), item name (品目名), storage location (保管場所), quantity (数量), unit (単位), and EOS.
Inventory unit prices can be calculated by several methods; the chosen method must be filed with the tax office (税務署に届出).
If no method is filed, the last-purchase-cost method (最終仕入原価法) becomes the default (standard) valuation method.
最終仕入原価法 is relatively simple to compute, so many small and medium-sized enterprises use it for inventory valuation.

Inventory valuation amounts have a large impact on reported performance for retailers, wholesalers, and manufacturers; therefore a method that better matches actual costs should be selected rather than defaulting to the simplest option.
棚卸資産の評価方法（inventory valuation methods）には、最終仕入原価法、先入先出法、総平均法、移動平均法、個別法、売価還元法などがある。
最終仕入原価法: 最後に取得した単価を用いて取得価額を評価する方法（last purchase cost / last-in cost method）。
先入先出法（FIFO）: 先に受け入れた棚卸資産から先に払い出されたと考えて取得価額を評価する方法。期末に残る資産の評価は、直近に仕入れた資産と同じ評価結果となる。
総平均法（periodic weighted-average method）: 年度内で取得した棚卸資産の総合計額を総数量で割った平均単価を用いて取得価額を評価する方法。
移動平均法（moving-average method）: 棚卸資産を取得するごとに、合計数量と合計金額から平均単価を求めて取得価額を評価する方法。
個別法（specific identification method）: 期末棚卸資産の全部について、その個々の取得価額で評価する方法。
売価還元法（retail inventory method）: 同じ種類の棚卸資産でグルーピングし、期末における販売価額に原価率を乗じて取得価額を計算し評価する方法。

At fiscal year-end, annual depreciation expense (減価償却費) must be calculated accurately using the method for fixed assets (as in section 2-15). Companies that already allocate monthly depreciation precisely in monthly closing may not need to recompute, but discrepancies between monthly and annual amounts are common, so the accurate annual total must always be computed and totals aligned.

Typical cases requiring year-end adjustment of depreciation against monthly amounts: (1) rounding/fractional-yen differences when allocating annual depreciation into monthly amounts; (2) monthly postings based only on beginning-of-period annual estimates that ignore assets acquired during the period; (3) monthly use of estimates rather than exact amounts from the fixed-asset ledger; (4) no monthly closing at all, with depreciation recorded only annually.

Year-end financial closing requires recording of unpaid debts (未払債務) on the accrual basis (発生主義). Even companies that record invoices received during monthly closing typically only capture those arriving by a cutoff date as accounts payable or accrued expenses; annual closing therefore needs a finer net, capturing more items.

Practical steps for complete year-end accrual of liabilities: request suppliers and field sites to submit invoices earlier so debts can be recorded promptly; for invoices discovered after year-end (payments arising in the following month) that relate to the closed period, record the liability retroactively as of the closing date.

For borrowings (借入金), if equal monthly repayments are in place, monthly entries typically consist of principal repayment plus interest. At annual closing, reconfirm that those monthly treatments are correct and that loan balances agree.
Loan (borrowing) balance checks should primarily use each bank's repayment schedule (返済計画表) as a reference to build an in-house loan details table (借入明細表).

Companies with multiple financing contracts typically have several loan contracts and their associated repayments running in parallel (same bank or different banks), so per-contract balances and the total balance often fail to match.
To prevent mismatches, list every financing contract the company has and maintain a summary table that shows monthly repayment amounts and outstanding loan balances.
Create this loan-details material and, at year-end closing, always reconcile and confirm it against the book (ledger) balances.

A typical loan details table includes: bank name, borrowing date, borrowing number, total loan amount, repayment due date, interest rate, then monthly columns for principal repayment, interest, and remaining balance, plus totals for principal, interest, total repayment, and overall outstanding balance.

Example (Bank A): start balance 1,000,000; monthly principal 20,000; interest declining from 100; rate 1.50%. Example (Bank B): start balance 500,000; monthly principal 12,000; interest declining from 62; rate 1.70%. Combined monthly principal 32,000 plus declining interest yields total remaining balance declining from 1,500,000.
An allowance/provision (引当金) is an accounting treatment that records future expenses or losses in advance when four specific requirements are met.

Four recognition criteria for 引当金 (provisions/allowances) in Japanese accounting: (1) it is a specific future expense or loss; (2) its occurrence is attributable to events of the current period or earlier; (3) the probability of occurrence is high; (4) the amount can be reasonably estimated.

Difference between 引当金 and 未払費用/未払金: 未払費用 (accrued expenses) and 未払金 (accounts payable) are actual debts that have already occurred, whereas 引当金 is not a present legal debt but an amount expected to arise in the future. Account classification must not be confused.

貸倒引当金 (allowance for doubtful accounts): recorded against the risk that receivables such as 売掛金 (accounts receivable) and 受取手形 (notes receivable) will become uncollectible due to a customer's bankruptcy or dissolution/liquidation.
賞与引当金 (bonus provision): recorded at the balance-sheet date for bonuses that will have to be paid in the future in accordance with the company's bonus payment criteria.
退職給付引当金 (retirement benefit provision): when the company participates in a defined-benefit retirement plan, future expected retirement-benefit payments are reasonably estimated and recorded.
修繕引当金 (repair provision): recorded for future repair costs when factory buildings or machinery already require repair at the present time.
製品保証引当金 (product warranty provision): recorded for expected warranty costs (returns, exchanges, repairs) arising from defects in goods already sold.

経過勘定 (keika kanjo / accrual adjusting accounts) are account titles used to adjust the timing of recognizing expenses and revenues on an accrual basis (発生主義) when goods/services are received or provided continuously and periodically under a contract.
The four 経過勘定科目 are: 未払費用 (accrued expenses / unpaid expenses), 前払費用 (prepaid expenses), 未収収益 (accrued revenue / uncollected revenue), and 前受収益 (deferred/unearned revenue / advance received revenue).
