未払費用 is a current liability (流動負債): under a contract for continuous receipt of services, the portion of services already received for which payment has not yet been completed. Examples: unpaid social insurance premiums (社会保険料の未払), unpaid salaries (給与の未払).

前払費用 is a current asset (流動資産): under a contract for continuous receipt of services, consideration paid for services not yet received. Examples: prepaid rent (賃料の前払), prepaid interest (利息の前払), prepaid insurance (保険の前払).

未収収益 is a current asset (流動資産): under a contract for continuous provision of services, services already provided for which payment has not yet been received. Example: uncollected license fees (ライセンス料の未収).

前受収益 is a current liability (流動負債): under a contract for continuous provision of services, consideration received for services not yet provided. Examples: rent received in advance (家賃の前受), advance receipts for maintenance services (保守メンテナンスサービスの前受).

These accounts exist specifically because of the matching principle under accrual accounting: they shift recognition of costs and income to the periods in which the related services are actually consumed or delivered, rather than when cash is paid or received.
経過勘定（accrual/deferral accounts）は似た名称が並び混同しやすい。覚えるコツは①役務・サービスの提供を受ける側か提供する側か、②前払いしているか後払いしているか、という2×2の組み合わせで4つのうちどの勘定科目を用いるかが決まる、と覚えること。
年度決算では、期中に行った一つひとつの仕訳処理での消費税判定が合っているかどうかを、改めて年度全体を通してチェックする。
消費税チェックは会計ソフトの帳簿データから「消費税集計表」を出力させることで、勘定科目別や税区分別に消費税集計結果が確認できるため、これを使ってチェックをかける。
消費税チェックの手順例：会計ソフトから消費税集計表を出力 → 勘定科目別・税区分別に消費税金額の全体をチェック → 気になる・間違えている可能性のある勘定科目や税区分を見つけたら、総勘定元帳や仕訳帳の1件別でのデータを確認して、間違いがあれば修正する → 勘定科目別・税区分別に消費税金額の全体を再チェック（繰り返し）。

For small and medium-sized enterprises (中小企業), financial statements (決算書) are composed of the Balance Sheet (貸借対照表), Profit and Loss Statement / Income Statement (損益計算書), Statement of Changes in Equity (株主資本等変動計算書), and Individual Notes (個別注記表).
Under the Companies Act (会社法), companies must also prepare a Business Report (事業報告書) and Supplementary Schedules (附属明細書) in addition to the financial statements.

In accounting and finance practice (経理財務の実務), the Balance Sheet and Profit and Loss Statement are the most important documents among the financial statements, so their preparation methods and composition must be thoroughly understood.
The Balance Sheet (貸借対照表) shows the company's property/financial position (企業の財産状態を示すもの). It is also called Balance Sheet or abbreviated as B/S.
The Balance Sheet consists of three main parts: Assets (資産), Liabilities (負債), and Net Assets (純資産).

A finer classification of the Balance Sheet divides it into five categories: Current Assets (流動資産), Fixed Assets (固定資産), Current Liabilities (流動負債), Fixed Liabilities (固定負債), and Net Assets (純資産). Adding Deferred Assets (繰延資産) would make six categories, though this is often not used in practice.

The balance sheet (貸借対照表, B/S) is called a stock-type financial statement (ストック型の財務諸表). At fiscal year-end it shows the company's assets (財産), i.e. stock information, from which financial safety (財産上の安全性) and asset efficiency (資産効率性) can be understood.
Typical current-asset items on a Japanese B/S include cash and deposits (現金/預金), inventory (棚卸資産), prepaid amounts (前払金), and prepaid expenses (前払費用).
Typical current-liability items include accounts payable (買掛金), accrued expenses (未払費用), unpaid corporate tax (未払法人税等), and short-term borrowings (短期借入金).
Typical non-current (fixed) liability items include long-term borrowings (長期借入金) and bonds (社債).
Typical non-current asset items include land (土地), tools/fixtures/equipment (工具器具備品), software (ソフトウェア), guarantee deposits (保証金), and investment securities (投資有価証券).
Equity (純資産) items typically shown include capital reserve (資本準備金), other capital surplus (その他資本剰余金), and retained earnings (利益剰余金).
The B/S is conventionally presented with assets on one side and liabilities plus equity on the other, split into current vs. non-current (fixed) categories.
損益計算書（P/L, Profit & Loss Statement）とは、企業の経営成績・業績結果を示す財務諸表である。
P/Lは本業の収入から費用を控除して本業利益を求め、営業外損益を加味し、さらに臨時的な特別利益・特別損失を反映したうえで税金を控除し、最終的な当期純利益を算出する段階的な構造を持つ。
利益は売上総利益（本業収入−本業費用）→営業利益→経常利益→税引前当期純利益→当期純利益という階層で示される。
The income statement (損益計算書) is called a flow-type financial indicator (フロー型の財務指標).
It captures activities throughout the year, i.e. flow information (フロー情報), rather than a point-in-time snapshot.
From the income statement one can understand a company's profitability (収益性) and growth potential (成長性).

Cash flow and profit/loss (損益) are fundamentally different: profit/loss consists of figures created according to established accounting rules, whereas cash flow is the actual increase or decrease in cash and bank balances and thus represents pure fact.
Key accounting principles that govern profit/loss figures include the accrual basis (発生主義), the realization principle (実現主義), and the matching principle of expenses and revenues (費用収益対応の原則).

Equipment-investment example: a cash purchase of 100 million yen of equipment immediately reduces cash/deposit balances, yet depreciation (減価償却) spreads the expense over several years. First-year cash flow is therefore largely negative while reported profit may remain only mildly negative or even positive if operations are healthy.
This mismatch is one cause of 'black-ink bankruptcy' (黒字倒産): accounting profit can be positive while cash flow is severely insufficient, so the company can no longer operate.

Cash-flow management (資金繰り) is the company's lifeline. Even when accounting profit exists, insufficient circulating cash leads toward bankruptcy; conversely, a company that is unprofitable on an accounting basis can continue if cash continues to circulate.

Profit management and cash-flow management look similar but serve completely different purposes and use different measurement scales; both perspectives must be applied according to the situation in order to grasp the company's true condition.
利益管理 (profit management) and 資金繰り管理 (cash-flow / funding management) have different purposes and should not be treated as the same control.

利益管理 is management for seeing a company’s normal earning power (会社の正常な収益力). If 営業利益 (operating profit) or 税引利益 (profit after tax) is positive, it indicates the company is in a state of continuous development and operation.

資金繰り管理 is management for checking cash shortages (資金ショート). Reviewing monthly or daily cash movements and their breakdowns is used to judge whether countermeasures such as additional financing (追加融資) or investment restraint (投資抑制) are needed.
A concrete method of 資金繰り管理 is to build a 資金繰り管理表 (cash-flow management table) and, for each 収支項目 (income/expenditure item), track 実績 (actuals), 直近見込み (near-term forecast), and future management.

A 資金繰り管理表 (cash flow / funds management table) is a practical back-office tool that tracks monthly beginning cash, operating inflows and outflows, investing activities, financing activities, net cash flow, and ending cash (which becomes the next month’s opening balance).

Typical operating inflows include 現金売上 (cash sales), collection of receivables (売掛金回収), and その他営業外収入 (other non-operating income). Operating outflows commonly include 仕入 (purchases), personnel costs, 法定福利費 (statutory welfare / social insurance), 地代家賃 (rent), utilities, 消耗品費 (consumables), 租税公課 (taxes and public charges), and other expenses.
The table separates operating cash subtotal from investing cash flows (固定資産売却収入, 有価証券売却収入, capital expenditure / loans given) and financing cash flows (短期借入金・長期借入金 借入, repayments, 配当支払).
Columns mix 実績 (actual) and 予想 (forecast) by month so that actual results feed the next forecast; a yearly total column is also shown.

Ending cash = beginning cash + period cash inflows − period cash outflows. Large one-off items (e.g., a 35,000 financing or investing movement) must be placed in the correct investing or financing section so the cash position remains accurate.

Example structure for 2023 (Jan–Dec): opening cash around 20,050 in January, monthly operating net that can turn negative (e.g., −340 in one month), investing/financing spikes, and a closing cash of 50,257 by year-end in the illustrated case.
When creating a cash flow management table (資金繰り管理表), do not cling to a predetermined format; management items must be changed to match the company's business model and income/expenditure situation.

Filling only a standard format does not guarantee that cash flow management will work without problems. Because cash flow management is the company's lifeline, it must be customized so that the daily, living-like movement of funds can be firmly grasped.

Customization example for store businesses with many payment methods and deposit cycles: set detailed operating-income deposit items by cashless payment type and by differing deposit cycles, so that deposit volume and trends by settlement method become visible.

Customization example when factory and sales-office department segments are separated: within operating income/expenditure items, set factory and sales office as medium classifications so that each side's cash flow can be grasped.

Customization example when near-term cash flow is unstable and payment adjustments to counterparties or loan-repayment rescheduling may be needed: prepare cash-flow tables on a daily or 5-day basis rather than monthly; further subdivide income and expenditure items by counterparty and use them as material for considering payment adjustments and rescheduling.

Companies raise funds mainly through two methods: receiving equity investment (stock) or receiving loans (debt financing). Accounting and finance departments are actively involved in loan financing, not equity.

Bank lending is often described with the phrase 'lending an umbrella on a sunny day and taking it away on a rainy day' (晴れの日に傘を貸して雨の日に取り上げる). The expression, popularized by the drama Hanzawa Naoki, is extreme but partly true.

Banks' business model is to lend to companies so those companies can invest, grow, and then borrow more, thereby expanding the bank's interest income in a cycle. Banks therefore typically will not lend to firms that already show visible deterioration in profitability and look close to collapse; that judgment is commercially natural.

Waiting until performance has already worsened before approaching banks is too late. Failure to monitor cash flow and funding until results deteriorate is a management judgment error, not solely the bank's fault.

While performance is still strong and growth investment is possible, management should negotiate loans and balance growth against investment. Approaching financial institutions only after conditions worsen exposes a lack of managerial capability.
A core practice of stable management is to always hold a management vision, read the company's situation two or three steps ahead, and proactively negotiate financing with financial institutions.
融資 (financing/loans) from financial institutions proceeds through multiple processes including negotiations, document preparation, and interviews, after which approval or rejection is decided.

Four main steps of the financing process: (1) Decide the target financial institution and financing program; (2) Prepare submission materials; (3) Conduct the financing interview (融資面談); (4) Receive the decision notice and execute the contract.
The area that should receive the greatest effort is preparation of the submission materials (提出資料の準備).
For accounting/finance staff, preparing submission materials is the most time-consuming task in a financing application.

Two especially important and time-consuming tasks: (1) properly closing recent financial-statement and bookkeeping information so it can be submitted; (2) converting future plans into a formal business-plan document (事業計画書).
Submission materials cannot be prepared overnight; accounting staff should consult and discuss with management and begin preparation with ample lead time before applying.

When applying for a loan (融資) from a financial institution, typical required documents include a loan application form (融資申請書). The form format is specified by each financial institution or loan facility.
Corporate registry information is submitted as proof of the company's basic legal information.
The representative's identification documents are required, such as My Number Card, driver's license, or passport.

Tax returns for the most recent 2–3 fiscal periods must be submitted, including corporate tax returns (法人税申告書), corporate inhabitant tax, corporate business tax returns, and account item breakdown statements (勘定科目内訳書).

Financial statements to submit include the balance sheet (B/S), profit and loss statement (P/L), selling, general and administrative expense details (販管費明細書), manufacturing cost details (製造原価明細書), statement of changes in equity (株主資本等変動計算書), and notes to individual financial statements (個別注記表).
If more than six months have passed since the latest fiscal closing, additional documents are recommended; monthly trend data should be attached if possible.
When applying for equipment/capital funds (設備資金), extra supporting documents are typically required.
Industries that cannot operate without permits or notifications (e.g., restaurants, beauty salons, construction, clinics) must submit those licenses or filings.
A business plan summarizing future strategy and income/expenditure projections should be prepared (detailed creation method referenced in section 6-4).
During financing, a financing interview (融資面談) is always conducted unless the financial institution has given prior approval (お墨付き).

The company manager's participation in the financing interview is mandatory. Financial/accounting or management-planning staff may also attend. For SMEs without an in-house management function, a tax accountant or certified public accountant may attend.
The financing interview is a critical judgment process used to confirm qualitative information that cannot be obtained from submitted financial statements and background documents.

Even a company with a strong financial position can have its financing decision reversed solely on the basis of the manager's perceived reliability; therefore the interview must be approached with care.

Interview checklist — appearance and language: Speech manners and interview attitude are basic. Even in contemporary industries, business-casual dress is acceptable provided cleanliness and professionalism are maintained.

Interview checklist — business explanation: Interview time is limited. Being able to explain the company's business content and distinctive features concisely and clearly conveys the reliability of the manager's management and sales capabilities.

Interview checklist — personal conviction: The manager should be able to speak in his or her own words about passion for the business. Articulating a social mission (not merely profit-making) builds trust. This is especially important for start-up financing, where there is no past track record, so the manager's background and founding vision receive heavy weight.

When seeking bank financing, a manager's career history and past achievements (such as sales performance and project results) are highly valued and should be communicated in as much detail as possible.

To differentiate from competitors, first research, analyze, and understand competitors' characteristics, then clearly and powerfully articulate the company's own strengths and unique selling points; this perspective is essential for long-term business growth and survival.

Market size and target customers must be clearly defined; consider the sales potential of the targeted customer segment and explain the specific characteristics of the layer the company aims to capture within the overall market.

Being able to explain the business plan in one's own words demonstrates numerical management capability and thus the reliability of management ability; it is important to distinguish past sales results from future projections.
Sales growth plans should be neither overly aggressive nor overly conservative; the rationale must be clearly explained based on past experience and achievements.

The required borrowing amount must be explainable. Fund usage divides into working capital (運転資金: short-term costs such as personnel, advertising, and rent) and equipment/capital funds (設備資金: based on actual quotes for real estate, interior construction, and equipment purchases).
Proof of self-funding (自己資金) is required; if the representative has personal assets, these should be submitted as supporting documents.

Banks strongly dislike officer loans or short-term lending to the representative or relatives (役員貸付金); if such items exist, a rational explanation is needed because banks suspect the funds may be diverted from business investment.

The representative's personal credit information must be unproblematic; history of personal bankruptcy, heavy use of revolving payments or cash advances, or credit-card payment delinquencies can become obstacles to financing.
Building relationships with banks is treated as one of the 'offensive' (proactive/strategic) duties of accounting and finance, not only a defensive or administrative task.
Financial institutions, especially a company's main bank (メインバンク), historically played a major role in Japan's economic growth and remain central to corporate funding.
Unlike large firms that can raise capital from equity markets, SMEs (中小企業) have limited funding options, so banks can effectively determine a company's fate.
Accounting and finance staff should keep daily communication with financial institutions smooth in order to build a foundation (土壌・地盤) for receiving various kinds of support when needed.
SMEs that currently bank with only one institution should, where possible, deal with multiple banks and consciously design a support-team structure of 'one main bank + several sub-banks'.
Good multi-bank relationships enable coordinated/syndicated lending (協調融資), which can secure larger funding amounts than a single bank would provide.
Making the main bank an ally helps prevent or stop lending reluctance (貸渋り) and loan pullbacks (貸し剥がし) from sub-banks.
Multiple banking relationships create leverage to negotiate lower settlement and transaction fees.
Deeper bank ties increase introductions for business matching, M&A, and partnership opportunities that support business growth.
Practical ways to deepen a bank relationship include: taking financing, opening accounts and raising deposit balances, and increasing settlement/transaction volume.

Corporate-bank relationships should be designed strategically by combining multiple transaction types and spreading them across banks rather than concentrating everything with one institution; both the company and the banks evaluate relationship rank (main bank vs. 2nd/3rd-tier) by depth and intimacy of dealings.

Key quantitative factors that determine a bank’s ranking with a company include overall loan outstanding (融資残高), proprietary/direct loan outstanding (プロパー融資残高—bank’s own credit, not credit-guarantee-association-backed loans), deposit balances, and settlement/transaction volumes (売上・仕入・給与などの決済取引量).

Worked example: even if Bank A holds the largest share of total loans (e.g., 60 % vs. 30 % / 10 %), if Bank B holds the largest proprietary-loan share (e.g., 65 %), the largest deposit balances and the largest settlement volumes, Bank B is treated as the company’s main bank, Bank A as second-tier and Bank C as third-tier.

There is no formal, universally accepted definition of a “main bank” (メインバンク). In practice it is the bank that the company most relies upon and that simultaneously takes genuine credit risk for the company.
Ongoing relationship maintenance requires regular, proactive provision of financial-statement information (決算情報) and business information to the banks.
Once a banking relationship has begun through financing, continue providing information continuously and proactively so the bank understands the company's situation.

Send monthly trial balances (月次試算表) at monthly timing; at year-end settlement, present annual tax returns (税務申告書) and financial statements (決算書) while proposing meetings as needed to share business conditions.

Bank officers typically handle dozens to about 100 financing clients, so time allocated per company is limited; regular meetings also serve as an opportunity to demonstrate the company's presence to the bank.
Maintain an appropriate distance with banks—neither too close nor too distant (付かず離れず).

Due to bank HR systems, branch managers, loan section chiefs, and officers rotate every few years; intra-branch handovers are incomplete, and new managers' policies can change the support stance toward the company.

Rather than investing time in overly personal ('wet') relationships with excessive expectations, strategically manage objective results such as loan balances, deposit balances, and settlement transaction balances, accumulate those results, and build mid-to-long-term bank relationships.

人事労務 (HR and labor affairs) is work that deals with 'people' (人). People are an indispensable asset (財産) for a company's growth, and the HR/labor department is a critical function that determines the growth of the company's business and organization itself.
HR/labor work encompasses many activities, including recruitment, designing systems, and creating education programs. These should first be classified and understood at a high level.

Main categories of 人事労務 work include: value formation and HR policy (バリュー形成・人事ポリシー); organization design and role-allocation design (組織設計・役割分担設計); creating personnel evaluation systems (人事評価制度づくり); payroll calculation and attendance management (給与計算・勤怠管理); social insurance procedures (社会保険手続き); labor law, employment contracts, and work rules (労働法・雇用契約・就業規則); labor troubles and labor-management response (労務トラブル、労使対応); safety and health management (安全衛生管理); recruitment (採用); development and training (育成・研修); and engagement and motivation management (エンゲージメント・モチベーション管理).
人事労務 (HR and labor affairs) covers organization/systems, labor management, and the full talent lifecycle to strengthen and activate the organization.

組織・制度 (organization and systems) work shapes company culture, HR policy, org charts, and departmental missions; management leads design while HR supports turning business strategy, organizational vision, and intent into concrete form.

労務 (labor affairs) is the function that applies labor law: Labor Standards Act compliance, social-insurance and employment-insurance administration, and accurate payroll. It demands legal/hard-skill expertise in addition to people-oriented communication.
The talent process spans entry (採用/recruitment), middle (日常業務), and exit (退職); managing join–grow–leave metabolism is the core mission that keeps the organization renewed and effective.

In HR and labor affairs (人事労務), three points to raise the results and quality of the work are: understanding of Mission, Vision, and Value; liking the company; and balancing hard skills and soft skills.

The most important point in performing HR and labor work is that all personnel, labor, and organizational systems are determined by the company's Mission (果たすべき役割, the role to fulfill), Vision (ありたい姿, the desired state), and Value (価値基準, value standards).

HR work targets people, who are diverse. Officers and employees must be assembled as a selected group from among those diverse talents so they can unite as a company, organization, or team to achieve one large goal.
The company must define the talent image needed to achieve its goals. That image is sometimes called Culture (カルチャー), shown as Credo (クレド), or expressed as Core Value (コアバリュー) or HR Policy (人事ポリシー).
The required talent image and every HR/labor-related measure are decided on the basis of the larger Mission, Vision, and Values.
人事制度の体系は、人事ポリシーを中心に、賃金制度・評価制度・キャリア運用・採用戦略などで構成される。
人事労務施策は人事ポリシーとの関係性を踏まえて設計する必要がある。
人事労務で働く者は、会社が目指す目標を常に意識しながら業務に取り組む必要がある。
人事労務施策をつくる際に常に考えなければならないのは「取捨選択」である。
採用の例：新たなメンバーを採用しようとするとき、「仕事はスピーディだけれど」といった要素を踏まえて取捨選択する。
When choosing between a candidate who lacks accuracy and one who is accurate but slow, the right choice depends on the company; HR/labor must derive the company's answer from its vision and values.
If HR/labor does not understand the company's vision and values, they will keep hiring people who do not match what the company needs, making both the hired person and the company unhappy.

Welfare and benefits cannot be people-pleasing policies that try to satisfy every employee; budgets are limited and excessive leniency can lower organizational performance, so HR must select only the benefits that fit the talent the company needs and discard the rest.
HR/labor is expected to have the ability to make such selection-and-discarding (取捨選択) among diverse talent.
A person suited to HR/labor is 'the person who loves the company the most.'

HR/labor work targets people's emotions and motivation: sharing joy when employees are promoted, while also having to persistently communicate harsh realities such as restructuring and pay cuts, and sometimes being betrayed by trusted employees.
The essential quality for fulfilling the HR/labor mission is loving the company, prioritizing the organization over oneself, and being able to treat people both strictly and with affection.
Because HR handles highly confidential personal and personnel information, selfish or self-centered people cannot do the job well; the ideal is someone who loves the organization and is trustworthy.

HR and labor have different natures: HR focuses on activating and maximizing internal talent and therefore values human charm, management ability, and the power to involve others more than pure logic or knowledge.
Labor deals more with laws and knowledge and therefore requires correct knowledge and understanding of legal structures; tasks such as payroll calculation must not contain errors.
HR/labor affairs (人事労務) require both interpersonal/communication skills and highly accurate operational work; people who possess both skill sets are rare.

Because dual-skilled talent is scarce, organizations typically split HR/labor tasks among team members, or (in small companies with few HR staff) outsource portions of the work to external specialists in order to keep the function balanced.
Labor affairs (労務), human resources (人事), and organizational systems (組織制度) are tightly interdependent; each domain reinforces the others so that the organization as a whole becomes stronger.
A strong organization cannot be built if any one of those three domains is missing.
Therefore, solid internal collaboration (内部連携) must be maintained across domains that demand different skill sets.
In Japanese HR and labor administration (人事労務), work proceeds through daily interactions with various internal and external stakeholders.

The Labor Standards Inspection Office (労働基準監督署) handles filings such as work rules (就業規則) and Article 36 agreements (36協定書), and is the counterpart for labor-law matters under the Labor Standards Act, Industrial Safety and Health Act, and workers’ accident compensation insurance (労災保険). It supervises workplaces and issues correction recommendations (是正勧告) that must be addressed.

Hello Work / Public Employment Security Office (公共職業安定所, ハローワーク) handles employment-insurance matters: workplace coverage, employee qualification acquisition and loss, and issuance of separation notices (離職票). Departing employees use it to claim unemployment benefits; recruitment via Hello Work is free.

Pension offices of the Japan Pension Service (日本年金機構) handle Employees’ Pension Insurance qualification acquisition and loss. They also serve as the social-insurance window (including health insurance). Companies enrolled in Kyokai Kenpo typically file health-insurance and pension procedures together at the pension office, increasing document volume.

Health insurance is obtained either through a Health Insurance Association (健康保険組合) or Kyokai Kenpo (協会けんぽ); most small and medium-sized enterprises join Kyokai Kenpo. Prefectural bodies handle procedures under the Health Insurance Act.

Health insurance associations (健康保険組合) can be established by organizations under Japan's Health Insurance Act; they are commonly formed around specific industries, regions, or large corporate groups, and each association sets different insurance premiums and benefit contents.

Startups often join Association Kenpo (協会けんぽ) at founding, but if membership requirements of a suitable health insurance association are met, companies should actively consider joining to obtain more favorable premiums and benefits.
A social insurance labor consultant (社会保険労務士) is a nationally qualified specialist in labor consultation and labor-related procedures.

As an organization grows, employment conditions, payroll calculation, attendance management, harassment response, and issues involving managerial supervisors become more complex, so labor problems and labor risk increase; it is important to manage those risks in cooperation with expert labor consultants.

Job media companies (求人媒体) sell advertising space so employers can post recruitment ads for a fixed period and collect applications; a key advantage is gathering many candidates in a short window, but short-term posting does not guarantee that hiring will actually be secured.
The four major Japanese job media are リクナビNEXT, エン転職, マイナビ転職, and doda; many smaller media specialized by industry or occupation also exist.

Recruitment agents (エージェント) match companies that need talent with job seekers via occupational introduction (職業紹介); they range from large firms to individual agents, so finding an agent that can introduce people suited to the company is essential.

Most agent contracts are success-fee based (for example, a fee equal to 35% of annual salary upon hire); hiring cost tends to be high, but the benefit is targeted, one-by-one introduction of well-matched candidates.

HR consulting firms (人事系コンサルティング会社) are used when internal resources or expertise are insufficient for projects such as evaluation-system design or organizational reform, and they are also engaged to deliver training programs for managers or new-graduate development.
人事労務は人を扱う職業柄、実にさまざまな関係者が存在する。
採用業務においては、良い候補者を常に見つけられるような人材プール市場を形づくるために、各関係者とのネットワークづくりも重要なミッションの1つである。
In modern management with diversifying work styles, the fixed idea that hiring people equals hiring full-time employees (正社員採用) is disappearing.
When labor is insufficient, two main options exist to reinforce personnel: employment contracts (雇用契約) and business consignment/outsourcing contracts (業務委託契約).

Both involve helping with company operations from the perspective of assisting with work, but their natures differ greatly, so they must be fully understood before deciding the form of company participation.
Employment contract vs. business consignment contract comparison: labor-related laws/regulations apply vs. do not apply.
Time management: necessary (depending on contracted hours) vs. not necessary.
Certain benefits or arrangements (e.g., insurance or leave-related): possible vs. not possible.
Working-hours constraints: exist vs. none.
What is provided: the labor force itself vs. deliverables (成果物) or task performance/execution.
Payment method: salary (給与) vs. remuneration/fee (報酬).
Tax treatment of certain payments (e.g., allowances): non-taxable vs. taxable.
Organizational culture formation: easier vs. more difficult.
Long-term commitment: easier to obtain vs. more difficult to obtain.
The decisive difference between an employment contract (雇用契約) and a business consignment contract (業務委託契約) is the presence or absence of worker status (労働者性).
Worker status (労働者性) is judged by whether two requirements are met: (1) existence of a command-and-control system (指揮命令系統) and (2) existence of business independence (事業独立性).

Indicators of a command-and-control system include: whether work methods are instructed in detail; whether arrival and departure times are managed; and whether the person is required to follow workplace service rules (服務上の規律).

Indicators of business independence include: whether work is performed under one's own responsibility and judgment; whether expenses are borne by oneself; and whether work is carried out based on one's own expertise, skills, and experience.
The stronger the command-and-control system and the weaker the business independence, the more strongly worker status (労働者性) is recognized.
Mismatch between contract form and actual working conditions can lead to a finding of disguised contracting (偽装請負) and elevated legal risk.
The actual nature of the requested work and the intended management methods should be designed and understood before choosing the contract type.
Without people, a business cannot start; business growth cannot be discussed without human resources.

Before recruiting, first formulate a recruitment strategy (even roughly). Recruitment strategy equals the 5Ws of recruitment: when (by when), how (which recruitment channels), where (which department), what kind of person (abilities, experience, and personality), and how many people are needed.
Recruitment takes time and people are not found overnight, so create a recruitment plan looking 1–3 years ahead that specifies how many people each department needs.
The most important point of a recruitment plan is to link it to the business plan (事業計画と連動した採用計画にする).
A business plan describes the intended speed of growth in sales and profits.
A common failure is when planned sales/profit growth is completely unlinked from the recruitment plan.
Contradictory business plans often arise in which sales and profits are projected to grow even though no specific hiring plan is shown.
A business plan represents management's major business goals, so a hiring plan must be created while verifying whether practical recruitment activities aligned with it are actually possible.
If a business plan is built on clearly unrealistic staffing premises, the HR/labor side should give feedback and the business plan itself may need to be revised.
Example of formulating a hiring plan: a quarterly (Q1-Q4) headcount table by role (e.g., Manager and other positions) showing planned incremental increases.
When planned headcount increases, corresponding hiring is required to match the growth.
When establishing a recruitment plan, simultaneously define the desired talent image (人材像), i.e., the target of 'what kind of person you want to join the company.'
Target setting for recruitment should be done from two viewpoints: (1) experience and skills, and (2) mindset and personality.
Experience/skills are more objective and easier to confirm; mindset/personality is information that typically cannot be known until interviews or after the person has joined.
In the early stages of selection, focus primarily on confirming experience and skills; as the process moves to later stages, also confirm mindset and personality.

Because target setting will be reflected as application conditions in actual job postings, it is recommended to divide conditions into 'required conditions' (必須条件) and 'welcome conditions' (歓迎条件) when possible.
A recruitment channel (採用チャネル) refers to the types/methods of recruitment, such as job advertising media.
The success or failure of recruitment activities largely depends on whether the company can select recruitment channels that match the desired talent and the required number of personnel.
In the past, using major job advertisement media was the mainstream method; currently recruitment channels have diversified, so it is important first to understand the various types available.

Recruitment channels (採用チャネル) are the methods companies use to source candidates in HR/back-office operations; common types include referral, job ads, agencies, direct scouting, SNS, and owned content/media.

Referral recruiting (リファラル採用) is hiring via employee introductions of people they know. Advantages: more stable talent quality and minimized cost. Disadvantages: limited pool of possible referrals and dependence on employee cooperation.

Job advertising (求人広告) means posting recruitment ads for a fixed period to generate applications. Advantages: large reach, high application volume, and relatively low cost if multiple hires are made. Disadvantages: applicant quality is hard to control and results depend heavily on company name recognition and brand strength.

Recruitment agencies (エージェント/人材紹介) match companies that need talent with job seekers. Advantages: higher chance of receiving well-matched candidates and lower internal hiring workload. Disadvantages: high cost, typically a success fee of around 35% of the hire’s annual salary.

Direct recruiting/scouting targets the latent (not actively applying) talent pool by searching for people and sending scout or offer emails. Advantages: access to passive job-changers and often higher-caliber talent. Disadvantages: significant operational effort to write and send personalized messages.

SNS recruiting uses platforms such as X, YouTube, and LinkedIn to broadcast company information and attract applicants. Advantages: low barrier to start and little or no initial cost. Disadvantages: requires ongoing operational resources and budget to keep content flowing.

Owned-media recruiting publishes articles and content on the company site to show employer attractiveness. Advantages: candidates who apply have researched the company, reducing post-hire mismatch, and it builds long-term recruiting power and brand. Disadvantages: content planning and production costs plus a long time lag before results appear.

Trade-off pattern across channels: lower-cost or higher-quality methods (referral, owned media) tend to have volume or time limitations, while high-volume methods (ads, agencies) trade quality control or higher fees.
募集要項では、採用戦略をつくった際に考えた人材条件を実際の募集条件として記載する。
募集要項は職業安定法に基づく指針等を遵守した記載内容にしなければならない。遵守しないと違法となり罰則を受けるため、募集条件を各種媒体に載せて公募する場合は十分に注意する。
SNS採用やメディア運用、リファラル採用などでは募集要項が必要ない場合もある。ただし候補者の視点に立てば、募集要項があるほうが入社前イメージと入社後のギャップを解消する材料になる。
職業安定法上、募集時に明示すべき労働条件（記載が必要な内容）：業務内容、契約期間、勤務場所、就業時間、休憩時間、休日、時間外労働時間、賃金（臨時に支払われる賃金や賞与などは除く）、健康保険・厚生年金・労災保険および雇用保険の適用の有無、募集者の氏名または名称、受動喫煙防止措置。
当てはまる場合に追加で記載が必要な内容：裁量労働制がある場合はその内容。

When a fixed overtime pay (固定残業代) system exists, required details include: (1) the amount of basic salary excluding the fixed overtime pay, (2) the breakdown of the fixed overtime pay, and (3) a statement that additional premium wages will be paid for overtime work exceeding the fixed overtime hours.
If hiring as a dispatched worker (派遣労働者), that fact must be stated.
When starting actual recruitment, the recruitment process and role assignments should be decided in advance.
A typical recruitment process consists of stages such as document screening (書類選考), first interview (1次面接), second interview (2次面接), and final interview (最終面接).
Document screening should generally be included except in the case of referral hiring (リファラル採用).

The number of interview rounds, as well as who serves as interviewers, should be determined according to the personnel composition of the hiring department and the matters to be confirmed in interviews.

Example for a small or medium-sized enterprise: if the relevant department has only about 1–3 members, the first interview can be conducted by department members and the final interview by the company representative, resulting in a two-round process.

Recruitment activities closely resemble sales activities: both involve attractively presenting an offering to a target audience using similar methods, differing only in the object being promoted and the counterpart.

In sales, the company's product is attractively expressed to customers; in recruitment, the company itself (its culture, workplace environment, and growth opportunities) is attractively expressed to candidates.
When conducting recruitment, practitioners should adopt a salesperson mindset, treating the company as the product and focusing on how to communicate its appeal to candidates.
Both sales and recruitment rely on funnel management (ファネル管理) to track sequential process metrics and conversion rates.

Sales funnel stages: potential customers in the market → number of prospects (見込客数) → number of negotiations (商談数) → number of closed deals (成約数). Key indicators include prospect and negotiation volumes plus rates such as close rate and negotiation rate.
Recruitment funnel stages: potential candidates → number of scouts → number of applicants → number of offers (内定数) → number of joiners (入社数). Funnel-style numerical management is equally critical.

Many veteran HR professionals have prior top-sales backgrounds, and sales performance often correlates with later recruitment effectiveness; successful HR practitioners may likewise transition into sales roles.
採用広報 (recruitment PR / employer branding communication) is the long-term, ongoing activity of communicating a company's attractiveness as an employer to people who may join in the future.

By conveying the overall company and workplace image, candidates apply already holding a workplace image. This can shrink the recruitment gap (mismatch between expectation and reality), raise applicant quality and selection pass rates, improve offer-acceptance rates, and lower post-hire turnover.

The hardest aspect of 採用広報 is that effects are medium- to long-term, not short-term. Operations should be run for at least 1–2 years, with a clear understanding that ongoing operational cost will be incurred over that period.
採用広報 (recruitment PR / employer branding) is a core HR back-office activity aimed at helping candidates deeply understand the company and form a concrete image of working there after joining.

A dedicated recruitment site or page should be created in addition to the corporate homepage. Typical content includes employee interviews, employee growth stories, workplace photos, welfare/benefits systems, HR systems, and department-by-department job introductions.
The purpose of that content is to make post-hire working life imaginable, thereby creating opportunities for candidates to understand the company more deeply than a generic corporate site allows.

Article content should also be produced and published on recruitment media and the company website. Typical topics are employee introductions, workplace introductions, job-site/field details, and in-depth explanations of the work itself.
Because such articles keep accumulating over time, they function as stock-type content that can continuously expand awareness (ストック型で認知拡大が可能).

Recruitment introduction materials (採用紹介資料) that communicate the company’s appeal should be created and then linked from the corporate homepage and from pages on various recruitment media, increasing the number of touchpoints through which candidates can learn about the company.
Before a new hire joins, the two documents to prepare for a candidate who has accepted an offer are the 労働条件通知書 (labor conditions notification) and the 雇用契約書 (employment contract).
労働条件通知書 is a written notice that informs the worker of labor conditions in advance. Under the Labor Standards Act it must be given in writing beforehand and is a legally required document.

雇用契約書 records the labor conditions that will apply after joining. It is not required by the Labor Standards Act; an employment contract can be legally formed without a written document, but concluding it in writing is desirable.

The two documents contain almost the same information. Because the notification is a unilateral company document, practice often combines them into a single 労働条件通知書兼雇用契約書 that both notifies the worker and records mutual agreement, reducing later disputes.
After the combined (or separate) document is prepared, the contract should be signed at some point before the joining date.

Before joining a company in Japan, besides concluding the labor conditions notification combined with the employment contract (労働条件通知書兼雇用契約書), the company should request the following documents/information from the new hire: identity guarantee and pledge (身元保証書、誓約書) only if necessary; My Number (マイナンバー); employment insurance insured person certificate issued by the previous employer (前職で発行された雇用保険被保険者証); withholding tax slip (源泉徴収票); and salary earner movement notification issued by the previous employer (前職で発行された給与所得者異動届出書).
Previously a pension handbook (年金手帳) was required for Employees' Pension Insurance qualification procedures, but from 2022 onward it is no longer required if the My Number can be confirmed.

After joining, the company must proceed with procedures related to social insurance, employment insurance, and resident tax, filing the relevant documents with government offices within the prescribed deadlines.

The Health Insurance and Employees' Pension Insurance Insured Person Qualification Acquisition Notification (健康保険・厚生年金保険被保険者資格取得届) should be processed early because the health insurance card is issued only after the procedure is completed. New employees therefore do not yet have a health insurance card immediately after joining and, if they visit a medical institution, must temporarily pay the full medical costs out of pocket and later seek reimbursement.

After an employee joins a company in Japan, required filings to government offices include social insurance (健康保険) and employment insurance (雇用保険) notifications, with specific destinations and deadlines.

健康保険被扶養者異動届 (health insurance dependent change notification) is submitted to the 年金事務所 (pension office) immediately after the employee's qualification acquisition date, but only if the employee has dependents.
雇用保険被保険者資格取得届 (employment insurance insured qualification acquisition notification) must be filed within 10 days from the day after the hiring date.
A related notification to the 市区町村 (municipality) is due by the 10th of the month following the joining date.
Social insurance and employment insurance filings are recommended to be done electronically; electronic filing is mandatory for corporations with capital exceeding 100 million yen.
Electronic applications can be submitted using the free government-provided e-Gov system.
Direct input into e-Gov often takes extra time for unfamiliar users and frequently results in errors that cause applications to be returned; using software that links to e-Gov is preferable.
Back-office work spans accounting (経理), HR (人事), legal (法務), general affairs (総務), management planning (経営企画), and DX.
Consider using labor-application software that supports electronic filing procedures.
人事評価制度は、基本方針の明確化から具体的な制度設計までのステップで作成する。各ステップは楽な道のりではなく、経営陣・人事労務・フロント部門・その他の管理部門のすべてを巻き込んだ一大プロジェクトとなる。
人事制度作成のプロセス STEP 1: 基本方針の明確化。内容はバリュー・人事ポリシーの制定、および中長期事業計画。
人事制度作成のプロセス STEP 2: 具体的な制度設計。内容は等級制度・ジョブディスクリプションの設定。
人事評価制度をつくるためには、まず人事上の基本方針を明確にする。これは経営の大方針でもあるため、人事労務が決めるというより経営陣が主体的に進める。

Company values (バリュー) are the value standards and behavioral standards that a company wants to cherish; they serve as guidelines for employees' values and actions and therefore have a close relationship with HR policies and measures.
A similar term is 'HR policy' (人事ポリシー), which is essentially a rephrasing of company values using language closer to HR measures.

Mercari established three values and reflects them in all HR measures including personnel evaluation, talent development, and job assignments/transfers: Go Bold (dare to make bold choices), All for One (all for the success of the company), and Be a Pro (maintain professionalism in the workplace).
When creating a personnel evaluation system (人事評価制度), it is essential that a business plan (事業計画) is already in place, typically covering sales and profit targets for the next 3–5 years.
A business plan that defines future sales and profit also determines (1) the outline of the future organization and (2) the allowable human-resource investment plan (人的投資プラン).

Future headcount should be projected by job grade/position so that salary levels and bonus targets can be set; having a human-investment budget target in the business plan makes HR/labor system design much easier.

Once the overall policy is set, design the concrete HR systems in this strict top-down sequence: (1) grade system and job descriptions (等級制度・ジョブディスクリプション), (2) evaluation system (評価制度), (3) wage system (賃金制度).
Never reverse this order. Starting with the wage system greatly increases the chance of failure.
A related principle is that wages alone do not motivate people (賃金だけでは人は動かない).
Herzberg's two-factor theory (motivation-hygiene theory) holds that human motivation arises from two kinds of factors: motivator factors (動機付け要因) and hygiene factors (衛生要因).

Hygiene factors, if absent at a minimum level, produce dissatisfaction, yet no amount of additional fulfillment of them satisfies desire or raises motivation above zero. Wages and working conditions belong to hygiene factors.
Wages can therefore move motivation from negative to zero, but they are poorly suited to making it positive.
Example: raising bonuses after a strong year produces temporary joy and higher motivation; paying the identical amount the next year often elicits dissatisfaction ('the same amount again...').
Wages behave like a narcotic: once people become accustomed to a given level, gratitude declines and wants become limitless.

People commonly assume that visible, tangible items such as pay drive motivation, yet the theory locates high motivation in motivator factors—sense of achievement, recognition, and similar intrinsic job elements.
Motivator factors raise motivation once a certain baseline of needs has already been met.

Motivator factors (turning zero into plus; sources of drive that come from the work itself) include: recognition (承認), achievement (達成), the work itself (仕事そのもの), responsibility (責任), promotion (昇進), and growth (成長).

Hygiene factors (turning minus into zero; their absence heightens dissatisfaction, but abundance never produces satisfaction or conviction) include: company policy and administration, relationship with supervisor, working conditions, salary, relationship with colleagues, and personal life.
Designing the wage system first raises the risk of failing to improve motivation and performance, because pay is not the primary driver of those outcomes.

Grade systems (等級制度) and evaluation systems (評価制度) assign work and missions, treat evaluation as acknowledgment, and enable promotion and new work. That design is the creation of motivating factors (動機付け要因).
To raise organizational performance and engagement, start with grade-system and evaluation-system design rather than wages.

Personnel evaluation design must choose a base of job-type (ジョブ型) or membership-type (メンバーシップ型). The distinction is what is evaluated; a finer split yields four types: job (職務), role (役割), seniority (年功序列 / 在年数), and ability (職能 / 能力).
Job-type (職務): evaluation against defined job duties; wages linked to work, which tends to raise acceptance (納得度); requires operational know-how to define jobs.
Role-type (役割型, often grouped with job-type thinking): evaluation against roles; wages linked to roles and high acceptance; employees who do not try to expand their roles are hard to evaluate.
Seniority (年功序列): evaluation against years of service; high employee sense of security; easily produces dissatisfaction toward people with insufficient ability.
Ability-type (職能型): evaluation against ability; pay can be maintained even when posts are scarce; generalists tend to accumulate ability and be evaluated more easily.
Recent trends in Japanese personnel systems show that approaches closer to job-type (ジョブ型) employment are being adopted more frequently than traditional membership-type systems.
There is no universally correct or generally right classification of personnel/HR systems; the choice depends on company-specific circumstances rather than a single standard answer.

The appropriate system should be selected based on the basic policy already defined in STEP 1 of the framework, evaluating which design best matches the company and whether it can sustain employee motivation.
To design an education and training system as part of talent development (人材育成), first map out the ideal career plans (キャリアプラン) that the company wants internally.

Contemporary organizations have multiple career paths, including: new-graduate hires who aim to become future executives; mid-career specialists with high expertise; and regionally limited employees who develop field-management skills.

Employment forms have diversified beyond regular full-time employees of a single company to include contracted members, employees with side jobs, and short-time employees, so individual career plans are becoming more varied.
In this environment, companies should prepare several model career plans that still allow diverse career and life designs while enabling the business to grow.
Once multiple career plans exist, design corresponding education and training programs (教育研修プログラム) for each plan.
Education and training programs can be classified by hierarchy and type (a subsequent diagram in the source illustrates the categories).

Corporate education and training programs (教育研修プログラム) are classified into new-employee training (新人教育研修), management training (管理職研修), Off-JT (Off-the-Job Training), OJT (On-the-Job Training), and self-development activities (自己啓発活動).

Off-JT (Off-the-Job Training) is structured training away from daily work and typically covers business manners (ビジネスマナー), new-hire guidance (入社ガイダンス), basic skills and OA/office-automation skills (基本スキル・OAスキル), company understanding (会社理解), compliance (コンプライアンス), job-specific skills (職種別スキル), logical thinking (ロジカルシンキング), and project management (プロジェクトマネジメント).
Management training (管理職研修) focuses on strategic thinking (戦略思考), numerical/financial management (計数管理), management and team building (マネジメント/チームビルディング), compliance, and mental health (メンタルヘルス).
OJT (On-the-Job Training) is learning through experience in actual job duties (実際の業務での経験).

Self-development activities (自己啓発活動) are commonly supported by e-learning, book-purchase subsidies (書籍購入補助), external-seminar participation (外部セミナー参加), in-company universities (企業内大学), and qualification-acquisition subsidies (資格取得補助).
Compliance (コンプライアンス) training is treated as a recurring, cross-cutting topic that appears in new-employee, management, and general training programs.
Career plans (キャリアプラン) must be linked to and coordinated with the personnel evaluation system (人事評価制度).
Define the requirements (要件定義) for what kind of career growth an employee needs in order to raise their grade or rank (等級).
When career plans, education/training programs (教育研修プログラム), and the personnel evaluation system are aligned, they function together as one consistent, integrated program.
This linkage creates a unified cycle: career plan → education and training program → personnel evaluation system.

就業規則 (employment rules / work rules) is a company-wide regulation that defines various labor conditions such as wages and holidays, as well as service discipline (服務規律). It serves as the rulebook for employees working at the company and is the highest-level concept among HR regulations (人事規程), making it a critical document that can exceed 100 pages depending on the company.

Creation of 就業規則 becomes legally mandatory once a company regularly employs 10 or more workers. Startups and small SMEs with fewer than 10 employees are not required to have them; absence of employment rules in that case is not illegal and remains at the company's discretion.

Because 就業規則 is the most important personnel regulation, it cannot be decided unilaterally by the company. When newly creating or amending employment rules, the company must obtain an opinion letter (意見書) from employee representatives or a labor union, then file the rules with the Labor Standards Inspection Office (労働基準監督署).
Created 就業規則 must be stored, distributed, or otherwise made available so employees can view them at any time, and they must be properly publicized/notified (周知) to employees.
就業規則 must include specified required items covering labor conditions and related rules (the detailed list of items begins on this page but is not fully shown in the excerpt).

Japanese employment rules (就業規則) have three layers of content: absolute mandatory items that must always be written, relative mandatory items that must be written if the company adopts those rules, and other optional company-defined rules.

絶対的必要記載事項 (absolute mandatory items) that must always be stated in the employment rules: (1) start and end times, rest periods, holidays, leave, and—for shift systems—matters on changing work shifts; (2) wage determination, calculation and payment methods, wage closing and payment dates, and pay raises; (3) retirement, including grounds for dismissal.

相対的必要記載事項 (relative mandatory items)—if the company sets the rule, it must be written: (1) retirement allowances; (2) temporary wages/bonuses and minimum wage amounts; (3) employee burden for meals, work supplies, etc.; (4) safety and hygiene; (5) vocational training; (6) disaster compensation and assistance for non-work injury/illness; (7) commendation and sanctions; (8) other matters that apply to all workers.

Employment rules are not only a document titled 「就業規則」. They can be a collection of multiple regulation documents. Separate 「賃金規程」(wage regulations) or 「慶弔金規程」(congratulatory/condolence money regulations) fall under the absolute mandatory wage-determination items, are treated as detailed rules forming one body with the employment rules, and must be filed with the Labor Standards Inspection Office (労働基準監督署).
Personnel evaluation systems are generally also regulations that constitute part of the employment rules, not a completely separate internal policy.

Employment rules (就業規則) are composed of various detailed sub-regulations (細則規程), including wage regulations (賃金規程), personnel evaluation regulations (人事評価規程), rank/grade regulations (等級・グレード規程), retirement allowance regulations (退職金規程), childcare and nursing-care leave regulations (育児・介護休業規程), business-trip regulations (出張規程), personal-information management regulations (個人情報管理規程), remote-work and work-from-home regulations (リモートワーク規程、在宅勤務規程), welfare-and-benefits regulations (福利厚生規程), and harassment regulations (ハラスメント規程).
Employment rules constitute the fundamental 'head temple' (総本山) of a company's human-resources rules and should therefore reflect the company's vision and values (ビジョン・バリュー) as core HR policy.

Excessively granular drafting of each individual provision tends to narrow perspective and produce either overly harsh 'black' rules driven by profit-supremacy or overly lenient 'white' rules that try too hard to please employees.
Once employment rules have been established they are difficult to change; disadvantageous amendments require not only employee opinions but also individual consent from each employee.

When newly creating employment rules, carefully design the provisions that affect important company guidelines (vision, values, and HR policy) while using standard templates as the base for overly detailed items rather than over-customizing them.

Templates (ひな型) for employment regulations (就業規則) are held by specialists such as certified social insurance labor consultants (社労士), and can also be downloaded from the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働省) website.

Creating employment regulations solely by a labor-affairs staff member is difficult: they are the most important HR regulation; the document is nearly 100 pages; including related detailed regulations (細則規程), roughly 10 regulations result; creation difficulty is therefore high.
Annual legal amendments must be understood and reflected in the articles of the regulations.
If the company has a highly specialized labor superior or a veteran employee holding a 社労士 qualification, that person can lead creation; in most companies this is not the case.
Recommendation: create employment regulations together with specialists such as 社労士, reviewing and confirming the content jointly.
As organizations grow larger and their systems become more established, employees experience more frequent personnel transfers (人事異動).
Personnel transfers consist of two main types: vertical (縦) and horizontal (横) movements.
Vertical personnel transfers include promotion and rank advancement (昇進・昇格) within the same job grade.
Horizontal personnel transfers include inter-departmental reassignment (配置転換), secondment (出向), and employment transfer (転籍) to group companies, changing job content or work location.

Job rotation (ジョブローテーション) is an HR talent-development system that periodically (typically every 2–5 years) reassigns employees across departments so they accumulate diverse experience, combining both transfers and promotions.

Purposes of job rotation include: developing future executive candidates from a medium- to long-term perspective; seeking optimal placement (適材適所); and deepening employees’ understanding of company-wide operations.
Horizontal-transfer policies such as job rotation are generally impractical unless the organization is sufficiently large.
A January 2017 Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare survey on corporate transfer practices found a strong correlation between company size and whether job rotation is implemented.

In organizations of several dozen people, lateral (horizontal) personnel transfers can temporarily reset previously acquired skills and know-how, or assign people to roles they do not want, which can lower motivation and reduce overall organizational performance.
Job rotation should be implemented strategically only after other HR systems—especially recruiting capability—have been sufficiently strengthened.

Larger companies are more likely to practice job rotation. Based on Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare 2017 survey on intra-company transfers: under 300 employees ~39%; 300–500 employees 51.3%; 1,000+ employees 70.3%.

The fundamental design of personnel transfers is shaped by whether the company’s HR policy and evaluation system is job-type (ジョブ型) or membership-type (メンバーシップ型); the two models produce very different approaches to mobility and role assignment.

Job-type (ジョブ型) vs membership-type (メンバーシップ型) HR/organization design: Job-type designs the organization around duties/jobs and develops specialists by raising expertise and execution ability; pay is tied to the job itself, so horizontal (lateral) transfers are a poor fit and the system centers on vertical transfers. Membership-type designs the organization around people’s capabilities, builds high-capability generalists through varied experience, and sets pay for the person rather than the job, so both vertical and horizontal transfers are needed.

Personnel transfers must be linked to talent-development career plans and career paths. Design several department- or person-level career paths that are win-win for company growth and individual growth, then intentionally use vertical and horizontal moves according to that growth plan.
Generalist career paths in back-office functions can branch into diverse roles such as marketing, new-business development, sales, and related operations, as shown across multiple illustrative cases.

Personnel transfers (人事異動) have a secondary role beyond ordinary rotation: they can change an employee’s duties or rank (職階) when life-stage changes, private circumstances, or internal organizational trouble make the current assignment unsustainable.
Such transfers function as an organizational “adjustment valve” (調整弁) that absorbs unexpected personal or workplace events that cannot be planned in advance.
Unavoidable-reason transfers therefore serve both the individual’s changing situation and the organization’s need to keep operations stable.

Unavoidable circumstances that may necessitate personnel transfers (人事異動) include life-stage changes such as childcare, childbirth, and nursing care; a spouse or family member being transferred overseas; return to the workplace after leave due to mental health issues; communication problems within a department; deterioration of interpersonal relationships; occurrence of harassment within a department; and dealing with problem employees.

Job transfers (配置転換) cannot be decided lightly or unilaterally by management or HR/labor staff. They impose a significant personal burden on employees, so labor-law compliance and legal-risk countermeasures are essential.
If a transfer is unjust, the employee has the right to refuse the order.

Before conducting a transfer, confirm that the work rules (就業規則) contain a provision stating that transfers may be carried out when there is business necessity. If no such provision exists, the work rules must be revised after agreement with the employee representative or union.
Separately from work rules, if an individual employment contract limits the employee’s work location or job type, a transfer cannot be ordered without the employee’s agreement.
A transfer must have a reasonable business reason and necessity (業務上の合理的な理由・必要性). A transfer lacking such a reason may be deemed an abuse of rights (権利濫用) and therefore invalid.

Examples of reasonable reasons for a transfer include proper allocation of the workforce (労働力の適正配置), improvement of business efficiency (業務効率の向上), improvement of motivation (モチベーション向上), talent development (人材開発), and maintenance of employment (雇用の維持).
When issuing 辞令 (personnel appointment/transfer orders) in back-office HR practice, a key check is whether the action imposes a significant disadvantage (著しい不利益) on the employee.
Personnel orders should not be issued as purely unilateral commands; as much as possible, confirm the employee's intentions before issuing the 辞令.
This guidance appears in the context of Japanese corporate back-office operations covering HR, legal, general affairs, and related functions.

36協定 (Article 36 Agreement) is formally named 「時間外・休日労働に関する協定」 (Agreement on Overtime and Holiday Work). It is required whenever employees work beyond statutory hours of 8 hours per day or 40 hours per week; the agreement must be concluded and filed with the Labor Standards Inspection Office under Article 36 of the Labor Standards Act.
Even 1 minute of statutory overtime in a day makes work illegal without a filed 36協定. In practice it is recommended to file as soon as even one employee is hired.

Procedure to conclude a 36協定: (1) decide upper limits on overtime hours and holiday-work days; (2) conclude the agreement with the employee representative; (3) file it with the Labor Standards Inspection Office; (4) notify employees.
A 36協定 is valid for only one year and must be renewed annually to avoid illegal overtime.

Filing a 36協定 does not permit unlimited overtime. Statutory caps still apply: monthly overtime must be less than 100 hours and annual overtime must be less than 720 hours (annual ceiling of 720 hours).
Under Japan's Labor Standards Act 36 Agreement, overtime exceeding 45 hours in a month is allowed at most 6 times per year.
One-month overtime maximum must be under 100 hours; multi-month average must stay within 80 hours.
Standard legal overtime limits are 45 hours per month and 360 hours per year; exceeding these requires filing a special-clause 36 agreement (特別条項付き36協定).
Overtime, holiday work, and late-night work require premium (overtime) wages as compensation for the extra burden on the worker.
Premium-wage formula: wage unit × hours worked × premium rate.

Wage-unit calculation: monthly salary = (monthly pay + allowances) ÷ [(annual prescribed workdays ÷ 12) × daily prescribed hours]; daily wage = (daily pay + allowances) ÷ daily prescribed hours; hourly wage uses the given hourly rate.
Statutory premium rates: overtime 25 % (50 % or more for hours beyond 60 in a month), statutory holiday 35 %, late night (22:00–05:00) 25 %.
Example: a 2,000-yen hourly worker who does 1 hour of overtime must receive an extra 500 yen (25 %), for a total of 2,500 yen for that hour.
Night-time work premiums can stack on top of overtime and holiday premiums. For example, work during night hours on a statutory holiday can require a combined premium of 35% + 25% = 60%.

In Japanese attendance and payroll practice, 「所定」(prescribed / company-set) and 「法定」(statutory / legal) must not be confused. Similar-looking terms include prescribed overtime vs. statutory overtime, and prescribed holidays vs. statutory holidays.
The Labor Standards Act rule that premium wages must be paid for overtime and holiday work refers to statutory (法定) standards, not company-set (所定) ones.
Statutory overtime is work exceeding 8 hours per day or 40 hours per week. A statutory holiday is one day of rest per week.

Many companies now use a two-day weekend and set daily hours below 8 (e.g., 7 hours). In that case, working on one of the two weekly days off for 7 hours or more but less than 8 hours is generally not statutory overtime/holiday work and does not require Labor Standards Act premium pay.

「法定」 means Labor Standards Act rules; 「所定」 means the company’s own rules. Whether extra premium is paid for prescribed (company) overtime or holidays is a company decision, and must be checked in the work rules and employment contract.

Attendance-management checks should include: prescribed working hours and holiday settings by contract type (hourly vs. monthly pay; full-time vs. part-time); and whether legally required rest/break time is actually taken.

When reviewing attendance (勤怠), check whether overtime that violates the 36 Agreement (36協定) is occurring; whether late-night work (深夜労働) or holiday work (休日労働) has become a regular/constant occurrence; whether there are departments or employees with monthly constant overtime; and whether paid leave (有給休暇) is actually being taken.
Japanese rest-period rules tied to working hours: work exceeding 6 hours generally requires a break of 45 minutes or more; work exceeding 8 hours generally requires a break of 1 hour or more.
To check attendance and connect it to payroll calculation (給与計算), the most important practice is to aggregate and manage working hours by attendance aggregation categories (勤怠の集計区分).

If category-based time aggregation is not done well, it becomes difficult to grasp the overtime upper limits required by the 36 Agreement, premium rates (割増率) may be applied incorrectly, and many operational problems arise.
Attendance is typically aggregated with attendance-management software or spreadsheets; confirm that hours can be totaled into the required legal/payroll categories.
Theoretically there are 18 time-aggregation categories (as in the book’s figure) to which premium rates can be linked.

Do not confuse predetermined overtime (所定時間外) with statutory overtime (法定時間外), or predetermined holidays (所定休日) with statutory holidays (法定休日); they are different and must be treated separately for compliance and premium pay.
勤怠の集計区分と割増率は、所定外労働を100%とし、月の法定残業が月60時間以内の場合に適用される。
労働時間の区分には日中と深夜があり、所定内、所定外残業、法定外残業、深夜所定内、深夜所定外、深夜法定外に分類される。
所定内労働の割増率は100%である。
所定外残業および法定外残業の割増率は125%である。
深夜所定内の割増率は125%である。
深夜所定外の割増率は125%である。
深夜法定外の割増率は150%である。
一部の区分（休日労働等を含む可能性）では135%の割増率が適用される。
これらの区分と率は日本のバックオフィス（経理・人事）における勤怠集計・残業代計算の実務知識である。

有給休暇 (paid annual leave) is leave granted to workers who have been employed for a certain period so they can recover from physical and mental fatigue and enjoy a more leisurely life; wages continue to be paid even when the leave is taken.

Two statutory conditions must both be met before paid leave is granted: (1) six months have elapsed since the hire date, and (2) the worker attended at least 80 percent of all working days during that period.
The first grant occurs at the six-month mark after hire; subsequent grants occur on a one-year cycle thereafter.

Statutory grant amounts for ordinary workers by continuous years of service: 0.5 years = 10 days, 1.5 years = 11 days, 2.5 years = 12 days, 3.5 years = 14 days, 4.5 years = 16 days, 5.5 years = 18 days, 6.5 years or more = 20 days.
Employers must pay attention to the legal obligation that workers take (digest) at least five days of paid leave each year (年間5日の消化義務).
Under Japan's Labor Standards Act, employers have a legal obligation to ensure that employees granted 10 or more days of paid annual leave (有給休暇) take at least 5 days of that leave within one year.

The 5-day annual paid-leave digestion obligation applies to employees who have worked for more than six months; therefore, in practice, it covers essentially all employees who have been granted paid leave.
Because paid-leave grant dates differ for each employee, companies must perform careful, individual paid-leave usage (消化) management.

Companies that already have a large number of annual holidays or that offer many special leave days often experience low actual usage of statutory paid leave. This can be addressed by timely announcements encouraging employees to take leave or by using 'planned granting' (計画的付与), in which the company designates the leave dates in advance.
Paid leave must be granted regardless of whether the worker is a part-timer (hourly) or a monthly-salaried employee. A common misconception is that part-timers are not entitled to paid leave.
A part-time worker who has been employed for five months and whose attendance rate exceeds 80 percent must be granted paid leave on the same basis as other workers.

Because many hourly part-timers work on a shift system in which days off are decided ad hoc, unplanned paid-leave requests can make it impossible to staff operations. When creating shift schedules, companies should incorporate paid-leave digestion plans so that work balance is maintained.

When a part-timer takes paid leave, wages are calculated as: (prescribed working hours per day) × (number of paid-leave days taken) × (hourly wage). Wage planning should therefore be prepared in advance taking expected paid-leave usage into account.

Workers who do not work five or more days per week (typical of many part-timers) receive a different number of paid-leave days from regular full-time workers; the grant is proportional rather than the standard full-time allotment.

For workers with weekly prescribed working days of 4 or fewer AND weekly prescribed working hours of less than 30 hours, annual paid leave (年次有給休暇) is granted on a proportional (比例付与) basis rather than the full statutory amounts.
Grant days depend on two factors: years of continuous service (継続勤務年数) and either weekly prescribed working days (週所定労働日数) or annual prescribed working days (1年間の所定労働日数).
Service-year breakpoints in the table are 6 months, 1 year 6 months, 2 years 6 months, 3 years 6 months, 4 years 6 months, 5 years 6 months, and 6 years 6 months or more.
4 prescribed days per week (or 169–216 annual prescribed working days) yields 7 / 8 / 9 / 10 / 12 / 13 / 15 paid-leave days at those service breakpoints.
3 prescribed days per week (or 121–168 annual prescribed working days) yields 5 / 6 / 6 / 8 / 9 / 10 / 11 paid-leave days.
2 prescribed days per week (or 73–120 annual prescribed working days) yields 3 / 4 / 4 / 5 / 6 / 6 / 7 paid-leave days.
1 prescribed day per week (or 48–72 annual prescribed working days) yields 1 / 2 / 2 / 2 / 3 / 3 / 3 paid-leave days.
When working days are defined by a period other than a week, the annual prescribed-working-days column of the same table is used instead of the weekly-days column.

Flex-time system (フレックスタイム制) and discretionary labor system (裁量労働制) both feature high freedom in start and end times and are considered for realizing flexible working styles that are not overly bound by working hours.

As career plans and working styles diversify, designing work that does not match traditional Labor Standards Act emphasis on specified attendance times and command-and-control can strengthen the organization and promote business growth.

Flex-time and discretionary labor systems are sometimes discussed in similar contexts but have completely different meanings and entirely different labor-law risks; correct understanding is essential.
Flex-time system: employees can freely choose their working hours. It grants employees advantageous rights, so flexible and free design is possible.
Discretionary labor system: actual hours worked are ignored and working hours are 'deemed.' It can impose excessive burden on employees, so many employee-protection rules and restrictions exist.
裁量労働制（discretionary labor system）はみなし労働時間制（deemed working hours system）の一種であり、「専門業務型裁量労働制」と「企画業務型裁量労働制」に分かれる。
みなし労働時間制には「事業場外のみなし労働時間制」もあり、これらはフレックスタイム制と制度内容が異なる。
職種の制限：専門業務型裁量労働制は情報処理システム分析、デザイナー、税理士などの業務、新聞記者などに限られる。企画業務型裁量労働制は事業運営に関する事項についての企画・立案・調査および分析の業務に限られる。事業場外みなし労働時間制は事業場外で労働した労働時間の算定が困難な業務に限り（例：外回りの営業）。フレックスタイム制は職種制限なし。
労働時間の判断：専門業務型・企画業務型・事業場外みなし労働時間制はみなし労働時間で判断する。フレックスタイム制は実際の労働時間で判断する。
残業代支給が必要な場合：みなし労働時間制（専門業務型・企画業務型・事業場外）では、みなし労働時間が法定労働時間を超えている場合に支給する。フレックスタイム制では、総労働時間（労働者が精算期間において労働すべき時間）を超えた場合に支給する。
深夜割増手当は、専門業務型裁量労働制、企画業務型裁量労働制、事業場外みなし労働時間制、フレックスタイム制のいずれでも必要である。
勤怠管理は、上記4制度のいずれでも必要である。
導入方法：専門業務型裁量労働制は労使協定の締結、監督署への届出、本人の同意が必要。企画業務型裁量労働制は労使委員会の決議、監督署への届出、本人の同意が必要。事業場外みなし労働時間制は就業規則で規定し労使協定を締結する（みなし労働時間が法定労働時間を超える場合は届出が必要）。フレックスタイム制は就業規則で規定し労使協定を締結する（届出不要）。
有効期間・報告：専門業務型裁量労働制は最大3年の有効期間ごとに労使協定を行う。企画業務型裁量労働制は6カ月以内ごとに所轄労働基準監督署へ報告を行う。フレックスタイム制には当該期間・報告の定めなし。

Introduction of flextime systems (フレックスタイム制) and discretionary labor systems (裁量労働制) is an important choice that must be linked to the company's ideal way of working, its relationship with employees, and its thinking about careers.
When introducing these systems, companies must also define required notifications (届出), regulation/policy development (規程整備), labor management (労務管理), and other related decisions.
Caution: introducing such systems without careful consideration merely because they 'seem good somehow' can later force large corrections; thorough review is required before adoption.

Whether to introduce the systems should be decided only after considering the culture and organizational climate sought by both employees and the company, as well as the HR policy (人事ポリシー) the company aims to achieve.
Under Japan's Industrial Safety and Health Act (労働安全衛生法), companies are legally obligated to conduct health examinations (健康診断) for employees as part of health management (健康管理).
Hiring health examination (雇入時の健康診断) must be conducted within 3 months of employment.
Periodic health examination (定期健康診断) must be conducted once per year.
Eligible employees (対象者) are those with a contract period of 1 year or more who work at least three-quarters of the prescribed weekly working hours of regular full-time employees.
For employees working at least one-half but less than three-quarters of prescribed weekly hours, it is considered desirable (望ましい) to have them undergo health examinations.
Because health examinations are a legal obligation under the Industrial Safety and Health Act, the company must bear the costs.
There are specific rules concerning wages for employees' constrained/working time spent undergoing health examinations (健康診断中の拘束時間に対する賃金).

Even if not legally mandatory, it is desirable for the company to bear the cost of employee health checkups; this should preferably be stipulated in the employment rules (就業規則) or wage regulations (賃金規程).

HR/labor should handle reservations and arrangements for health checkups so the company can properly grasp employees' health status. If each employee freely chooses a medical institution, results may not be sent to the company and information gaps can occur.
Individual health checkup results constitute personal information, so their management methods require careful attention.
