Using checkup institutions affiliated with a health insurance association or Kyokai Kenpo (協会けんぽ) is practical because they can handle reservation/implementation management and bulk billing.
Mental health care and related risk countermeasures have become increasingly important.

Failure of mental health care can lead to employee leave of absence, increased resignations, decline in overall organizational productivity, litigation, reputational damage, and business continuity risk.
Japan's Stress Check System (ストレスチェック制度) started in December 2015. Workplaces with 50 or more employees are obligated to conduct a stress check once a year.
Stress checks are used to grasp workplace stress conditions for each employee; based on analysis results, workplace environment improvement activities must be carried out regularly.

Stress checks should be implemented via external services (HR service companies or occupational health service companies). Doing them solely with in-house HR staff is not realistic due to the burden of statutory questionnaires, post-implementation aggregation/analysis, and information storage.
When selecting a stress-check service, implementation cost is one of the key points to consider.

Stress checks can be administered via Web-based diagnosis or paper mark-sheet diagnosis, and results may be used for other HR purposes such as simultaneous implementation with engagement surveys or other personnel surveys, followed by collaboration with an industrial physician after aggregation.
Companies with 50 or more employees must appoint not only stress-check arrangements but also a safety manager (安全管理者), health manager (衛生管理者), and industrial physician (産業医).

These appointments must be made within 14 days from the date the employee count reaches the statutory threshold and reported to the Labor Standards Inspection Office (労働基準監督署); each role has defined qualification requirements that must be verified.
When the employee count reaches 11 or more, a health promotion officer (衛生推進者) must be appointed even though no government notification is required.

The Industrial Safety and Health Act (労働安全衛生法) imposes different appointment/installation obligations according to headcount bands (typically 11–49, 50–99, 100–999, and 1,000+ employees), with some roles limited to designated industries.
Payroll calculation (給与計算) is one of the most important practical tasks for labor/HR staff (労務担当). To perform it, first understand the company's own payroll calculation schedule.
The first items to confirm in a payroll schedule are the closing date (締日) and the payment date (支払日). These differ by company.
A common setting at small and medium-sized enterprises (中小企業) is 'end-of-current-month closing, payment on the 25th of the following month' (当月末締め翌月25日払い).

Large companies or companies that consider employees' cash flow may use 'end-of-current-month closing, payment on the 20th of the current month' (当月末締め当月20日払い). In some cases overtime pay is finalized only at month-end and paid on the 20th of the following month.

After the closing and payment dates are confirmed, the following work is performed between those two dates: (1) closing of each employee's attendance input (勤怠入力締め); (2) attendance-input check by the labor/HR side; (3) new registration or deletion in the payroll system for employees who joined or left (入退社); (4) changes to deductions for social insurance premiums, employment insurance premiums, resident tax, and income tax (社会保険料・雇用保険料・住民税・所得税の天引変更); (5) bank-account transfers (銀行口座での振込).
Payroll calculation (給与計算) must be performed using a variety of items and cannot be done simply; it involves multiple data sources and settings.
Based on the author's experience reviewing payroll at many companies, the large majority of companies that calculate payroll without a dedicated payroll system have serious calculation errors.
To reduce both the frequency and the magnitude of payroll errors as much as possible, a payroll calculation system should always be used.
When choosing a payroll system, a practical option is to select one that can be contracted together with the accounting system (会計システム).
Payroll processing produces complex accounting journal entries (会計仕訳); using systems from the same vendor therefore has the advantage of easier data linkage and integration.

Typical payroll-calculation schedule / workflow includes: attendance input (勤怠入力) → attendance check (勤怠チェック) → setup of joining/leaving employees (入退社従業員の設定) → changes to deduction settings (天引設定変更) → reflection of expense-reimbursement information (経費精算情報反映).

Payroll systems can streamline bank transfer work: after payroll calculation is complete, they output each person's transfer amount as bank-transfer data (全銀データ / Zengin format or CSV), which can then be imported into internet banking.

Accurate payroll calculation (給与計算) depends on master data (マスター) setup. Aim for a state in which all relevant system settings are complete; if masters are solid, roughly 70–80% of calculation accuracy is already secured.

Master items that affect payroll include: wage type (月給 / 日給 / 時給 and the corresponding monthly, daily, or hourly system); prescribed working hours (所定労働時間数) and annual working days (年間労働日数); hours by category (所定時間内, 所定時間外, 深夜, 法定休日労働, etc.); paid-leave days and hours; commuting allowance (通勤手当) and expense reimbursements (経費精算額); premium rates for overtime, legal overtime, night, legal holidays, and prescribed holidays; fixed overtime pay (固定残業代); presence of flextime or discretionary-labor systems; standard remuneration monthly amount (標準報酬月額); social-insurance qualification acquisition and loss dates and collection month (normally next-month collection); inhabitant-tax special collection (特別徴収) flag and monthly amounts (typically June of the current year through May of the following year); income-tax withholding columns (甲欄 / 乙欄); and number and ages of dependents (扶養人数・年齢).
Payroll calculation (給与計算) is a critical back-office task that must not be mistaken, because calculation volume is overwhelmingly large and complex while errors have large impact.
Core difficulty of payroll work: it is both computationally heavy/complex and a high-stakes important operation.

Many applicable laws and internal rules must be applied, including employment insurance (雇用保険), workers' accident compensation insurance (労災保険), the Health Insurance Act (健康保険法), work rules (就業規則), and welfare benefit regulations (福利厚生規程).
Payroll is an extremely important function that supports employees' livelihoods, creating strong pressure not to make mistakes.
Accurate payroll is impossible without visibility into each employee's actual working conditions (勤務実態); without that grasp, truly correct calculation cannot be performed.
Time constraints are severe: payroll cutoff dates and monthly closing (月次決算) deadlines must both be met, so calculation must be done rapidly.
The book frames payroll as part of comprehensive back-office knowledge covering accounting, HR, legal, general affairs, management planning, and DX.
When performing payroll calculation (給与計算), divide the work into several influencing checkpoints and run calculation checks against them.

Attendance (勤怠) checkpoints: confirm attendance is entered every day; weekday vs. prescribed holiday (所定休日) vs. legal holiday (法定休日) distinctions are correct; prescribed working hours (所定労働時間) settings are correct; time is calculated to the 1-minute unit; break time is entered and meets legal requirements (45 minutes / 1 hour); hours are aggregated into the correct buckets (overtime, late-night, legal holiday, prescribed holiday).
Confirm successful data transfer from the attendance system to the payroll system.

Premium-rate checkpoints: premium rates for each aggregation category are set correctly; if the company uses unique premium rates that exceed the Labor Standards Act, those rates are reflected in the system; fixed overtime pay (固定残業代) is calculated correctly.

Social-insurance checkpoints: social-insurance settings are in place for joiners/leavers and for employees subject to monthly change (月変); for employees whose fixed wages changed, check whether the 3-month average salary causes a grade change of 2 grades or more; collection-month settings are not wrong.

Income-tax / resident-tax checkpoints: Kou-ran vs. Otsu-ran withholding-table settings are not wrong; number of dependents and ages (especially whether 16 or older) are not wrong; whether the employee is subject to special collection (特別徴収) of resident tax is correctly reflected in system settings.
These checkpoints span attendance data quality, system configuration (premiums, tax tables, insurance), and statutory vs. company-specific rules in Japanese payroll operations.
所得税と住民税は、給与支払い時に天引き（源泉徴収）を行い、その後、国や地方自治体に納付する。
所得税と住民税の共通ルール：毎月従業員から徴収し、徴収した月の翌月10日までに納付する。
所得税の納付先は国税（国）、住民税の納付先は市区町村（地方税）。
所得税の納付書類：所得税徴収高計算書（納付書）。住民税の納付書類：納入済通知書。
所得税の徴収方法：その年の所得に対して毎月概算で徴収し、年末調整時に確定額を最終調整する。
住民税の徴収方法：前年に確定した所得に対する税額を、翌年6月から翌々年5月にかけて分割して徴収する。
所得税の徴収対象者：全従業員（年の途中入社した従業員も含む）。
住民税の徴収対象者：前年末に年末調整を行った従業員。途中入社でも、前職が作成した住民税の異動届出書を提出した場合は徴収可能。
所得税の電子納付：e-Tax経由でインターネットバンキングまたはダイレクト納付。
住民税の電子納付：eLTAX経由でインターネットバンキングまたはダイレクト納付。
The book covers all back-office operations (バックオフィス業務), spanning accounting (経理), human resources (人事), legal affairs (法務), general affairs (総務), and management planning (経営企画).
所得税徴収高計算書 (所得税) is an official Japanese form used for calculating and reporting withheld income tax amounts.
領収済通知書 is an official receipt-completed notification document associated with tax payments.
When completing such official tax forms, the received amount must be entered as instructed, and the form must not be soiled or folded.
所得税の源泉徴収額は、扶養家族の人数と甲欄・乙欄の区分によって変わる。
実務上の所得税計算は、国税庁が公開している「源泉徴収税額表」を用いて行う。給与計算システムを使用している場合、扶養情報と甲乙欄情報が設定されていれば自動計算される。
具体例：その月の社会保険料控除後の給与金額が180,000円で、扶養家族が1名の甲欄の従業員の場合、その月の所得税徴収額は2,430円となる。
源泉徴収税額表の見方：その月の社会保険料等控除後の給与等の金額のレンジ（例：167,000円〜169,000円など）ごとに、扶養親族の数（0人〜7人以上）に対応する税額が示される。甲欄は扶養人数に応じて税額が減り、乙欄は扶養を考慮せず高めの税額となる。

In Japanese income-tax withholding on salaries, two main columns of the withholding tax table apply: Ko-column (甲欄) and Otsu-column (乙欄). A third Hei-column (丙欄) exists but is almost never used in practice.
Ko-column withholding produces a substantially smaller income-tax deduction than Otsu-column; Otsu-column requires a considerably larger amount to be withheld.

Ko-column applies to officers and employees who have submitted the “Salary Earner’s Dependent Deduction etc. (Change) Declaration Form” (給与所得者の扶養控除等（異動）申告書) and who receive their principal salary from that company.

The dependent-deduction declaration form may be submitted to only one employer. An employee who receives salary from two or more employers (e.g., dual employment) must choose the company that pays the main salary and submit the form there.
Otsu-column applies to employees who receive salary from two or more places and who have not submitted the dependent-deduction declaration form to that employer.

When preparing the income-tax payment slip (所得税徴収高計算書), the company must combine (1) income tax withheld from payroll and (2) withholding tax collected on payments to individual business owners or freelance contractors, and remit the total together.
Because HR/labor typically does not hold data on external expense payments, accounting must supply those figures; the two departments should cross-check before the combined payment is made.

Resident-tax (住民税) collection: around April–May each year the municipality sends the company a “Resident Tax Decision Notice” for every employee who underwent year-end adjustment the previous December, together with payment slips covering the 12 months from June of the current year through May of the following year.
The labor administrator withholds the exact monthly resident-tax amounts shown on the decision notice from each employee’s salary and remits them by the 10th of the following month.
In Japanese corporate back-office / HR practice, social insurance relating to people who work at a company is divided into a broad sense (広義の社会保険) and a narrow sense (狭義の社会保険).
Narrow-sense social insurance (狭義の社会保険) consists of three programs: Employees' Pension Insurance (厚生年金保険), Health Insurance (健康保険), and Long-term Care Insurance (介護保険).
Labor insurance (労働保険) consists of two programs: Employment Insurance (雇用保険) and Workers' Accident Compensation Insurance (労災保険).
The broad scope of social insurance (広義の社会保険の範囲) encompasses both the three narrow-sense social insurance programs and the two labor-insurance programs.

This classification (narrow social insurance vs. labor insurance, together forming broad social insurance) is the standard way Japanese companies organize statutory insurance obligations for employees.

Japanese social insurance (社会保険) systems compared include health insurance (健康保険 / 協会けんぽ), long-term care insurance (介護保険), and workers' accident compensation insurance (労災保険), each with distinct purposes, premium rates split between company and individual, and collection/payment methods.
Health insurance (協会けんぽ, Tokyo example): purpose is medical security; premium rate approximately 9.15% each for company and individual; collected and paid the following month (翌月納付).
Long-term care insurance (介護保険) applies only to persons aged 40 and above; premium rates around 0.95% (company) and 0.6% (individual) in the comparison; tied to medical security.

Workers' accident compensation insurance (労災保険) provides coverage for accidents occurring during work (労働中の事故への保障); generally company-borne; uses lump-sum payment method (一括納付方式) for certain businesses; rates vary by industry (e.g., general businesses vs. other businesses, with figures such as 16.19% / 15.54% appearing in the comparison).
Premium rates and burdens differ by insurance type: some are split equally between company and employee, others are employer-only; calculation and collection methods (翌月納付 vs. 一括納付) also differ.
The comparison table covers purpose (目的), premium rates (保険料率), collection/payment (徴収納付), company vs. individual shares, and key differences among the insurances.

To understand social insurance, first memorize the content and purpose of each insurance type, then start by comparing differences in how premiums are determined and their rates, as well as how premiums are collected and paid.
Social insurance in the narrow sense (社会保険 (狭義)) uses the concept of standard monthly remuneration (標準報酬月額) to determine premiums.
Formula: Social insurance premium = Standard monthly remuneration × Insurance premium rate (社会保険料 = 標準報酬月額 × 保険料率).
Standard monthly remuneration is divided into grades (等級).
Insurance premiums are split equally between labor and management (労使で折半); this must be noted.

Example: For a 45-year-old mid-career hire whose contracted salary at joining is 205,000 yen, the remuneration monthly amount falls in the 195,000–210,000 yen range, so the standard monthly remuneration is set at 200,000 yen. Employees' pension insurance is grade 14; health insurance / long-term care insurance is grade 17.
Premium calculation in the example: Employees' pension = 200,000 yen × 18.3% = 36,600 yen; Health insurance / long-term care insurance = 200,000 yen × 11.58% = 23,160 yen.
Japanese social insurance premiums for health insurance (健康保険) and employees' pension insurance (厚生年金保険) are calculated from a standard monthly remuneration (標準報酬月額) grade table.
Example rates for Tokyo Association Kenpo (全国健康保険協会管掌健康保険 / 協会けんぽ): 9.98% when the insured is not a Category 2 long-term care insurance (介護保険第2号) person, and 11.58% when they are.
Employees' pension insurance rate shown is 18.300% (excluding members of employees' pension funds / 厚生年金基金加入員を除く).
Premiums are generally split equally between employer and employee (折半); tables list both the full amount and the half (employee/employer) amount for each remuneration grade.
The page presents a worked example table of yen amounts corresponding to successive standard remuneration bands (starting from the 63,000-yen grade upward).
Labor insurance (労働保険) premiums are noted as having a separate calculation method.

Labor insurance (労働保険) premiums for employment insurance (雇用保険) and workers' accident compensation insurance (労災保険) are calculated using April through the following March as the computation period: sum total wages for that period, then multiply by the applicable premium rate.
Formula: labor insurance premium = (total wages from April to the following March) × premium rate.
Unlike narrow-sense social insurance, which estimates premiums using 標準報酬月額 (standard monthly remuneration), labor insurance premiums are calculated from actual wages paid.
The employer–employee burden split is not 50/50 as in social insurance; it follows industry-specific rates.
Employment insurance (general businesses): employer 0.95% + employee 0.6% = 1.55% total.
Workers' accident compensation insurance (other businesses): employer 0.3% (borne entirely by the company in the example given).
Both employment-insurance and workers'-compensation premium rates are set by industry; companies must enter the rate that matches their industry into the payroll system.
Premium rates are revised each year and should be checked regularly; they are published on the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働省) website.
Employment-insurance rates fall into one of three industry groups: general, agriculture/forestry/fishery/sake manufacturing, or construction.
Workers'-compensation rates are determined separately for 54 industry classifications.

Social insurance standard remuneration (標準報酬) in Japan is revised periodically. The three main timings for revising 標準報酬月額 (standard monthly remuneration) are: 資格取得時決定 using 資格取得届 (determination at qualification acquisition), 定時決定 using 算定基礎届 (regular/annual determination), and 随時改定 using 月額変更届 (occasional revision when pay changes significantly).
Less frequently, there is also a revision after returning from childcare leave (育児休業明けでの改定).
定時決定 (算定基礎届) is a procedure covering all employees: the employer prepares and submits the 算定基礎届 document, which revises the 標準報酬月額 collectively for one year starting from September.
定時決定 (teiji kettei) is the annual regular determination of 標準報酬月額 (standard monthly remuneration) used for Japanese social insurance (health insurance and employees' pension).
The process uses 算定基礎届 (santei kiso todoke, Calculation Basis Notification), submitted to the 年金事務所 (Pension Office).
In principle, all employees are covered by the regular determination.

People excluded from this revision: those who left on or before June 30; those who newly acquired insured status on or after June 1; and those who became subject to 随時改定 / 月変 (ad-hoc monthly revision) in July–September.
The new standard monthly remuneration applies from the September portion (October payment).
The calculation uses wages actually paid in April–June, based on the month of payment—not the month the wages were earned.
Months in which payment-eligible days are fewer than 17 are excluded from the April–June average.

随時改定 (ad-hoc/occasional revision) is a Japanese social-insurance procedure that changes an employee's 標準報酬月額 (standard monthly remuneration) mid-period. It applies only to people whose 固定的賃金 (fixed wages) have changed, and is done by preparing and submitting a 月額変更届 (monthly amount change notification).
The 月額変更届 is submitted to the 年金事務所 (Japan Pension Service office).
Submit the notification promptly once all of the following conditions are met.

All three conditions must be satisfied for 随時改定: (1) 固定的賃金 fluctuated because of a raise (昇給) or reduction (降給) etc.; (2) the 標準報酬月額 calculated from average remuneration over the three months starting from the fluctuation month differs by two grades or more from the previous 標準報酬月額; (3) each of those three months has 支払基礎日数 (payment-base days) of 17 days or more.
The revised 標準報酬月額 takes effect from the fourth month after the month of remuneration fluctuation.
Remuneration for the three-month average is calculated by the month in which it was paid (支払った月), not the month in which it was earned/occurred (発生月).
When calculating 標準報酬月額 (standard monthly remuneration) for Japanese social insurance, both 定時決定 (regular determination) and 随時改定 (occasional revision) use the average of 3 months of remuneration.

Items included in 報酬 (remuneration) for 標準報酬月額: 本給 (base salary), 役付手当 (position allowance), 勤務地手当 (work-location allowance), 家族手当 (family allowance), 通勤手当 (commuting allowance), 住宅手当 (housing allowance), 残業手当 (overtime allowance), 現物支給 (benefits in kind), and bonuses paid 4 or more times per year.

Items not included in 報酬: bonuses paid 3 times or fewer per year (年3回以内の賞与), 退職手当 (retirement allowance), 出張旅費 (business-trip travel expenses), 解雇予告手当 (dismissal-notice allowance), and 傷病手当金 (injury/sickness benefits).
通勤手当 is treated as remuneration under social insurance even though it is commonly paid to many employees; it must not be omitted from the calculation.
Allowances paid every month are generally included in remuneration regardless of the allowance name or company-specific nature.
Actual-expense reimbursements (e.g., travel or transportation expense settlements) are business expenses, not remuneration, and are therefore excluded.
Bonuses paid 3 times or fewer per year are excluded from 標準報酬月額; when such bonuses are paid, separate documentation must be submitted and social-insurance premiums paid on them.

In Japanese social insurance (社会保険), premiums also apply to bonuses (賞与), not only to regular wages. When a bonus is paid, the employer must create and submit a 賞与支払届 (Bonus Payment Notification) so that the corresponding social insurance premiums can be assessed and paid.
The 賞与支払届 must be prepared and submitted within 5 days of the bonus payment date. Late or forgotten filings are a common compliance risk and should be avoided.

Typical procedure for social insurance on bonuses: submit the 賞与支払届 to the 年金事務所 (pension office) within 5 days of payment; the related social insurance premiums are then due by the end of the month following the bonus payment date.

The most important practical rule for 賞与支払届 is that the name of the payment does not matter. Any remuneration paid three times or fewer per year must be treated as a bonus and social insurance premiums must be collected on it.

Examples of payments that count as bonuses for social insurance even if not labeled “bonus”: referral (リファラル) allowances paid to an employee who introduced a new hire; sign-up bonuses (サインアップボーナス) paid to offset a drop in the new hire’s previous annual income.
A frequent error is failing to file the 賞与支払届 and pay premiums because the company did not realize that the full amount paid to employees was remuneration subject to the bonus notification rules.

One-time bonuses (一時金), sales incentives paid for achieving half-year or one-year quotas, and merit awards for intellectual property such as patent registrations are all treated as remuneration that requires submission of a bonus payment notification (賞与支払届) and payment of social insurance premiums.

Japanese social insurance (社会保険) premium revisions follow a defined annual schedule consisting of three determination types: 随時改定 (occasional/monthly revision, also called 月変), 取得時決定 (determination at the time of insurance acquisition), and 定時決定 (periodic/regular determination).

The yearly social-insurance premium cycle is based on calculating a new average remuneration (平均報酬額 / 標準報酬月額) from three months of pay, then applying revision and subsequent premium payment; typical calendar windows run from April through October (and into the following April).

3-month average remuneration is the core input used both for regular (定時決定) and occasional (随時改定) recalculations of the standard monthly remuneration that determines the amount of social-insurance contributions.

Labor insurance (労働保険) premiums in Japan are determined and paid through a two-part mechanism: (1) payment of estimated premiums (概算保険料の納付) at the start of the fiscal year as an advance estimate of premiums expected to arise that year, and (2) payment of confirmed premiums (確定保険料の納付) after the fiscal year ends, calculating actual premiums incurred the previous year and settling any difference against the estimated amount already paid.

Both the estimated-premium and confirmed-premium calculations are performed in the same window of 6/1–7/10. Submitting the calculation documents to the Labor Bureau (労働局) and making the corresponding payment is the procedure known as the annual update (年度更新).

Labor insurance comprises two distinct programs—employment insurance (雇用保険) and workers’ accident compensation insurance (労災保険). Although their purposes differ completely, they are calculated and paid together during the annual update, so the differences in how each is computed must be understood.
雇用保険は会社と従業員の双方が負担するため、毎月の給与計算で従業員から天引き徴収する。労災保険は会社負担のみのため、給与計算の天引き項目には現れない。
会計処理では、雇用保険は「預り金」が生じる一方、労災保険は預り金が発生せず未払費用のみ生じる点が異なる。
役員は雇用保険・労災保険のいずれも対象外である。
労災保険は全従業員が対象だが、雇用保険は週労働20時間未満の従業員は含まれない。
雇用保険の対象は週労働20時間以上の従業員。昼間学生、季節的な雇用、1カ月未満の短期雇用は除く。
保険料率は令和6年度時点で、雇用保険は「一般の事業」、労災保険は「その他事業」を想定した率（雇用保険に従業員負担分0.6%、労災保険は従業員負担なし）。
労働保険は年度更新を含め、保険料の徴収・計算・納付のスケジュールで管理する。
労働保険料（労災保険・雇用保険）の全体スケジュールと1年サイクルが、4月から翌年7月にかけて図示されている。
労働保険の申告期間は毎年6月1日から7月10日である。
前年度に納付した概算保険料と実際の確定保険料の差額を精算する。
前納した概算保険料との差額処理を行い、確定納付を実施する。
当年度分の概算保険料を新たに計算・納付する。
労働保険料の政府への納付は年次申告で足り、月次での徴収対応は不要である。
労働保険料は概算（見込）と確定（実績）の2段階で管理される。
労働保険料は通常、年度更新の時期に年1回納付するのみだが、「概算保険料が40万円以上」になる場合は3回に分けて納付（分割納付）する必要がある。
分割納付時は、年度更新のように毎回書類を作成する必要はなく、労働局から納付書が届くので、届き次第納付すればよい。
労働保険を分納する際のスケジュール：計算期間4/1～7/31の納付期限は7月10日、8/1～11/30は10月31日、12/1～3/31は1月31日。土・日・祝日の場合はその翌営業日。
7月は労務担当者の繁忙期である。社会保険の定時決定（算定基礎届）と労働保険の年度更新が重なり、どちらも7/10が締切となるため。
定時決定は4～6月の報酬を支払ってから計算を始め、提出期限が7/1～7/10と非常にタイトなスケジュールであり、人数の多い会社で全社員の報酬計算を行うのは大変である。
労務担当者のもう一つの繁忙期は年末調整の時期で、特に11月後半から各種の書類チェックや計算チェックで忙しくなり、12月の給与処理に続く。

In Japanese year-end tax adjustment (nenmatsu chosei / 年末調整), labor/HR staff calculate refund amounts and, in January, submit salary payment reports (給与支払報告書) to each municipality (市区町村). This practical work is quite demanding.
Much of this year-end/January work is internal labor-affairs practice; other departments often do not know how busy this period is for HR/labor staff.
During this period, labor affairs staff process a large volume of information and field many questions, so other departments are asked to understand the workload and treat them considerately.
源泉徴収 (withholding tax) is deducted from employee salaries each month, but the withheld amount is only a monthly estimated (概算) figure and is not the same as income tax on full-year income.
Once annual income is finalized, tax must be recalculated and the difference versus amounts already withheld must be settled. This process is 年末調整 (year-end tax adjustment).
Monthly payroll withholding often collects slightly more tax than the true amount, and may not yet reflect income deductions (所得控除) such as insurance premiums (保険料).

Year-end adjustment additional/refund amount = income tax already paid each month minus the confirmed annual income tax. A positive result is a refund (還付); a negative result is additional collection (追徴).
Performing 年末調整 requires first understanding how income tax itself is calculated; income tax is obtained from a defined calculation formula.

Japanese income tax (所得税額) is calculated with the formula: 所得税額 = 課税所得 × 税率 − 税額控除額, where 課税所得 = 給与収入 − 給与所得控除 − 所得控除 (taxable income = salary/gross income minus employment income deduction minus income deductions).

Three operations are required to compute income tax: (1) determine annual salary income, i.e. face-value/gross income (年間の給与収入／額面収入); (2) calculate the employment income deduction (給与所得控除) in order to determine salary income (給与所得); (3) collect income-deduction (所得控除) information in order to determine taxable income (課税所得).
After taxable income is obtained, the applicable tax rate is applied and tax credits (税額控除) are subtracted as needed.
In Japanese year-end tax adjustment (年末調整), the following declaration forms must be completed for the relevant deduction items: 扶養控除等(異動)申告書, 保険料控除申告書, and 基礎控除申告書・配偶者控除等申告書・所得金額調整控除申告書.
The three forms correspond to specific deduction categories. Because the official names are long, they are commonly nicknamed 「マル扶」, 「マル保」, and 「基・配・所」(キ・ハイ・ショ).

Year-end adjustment example (annual figures in yen): gross salary (額面) 4,000,000; salary income deduction (給与所得控除) 1,240,000; social insurance deduction from salary 600,000; basic deduction (基礎控除) 480,000; income amount adjustment deduction (所得金額調整控除) 0; spouse deduction (配偶者控除) 380,000; dependent deductions etc. (扶養控除等) 380,000; life insurance premium deduction (生命保険料控除) 50,000; earthquake insurance premium deduction (地震保険料控除) 20,000; additional social insurance deduction 0; small-scale enterprise mutual aid etc. contribution deduction (小規模企業共済等掛金控除) 120,000.

In the example, total deductions equal 3,270,000, taxable income equals 730,000, calculated tax (算出税額) equals 36,500, amounts already withheld monthly equal 53,760, and the resulting refund is 17,260.

年末調整 (year-end tax adjustment) is the process of reconciling annual income tax on salary and bonuses against amounts already withheld monthly, using a structured calculation and specific declaration forms.
Calculation starts from 給与 & 賞与の額面 (gross salary and bonus amount, labeled ①).

Deductions subtracted from gross pay include: 給与所得控除 (salary income deduction), 社会保険料控除 (social insurance premium deduction on salary), 基礎控除 (basic deduction), 所得金額調整控除 (income amount adjustment deduction), 配偶者控除 (spouse deduction), 扶養控除等 (dependent and related deductions), 生命保険料控除 (life insurance premium deduction), 地震保険料控除 (earthquake insurance premium deduction), 社会保険料控除 (further social insurance deduction), and 小規模企業共済等掛金控除 (small-scale enterprise mutual aid and similar contribution deduction).
控除額計 (total deductions) is labeled ②; 課税所得 (taxable income) is ① − ② = ③.
算出税額 (calculated tax due) is ③ × 税率 (applicable tax rate) = ④.
毎月源泉徴収した金額 (total amount already withheld at source each month) is labeled ⑤.
年末調整の過不足額 (year-end adjustment additional payment or refund) is computed as ⑤ − ④.

Documents required to claim the various deductions include: 保険料控除申告書 (insurance premium deduction declaration form), 扶養控除等申告書 (dependent deduction etc. declaration form), 配偶者控除等申告書 (spouse deduction etc. declaration form), and 所得金額調整控除申告書 (income amount adjustment deduction declaration form).

For Japanese year-end tax adjustment (年末調整), three documents are used to claim various deductions. Because the forms are highly detailed, do not try to memorize every field; instead understand the structure of each document—where to enter which information—to avoid errors and confusion in practice.
These tax documents can be revised, so always confirm and use the latest versions. The forms discussed are the Reiwa 5 (2023) versions.
The first year-end adjustment form is the 令和5年分給与所得者の扶養控除等（異動）申告書 (Reiwa 5 Salary Income Earner’s Declaration of Dependent Deductions etc.).

Spouse deduction (配偶者控除): deduction amount of 380,000 yen. Applies to a spouse in the same household (同一生計) whose total income is 480,000 yen or less (if the spouse has salary income, 1,030,000 yen or less).

Dependent relative deduction (扶養親族控除): 380,000 yen per person. Applies to relatives in the same household; only those aged 16 and older are listed. For specific dependents (特定扶養) or elderly dependents (老人), the deduction amount is 480,000–630,000 yen.
The form also has a section for additional statuses: disabled persons (障害者), widows (寡婦), single parents (ひとり親), and working students (勤労学生).
Year-end tax adjustment (年末調整) materials include several premium-related income tax deductions that employees must report on designated forms.

生命保険料控除 (life insurance premium deduction): premiums must be classified into life insurance, 介護医療保険 (nursing-care/medical insurance), and 個人年金保険 (individual pension insurance); life insurance is further split between 新制度 (new system) and 旧制度 (old system); the maximum deduction is 120,000 yen.
地震保険料控除 (earthquake insurance premium deduction): the maximum deduction amount is 50,000 yen.

社会保険料控除 (social insurance premium deduction): only premiums paid individually by the employee are eligible; amounts already withheld by the company are excluded. Report items such as 国民健康保険 (National Health Insurance), 国民年金 (National Pension), 国民年金基金 (National Pension Fund), and 任意継続 (voluntary continuation).

小規模企業共済等掛金控除 (small-scale enterprise mutual-aid etc. contribution deduction): record contributions to 小規模企業共済 (small-scale enterprise mutual aid), 確定拠出年金 (defined-contribution pension), iDeCo, and similar plans if applicable.

Year-end tax adjustment (年末調整) in Japan uses dedicated declaration forms for salary earners, including 給与所得者の基礎控除申告書 (basic deduction declaration), 配偶者控除等申告書 (spouse deduction etc. declaration), and 所得金額調整控除申告書 (income amount adjustment deduction declaration) for Reiwa 5 (2023).

When preparing year-end adjustment materials, salary income plus other income must be entered; if total income exceeds 24 million yen (2,400万円), the standard basic deduction of 480,000 yen (48万円) is reduced according to a sliding scale.
Spouse deduction (配偶者控除等) amount is not fixed: it is determined in the range of 10,000–480,000 yen depending on both the spouse’s income and the taxpayer’s own income.

Income amount adjustment deduction (所得金額調整控除) must be entered when salary income exceeds 8.5 million yen (850万円). If the taxpayer has a specially disabled dependent or a dependent under age 23, 10 % of the excess over 8.5 million yen is deducted.
The forms and calculations apply to persons who are targets of year-end adjustment (年末調整の対象者) and constitute core back-office payroll/tax work.
Year-end tax adjustment (年末調整) in Japan is required for virtually all officers and employees, regardless of employment type (full-time, contract, part-time/arubaito, etc.).

People excluded from year-end adjustment: those whose annual salary exceeds 20 million yen (2,000万円); those with dual employment who undergo year-end adjustment at another company; those who changed jobs near year-end and will have year-end adjustment performed by the new employer.
Year-end adjustment is normally processed together with the December payroll (refunds/還付 or additional withholding/追徴).
If the December payroll cannot be completed in time or if a calculation error occurs in December, refund/additional-collection corrections can be processed in January.
To finish in time for December payroll, companies must collect the necessary year-end-adjustment information from employees starting in late October and no later than November.

Japanese corporate year-end tax adjustment (年末調整) requires dedicated schedule management around December and January payroll dates, building on monthly withholding already taken from salaries based on estimated amounts.

Employees (従) must obtain and submit deduction certificates (控除証明書) covering items such as life/medical insurance and housing loans (住宅ローン) so that year-end adjustment calculations can be performed accurately.

The labor/HR function (労) is responsible for announcing the start of year-end adjustment, calculating the adjustment amounts after employee data input, executing the actual additional payment or refund (often in a designated reserve/preliminary month), and issuing the salary payment report (給与支払報告書) together with other statutory statements (法定調書).

The overall back-office reference covers integrated processes spanning accounting, HR/payroll, legal, general affairs, management planning, and DX, of which year-end adjustment scheduling is one concrete operational workflow.

Year-end tax adjustment (年末調整) in Japanese companies requires entering and verifying a large volume of information and performing accurate calculations based on income-tax knowledge; it is difficult for a single person in charge to do everything perfectly from scratch.
Do not perform year-end adjustment on paper or spreadsheets. Use a dedicated year-end adjustment system that can data-link with the payroll calculation system.
A linked year-end adjustment system removes the need to create forms such as the Dependent Deduction etc. (Change) Declaration (扶養控除等(異動)申告書) from scratch.
Users simply follow the system's input fields and enter information item by item; the system then calculates through to the final additional tax collection (追徴) or refund result.

Information that must be entered into a year-end adjustment system includes: the employee's own personal information, dependent family members, insurance-premium details, housing-loan tax reduction (住宅ローン減税), and previous-job salary + social-insurance premiums + withholding income tax.
Year-end tax adjustment (年末調整) in Japanese back-office HR operations uses dedicated systems with input screens for employee personal data.

A typical personal-information screen captures data as of a reference date (example: 2022年1月1日時点での本人情報) including hire date (入社日), job title (肩書), prefecture, address (住所), phone number, employee name, and employee ID.
The illustrated interface is from the commercial SaaS product freee 人事労務.
Dummy example data shown: company FURR Co, employee ウエニシコウスケ, ID 001.

Year-end tax adjustment (年末調整 / nenmatsu chosei) in Japanese companies may be performed by either the accounting (経理) department or the labor/HR (労務) department; the split varies considerably by company and there is no single correct answer.
Labor/HR rationale: they already perform monthly payroll calculation, and year-end adjustment results are ultimately reflected in payroll, so it is viewed as a natural extension of that work.
Accounting rationale: they handle taxes and money, and year-end adjustment calculates income tax plus the subsequent resident tax, so it is considered part of their tax-related duties.
Both perspectives are valid when viewed through each department’s everyday role division.

General trend: as organizations grow larger, labor/HR staff more often take the lead. Key reasons include (1) the work involves highly sensitive personal information (My Number, income, address, family details) whose possession by non-HR departments creates significant risk, and (2) payroll calculation is a core, high-importance task for labor, making it impractical to isolate year-end adjustment.
In small companies with few back-office staff, accounting and labor functions are often not strictly separated; year-end adjustment is simply handled as part of daily operations.
How a company divides this work reflects the back-office department’s policies and its overall view of the business, offering a window into company-specific characteristics.
When an employee resigns in a Japanese company, multiple sequential labor/HR (労務) procedures must be completed rather than a single action.
Step 1: Receive the employee's expression of intent to resign (退職の意思を受け取る).
Step 2: Collect the formal written resignation request (退職願を預かる).
Step 3: Process remaining attendance records, unused paid leave (有給休暇), and expense reimbursements (経費精算) through the last working day.
Step 4: Recover company-issued items (貸与品) and the employee's health insurance card (保険証).
Step 5: File social insurance (社会保険) and employment insurance (雇用保険) qualification-loss procedures (資格喪失手続き).
Step 6: Delete the employee's email address and all related system accounts.
Step 7: Calculate and pay the final salary, issue the withholding tax certificate (源泉徴収票), and calculate/pay any retirement allowance (退職金).
Step 8: Prepare and send a retirement certificate (退職証明書).
Step 9: Prepare and send the resident-tax change notification (住民税の異動届出書).
Retirement-pay calculation and payment is listed as a distinct closing step in addition to the final-salary process.
Resignation intent is typically expressed by the employee to their direct supervisor; HR/labor then receives it from the supervisor or from the employee if the supervisor asked them to contact HR.
Whenever a resignation is reported, HR must check whether the resignation itself complies with the Labor Standards Act (労働基準法).
Resignation is energy-intensive for both the company and the employee, so the process should be kept as amicable and smooth as possible; this requires HR to have a firm grasp of the situation.
Confirm the employment-contract type: whether the departure is due to expiry of a fixed-term contract, resignation from indefinite-term employment, or mandatory retirement.
Japanese law imposes dismissal restrictions, so a company generally cannot unilaterally dismiss an employee.
Even fixed-term (contract) employees who have had repeated renewals and whose status is close to indefinite employment are subject to restrictions on non-renewal (雇止め).
The workplace must not forcibly try to retain the employee; workers have the legal right to resign of their own free will.
Check whether the resignation is escalating into a workplace dispute, whether handover is insufficient, or whether operations are being disrupted.
Record the reason for resignation so it can be used as feedback for future HR/labor countermeasures.
Be especially cautious if there are signs of poaching by another company or of information leakage.

When setting an employee's resignation date, consider both the advance-notice period required by the work rules (就業規則) and the time needed for business handover. Confirm whether timing is already coordinated with the field supervisor or will be finalized during the handover process.

Remaining paid annual leave (有給休暇) must be taken into account because it determines the last working day. Buying back unused paid leave is generally illegal in Japan, but an exception is recognized at resignation; buyback is possible only if the company has a buyback provision.

To avoid disputes over what was said, always receive a written resignation document. Distinguish 退職願 (resignation request): a document by which the employee 'requests' to leave and the parties proceed by mutual agreement; versus 退職届 (resignation notice): a document that 'notifies' resignation and unilaterally confirms it. Normally the document submitted in advance is 退職願, because both company and employee should complete procedures by agreement rather than one-sided notice.

While the employee completes final business handover, decide the policy for remaining attendance records and paid leave. That policy affects both the resignation date and the length of the handover period. After resignation, internal system accounts are disabled, so attendance and paid-leave processing must be completed while the person is still employed.

If the employee has outstanding expense reimbursements in the final month, process them before accounts are stopped. Because expense applications are often submitted after the monthly cutoff, both HR/labor staff and the departing employee should be reminded not to miss the application.

On an employee's last working day, all company-loaned items must be collected and returned. Typical items include entrance/ID cards (入館証), employee ID cards (社員証), loaned PCs, company mobile phones, and business cards (名刺). The exact list varies by company, so the company's own loaned-item checklist should be used for verification.
Health insurance cards (健康保険証) must be returned as well, including cards issued for dependent family members (扶養家族). This is required for subsequent social-insurance procedures.
After an employee leaves, social-insurance (社会保険) and employment-insurance (雇用保険) qualification-loss procedures (資格喪失手続) must be completed promptly.

Typical statutory filing windows mentioned for these qualification-loss filings are within 10 days counted from the day after the retirement date (or from the second day after retirement, depending on the specific form).

After the retirement date, the departing employee's email address and accounts for internal tools must be deleted or disabled without delay. Leaving accounts active can disrupt internal operations and raise the risk of information leakage.

Upon employee retirement, calculate and pay the final salary for work performed through the retirement date, send the withholding tax certificate (源泉徴収票), and calculate and pay retirement benefits (退職金).

Final-month payroll and social insurance premium collection depend on whether the employee retires on the last day of the month. Two governing rules: (1) social insurance qualification loss date = the day after the retirement date; (2) social insurance premiums are collected only through the month preceding the loss month.
Month-end retirement: collect and pay social insurance premiums for the retirement month. Retirement on any other day: do not collect or pay premiums for the retirement month.

Whether premiums are actually deducted from the final paycheck also depends on the company’s collection method (current-month vs. next-month collection) and whether the payroll closing date and payment date fall in the same calendar month. Avoid missed collection or double collection.

Example 1: October 31 retirement, next-month collection, month-end closing with payment on the 25th of the same month → deduct two months of social insurance premiums from the final salary paid on October 25.

Example 2: October 18 retirement, next-month collection, month-end closing with payment on the 25th of the following month → do not deduct social insurance premiums from the final salary paid on November 25.

If collection looks uncertain, confirm with accounting. Incorrect deduction causes the balances of accrued expenses (未払費用) and withheld amounts (預り金) to mismatch, so the amounts cannot be properly offset at payment time; accounting can therefore detect errors as well.

A retirement certificate (退職証明書) is not automatically required; the employer has a duty to issue it only when the employee requests it. No fixed format is mandated, but the document must include the required items typically found on a standard form.
A 退職証明書 (certificate of resignation/leaving) is a document in which the employer certifies that the person has left the company, typically issued on request.

Standard format/listed items for 退職証明書 include: 退職年月日 (date of leaving), 使用期間 (period of employment), 業務の種類 (type of work/duties), その事業における地位 (position in the business), wage-related information, and 退職の事由 (reason for leaving).

退職の事由 (reason for leaving) is recorded under categories: (1) 離職者の自己都合による (employee’s own convenience); (2) 定年、労働契約期間満了等による (mandatory retirement, expiration of labor contract, etc.); (3) 事業主からの働きかけによる (due to employer’s encouragement); (4) その他 (other, specified); (5) 解雇 (dismissal, specified).
Key rule on the certificate: 「尚、本人が証明を求めた項目に限って記載しています。」Only the items that the departing person actually requested to have certified are entered; other items are omitted.
The sample form is dated in the Reiwa era and is presented as a practical HR/legal template for back-office use (人事・法務).
退職金制度を作る目的は、従業員の老後の資産形成のサポートと、それにともなうモチベーション向上である。
退職金制度にはさまざまなものがあり各制度の効果も異なるため、違いをしっかり理解したうえで導入を進める。実際の導入時にはそれぞれの運用機関との契約が必要で、説明を聞いたうえで慎重に導入を進める。
確定給付企業年金（DB）：メリットは従業員が安全に低リスクで退職金や年金資産を受け取れること。デメリットは積立不足や運用失敗などによって追加負担が必要になること。
企業型DC（確定拠出年金）：メリットは従業員が自由に運用でき、企業側で追加負担が不要なこと。デメリットは従業員の運用失敗のリスクがあること。
中小企業退職金共済（中退共）：メリットは中小企業でも手軽に始められ、企業側で追加負担が不要なこと。デメリットは掛金限度額が月3万円と低めであること、退職するまで掛金拠出をし続ける必要があること。
特定退職金共済（特退共）：中退共と同様のメソッドだが、中退共と違い中小企業でなくとも加入可能。また中退共と違い、1年未満の退職でも支給される。
Under Japanese labor law there is no obligation to introduce a retirement-benefit (退職金) system; introduction is entirely at the company’s discretion.
Retirement benefits are an HR measure whose distinctive features are generating mid- to long-term employee commitment and serving as a long-horizon rather than short-term policy.

Retirement benefits are typically contrasted with short-term HR measures such as bonuses (賞与), incentives (インセンティブ) and welfare benefits (福利厚生); design should therefore balance both mid-/long-term and short-term elements.

Introduction timing depends on HR policy: if the business is still growing, retention is unstable, or short-term measures (bonuses, welfare, etc.) have not yet been introduced, it is acceptable to defer retirement-benefit introduction until a later stage.

Because retirement pay is treated as an element of “wages” (賃金), starting a system requires revision of the work rules (就業規則) and wage regulations (賃金規程), possible creation of a dedicated retirement-benefit regulation (退職金規程), and notification to the Labor Standards Inspection Office (労働基準監督署).
If a new operational agreement (運用規約) is needed, it must be drafted in consultation with the retirement-benefit management institution.
Retirement income is taxed separately (分離課税) from ordinary salary or bonus income and is therefore calculated and paid independently.
Retirement income enjoys preferential tax treatment: a large income deduction is first applied and then only one-half of the remaining amount is subject to income tax.
Resident tax (住民税) is also withheld at the same time; the resident-tax amount is 10 percent of retirement income.
退職所得の所得税及び復興特別所得税の源泉徴収税額は、退職金の額から退職所得控除額を差し引いた額に1/2を掛けて課税退職所得金額を算出し、これに所得税の税率を掛けて控除額を差し引いた残額（基準所得税額）と、基準所得税額に2.1%を掛けた復興特別所得税額を合計して求める。
課税退職所得金額 = (退職金の額 − 退職所得控除額) × 1/2。1,000円未満の端数は切り捨てる。
退職所得控除額の計算（勤続年数30年の場合）: 800万円 + 70万円 × (30年 − 20年) = 1,500万円。
計算例: 勤続30年で退職金2,500万円を受け取った場合、課税退職所得金額は (2,500万円 − 1,500万円) × 1/2 = 500万円。
同例の所得税額（基準所得税額）: 500万円 × 20% − 427,500円 = 572,500円（課税所得330万円超695万円以下の税率・控除額を適用）。
同例の所得税及び復興特別所得税の源泉徴収税額: 572,500円 + (572,500円 × 2.1%) = 584,522円。
上記に加え、住民税として50万円が特別徴収される。
この計算方法は国税庁ホームページを基に作成されている。
退職所得控除額は勤続年数に応じて算出する。勤続年数が20年以下の場合は40万円×勤続年数（最低80万円）。
勤続年数が20年を超える場合の退職所得控除額は800万円＋70万円×（勤続年数−20年）である。
退職所得の計算は（収入金額−退職所得控除額）×1/2 で行う。
退職所得に対する住民税は、市民税が退職所得×6%、県民税が退職所得×4%で計算される。
When a company pays retirement benefits (退職金), it must complete specific documents and tax filing/payment procedures with the tax office (税務署) and municipalities (市区町村).

Required document: 退職所得の申告を行う書類 (retirement income declaration form). Failure to submit it means income tax must be withheld at a flat rate of 退職金 × 20.42% instead of the preferential (normally calculated) retirement income tax.
The retirement income declaration form is often prepared by the company and confirmed by the retiree. It is not submitted to the tax office; the company retains it.

所得税徴収高計算書 (納付書) (income tax collection/withholding calculation form / payment slip) is submitted to the tax office. It is the same form used for monthly salary income-tax payments (due by the 10th of the following month). The retirement payment amount and corresponding tax must be added so that they are declared and paid together with regular payroll taxes.

退職手当等に係る市民税・県民税の内訳書 (breakdown of municipal and prefectural inhabitant taxes on retirement allowances) is prepared for the municipality. It records retirement-income information and is used to file the payment declaration.
Corporate legal affairs (企業法務) deal with the many kinds of laws surrounding a company; relevant regulations also differ by industry and business model.
Corporate legal work is broadly divided into three areas: ビジネス法務 (business legal affairs), コーポレート法務 (corporate legal affairs), and その他コンプライアンス (other compliance).

ビジネス契約書対応 (business contract handling): review contracts with counterparties that come up from front-line departments; create and provide contract templates so the front line can carry out contracting practice; manage executed contracts including renewals.
新規ビジネスへのリーガルチェック (legal check for new business): when expanding into a new business or area, investigate applicable laws and check risks.
債権管理・与信管理 (credit and receivables management): reduce counterparty default risk and ensure collection of receivables; handle recovery after bad debts arise.
知的財産権 (intellectual property): manage acquisition of trademarks, patents, and copyrights, and license agreements with other companies.
労務問題対応 (labor issues): manage compliance with the Labor Standards Act and related laws, covering issues such as illegal overtime and unfair dismissal.
Industry-specific regulation: legal also manages laws unique to each industry (example cited: 下請法 / Subcontract Act).
Legal affairs (法務) in back-office operations includes managing and operating both regular and extraordinary shareholders' meetings (株主総会) in accordance with the Companies Act (会社法).
In M&A, legal work covers designing organizational restructuring schemes, reviewing Antimonopoly Act (独占禁止法) implications, checking M&A contracts, and performing legal due diligence.
Corporate finance legal support (コーポレート・ファイナンス) focuses on the Financial Instruments and Exchange Act (金融商品取引法) for listed companies raising capital from the stock market.
Dispute and litigation response handles cases from counterparties or internal officers/employees that may escalate into disputes or lawsuits.
Governance and compliance work addresses internal-control themes such as J-SOX, the Corporate Governance Code, and ISO, including system design and implementation.

Harassment response (ハラスメント対応) includes operating consultation windows for power harassment and sexual harassment, establishing regulations, post-report handling, recurrence-prevention measures, and ensuring handling rules (取扱規程) are created and thoroughly disseminated inside the company.
Another framework for organizing legal (法務) work focuses on the time axis of legal response rather than only on types of tasks.
臨床法務 (clinical legal affairs): legal work that responds after a legal problem has already arisen, such as disputes or litigation.
予防法務 (preventive legal affairs): legal work that identifies risks in advance, before a legal problem occurs, in order to prevent the problem from arising at all.

戦略法務 (strategic legal affairs): legal involvement from an early stage of the business so that legal perspectives are combined with business perspectives and the accuracy of decision-making is improved.
Legal affairs (法務) is often perceived as rigid or strict because the legal department functions as the company's last bastion or last line of defense.
The primary role of legal affairs is to protect the company from legal risks. Overlooking issues or proceeding in an ambiguous state is not permitted in legal work.
Legal affairs serves as the 'last conscience of the company' (会社の最後の良心), fulfilling an important mission as a safety-net function and as a brake.
In recent years, 'offensive legal affairs' (攻めの法務) has become expected: legal must press the accelerator for business at the same time as applying the brake.

Example of strategic legal affairs: When a business unit is advancing a new venture, legal conducts thorough prior legal research and analysis, theoretically arms the company, and proactively designs structures and business setups that allow the business unit to accelerate safely.
Legal work requires a delicate balance of offense and defense.

Required skill ① Logical thinking: Laws fundamentally have a logical structure. In contract negotiations, one must understand the logical structure among contract clauses, check for contradictions, and compare against business realities and general law to assess appropriateness. The minimum required ability is to logically read, interpret, and rewrite written text.
Required skill ② Curiosity and pursuit of knowledge (知識への探求心) is listed as essential (page content cuts off here).
Legal affairs (法務) work is surrounded by a large number of laws and rules; laws are amended and updated every year, so one-time knowledge acquisition is insufficient.
To conduct internal legal education, understanding must be raised to a level that can be conveyed to others rather than remaining half-baked.

In the Learning Pyramid (ラーニング・ピラミッド) knowledge-retention framework, teaching or conveying knowledge to others is the deepest form of understanding and is associated with a 90% retention rate; this cannot be achieved overnight.
Intellectual curiosity (知的探求心) is therefore required of legal-affairs personnel.
Related Learning Pyramid levels referenced include demonstration, group discussion, practice through experience and training (75% retention), and lecturing/guiding others.

Legal staff do not need to memorize the vast body of laws; the more important quality is continuously maintaining intellectual curiosity, proactively investigating and analyzing new information, and communicating findings to others.

In-house legal personnel are necessary (as opposed to relying solely on external advisory lawyers) because the absence of an internal legal function leads to insufficient communication with the business front line, increased legal risk, and lower precision in business decision-making.

External lawyers typically review general clauses thoroughly but often cannot identify the issues the business actually cares about, and therefore cannot judge the balance between legal stability and profitability.

Even highly capable external lawyers tend to lack sufficient information on business-linked legal matters because they cannot maintain constant communication with the front line; they therefore lose the information contest.
The most direct way to raise the accuracy of legal judgments is smooth communication and information sharing with the business field.

A core principle of business is that risk and return are correlated (high-risk/high-return, mid-risk/mid-return, low-risk/low-return). Every transaction, scheme, or contract therefore contains a variable of how much risk and return each party will bear or enjoy.

Understanding a business model is essentially the same as understanding its risk–return balance. Without that understanding, legal review cannot grasp how the business side intends to earn returns or which risks it is willing to accept, and contracts may proceed without that balance being properly considered.

Example (SaaS model): the most important KPI is customer retention (lowering churn). Legal review should therefore check whether contracts and terms of use contain clauses that reduce cancellation risk.
Sound general common sense is also required when evaluating risk–return relationships, because people deeply immersed in a business can lose the ‘generally speaking’ perspective.
Front-line (front-office) operations that are sweating on the business front lines tend to lose the ability to think in terms of ordinary common sense (「常識的には……」).
The legal department must fulfill its function as the company's last bastion (最後の堡).
Doing so requires the ability to combine the business model with general common sense in order to examine the optimal and acceptable risk-return balance.
Business legal decision-making starts from understanding the business background of each negotiation counterpart.
That understanding then feeds into legal decision-making and judgment (法的意思決定・判断).
Corporate legal affairs (法務) involve multiple internal and external stakeholders with distinct roles in supporting business operations, compliance, and governance.
Business-front departments advance commercial activity and are the primary counterpart for legal work centered on business contracts.
External specialists (e.g., lawyers) serve as advisors on highly specialized matters such as litigation, M&A, and antitrust (独占禁止法) responses.

Government registration offices process applications when corporate registry information changes, including director appointment/resignation, head-office address change, company-name change, and capital increase/decrease.
Intellectual-property experts (trademark/patent specialists) support the full cycle of IP work: investigation and clearance, filing practice, and correspondence with the Patent Office (特許庁).
Shareholders interact with the company mainly around shareholder-meeting operations; communication style differs substantially between listed and unlisted companies.
Governance bodies prescribed by the Companies Act (officers and committees) function as internal control organs; the legal department acts as the liaison/pipe that communicates with them.

Additional public authorities that legal affairs routinely encounter include the Labor Standards Inspection Office (労働基準監督署), Fair Trade Commission (公正取引委員会), courts, stock exchanges, and the Patent Office.

A contract (契約) is an agreement between both parties (双方での合意). A common misconception is that a contract has no binding force without a written contract document (契約書); in fact, a contract as an agreement can be formed even orally.

Written contract documents are still essential in business. Business transactions involve many discussions, processes, and stakeholders, so without written confirmation of agreement both parties would feel insecure and deals would not proceed smoothly. In the event of litigation, the contract document is strong proof that an agreement existed.

Three main reasons to conclude a contract document: (1) to prevent future disputes and problems in advance; (2) to conduct transactions smoothly and safely; (3) to serve as proof of the agreement if the matter goes to court.

Business uses many types of agreement documents besides a 契約書 (contract), including 覚書 (memorandum), 合意書 (agreement document), Agreement, MOU (Memorandum of Understanding), and LOI (Letter of Intent).

The legal nature of an agreement document does not depend on its title. Sales staff sometimes suggest using a 'lighter' 覚書 instead of a 契約書, but the title itself does not determine the document's effect.

Legal staff must review and evaluate the content of any document they stamp/seal and agree to, because if both parties agree on the content, the legal effect does not change regardless of the type of document. Key statement: 「双方が合意する内容であれば、法的効果は変わらない」.
契約内容の自由 (freedom of contract content): If both parties agree, they may decide any contract content. This is a core basic rule of contracts.

In contract practice, a request such as 「民法・商法では○○という規定があるので変えてもらえますか?」 is not an assertion of a legal obligation to follow the Civil Code or Commercial Code. It is a negotiation to adjust discrepancies that would arise if the general law were applied as-is.

Freedom of contract is not unlimited. Two rules must always be observed: (1) 公序良俗に反しない (must not violate public order and morals); (2) 強行法規/強行規定には逆らえない (must not contradict mandatory provisions). Content that violates these is invalid; public order/morals and mandatory law take precedence over the contract.

Examples of contracts that become invalid: gender-discriminatory content; usurious/excessive-interest (暴利) arrangements such as 高利貸し; contracts premised on crime; contracts that are extremely one-sided and disadvantageous to one party.

Relationship of rules (from the diagram): Content contrary to 公序良俗 or 強行規定 is invalid. 任意規定 (optional/default provisions) may be freely decided or overwritten by the contract. For matters not stipulated in the contract or in optional provisions, the general provisions of 民法・商法 etc. apply. The legally binding range that both parties must observe is the valid contract area after excluding public-order and mandatory-law violations.

Business contracts come in many types; common titles include 販売基本契約書 (basic sales agreement), 秘密保持契約書 (NDA), ライセンス契約書 (license agreement), 投資契約書 (investment agreement), 業務提携契約書 (business alliance agreement), ジョイントベンチャー契約書 (joint venture agreement), and 業務委託契約書 (outsourcing/service agreement).
All contracts share common review points, plus additional points specific to each contract type.
General contract-review checklist: check whether a 契約不適合免責特約 (disclaimer of liability for non-conformity / former 瑕疵担保) exists and whether the warranty period is extremely short or long.
Check whether damages are owed even when the company itself has no negligence (自社に過失がない場合の損害賠償).
Damages clause: confirm whether liability is limited to direct damages or also covers indirect/consequential damages (機会損失 / opportunity loss) and the counterparty’s attorney fees.
Contract term: check whether the period is excessively long or short and whether automatic renewal (自動更新) applies.
Exclusivity: granting the counterparty overly broad exclusive rights can create strong future business constraints.
Termination: watch for unreasonable or one-sided termination conditions (理不尽な契約解除の条件).
Governing court / jurisdiction: a distant or overseas court sharply increases litigation burden and cost; prefer a convenient venue.
株主総会 (shareholders' meeting) is the highest decision-making organ of a Japanese 株式会社 (stock company).

In capitalism, a stock company divides ownership rights into shares held by shareholders (investors). Shareholders hold control (支配力) in proportion to the number of shares they own and exercise voting rights (議決権) to make decisions.
The shareholders' meeting is the venue where shareholders pass resolutions and make decisions on company matters.

Under the Companies Act (会社法) institutional design, companies that establish a Board of Directors (取締役会) delegate part of their decision-making authority to the board. Therefore not every matter is decided at the shareholders' meeting; only important agenda items are resolved there.

Two main types of shareholders' meetings exist: 定時株主総会 (ordinary/annual general meeting), which must be held within three months of the fiscal year-end (決算日) and always includes approval of the financial statements (決算承認) as an agenda item; and 臨時株主総会 (extraordinary general meeting), which can be convened at any time by the Board of Directors (or by the directors if the company has no board).
The ordinary shareholders' meeting is held once every year; this section focuses on how it is conducted, especially the process for approving the financial results as one of its resolution items.

The schedule from fiscal year-end (決算日) until the ordinary general meeting of shareholders (定時株主総会) varies mainly by company type: public company with a board of directors (公開会社かつ取締役会設置会社) versus non-public company without a board (非公開会社かつ取締役会非設置会社).

Two legal factors create the schedule difference: (1) the obligation to appoint auditors (監査役) under Companies Act Article 327(2) for public companies with a board, which also requires an audit report (監査報告); (2) different statutory deadlines for the notice of convocation (招集通知).

Convocation notice deadline: 2 weeks before the meeting for public companies with a board of directors; 1 week before for non-public companies without a board (and the articles of incorporation may shorten this further).

The AGM date is constrained by the tax-office filing deadline for financial statements (決算書) and the related tax return (税務申告書). The tax office will only accept financials that have already been approved by the shareholders’ meeting.
Default tax filing deadline is within 2 months of fiscal year-end; it can be extended to 3 months only if a prior extension notice is filed with the tax office.

Consequently, ordinary AGM schedules fall into two typical patterns: hold the meeting just before the 2-month tax deadline, or (when the 3-month extension is available) just before the 3-month deadline.

Public companies with a board typically use the 3-month tax-filing extension and therefore hold the AGM shortly before the 3-month mark; non-public companies without a board generally must file within 2 months and hold the AGM shortly before that 2-month deadline.

For Japanese companies with a March 31 fiscal year-end (3月決算), back-office legal procedures follow a defined schedule leading to the shareholders' meeting (株主総会), with timelines differing by company type and tax-filing deadline.
Public companies that have a board of directors (公開会社かつ取締役会設置会社) have a corporate tax filing deadline of the end of June (申告期限6月末).
Private companies that do not have a board of directors (非公開会社かつ取締役会非設置会社) have an earlier tax filing deadline of the end of May (申告期限5月末).
Fiscal year-end (決算日) is March 31 for both company types; preparation of financial statements (決算書の作成開始) typically begins the next day, April 1.
Key deliverables that must be completed before the meeting are the calculation documents / financial statements (計算書類) and the business report (事業報告).
In companies with a board, the board of directors (取締役会) must approve the calculation documents and business report and formally decide to send the convocation notice (招集通知発送の決定).
Where a statutory auditor (監査役) exists, the completed documents are submitted to the auditor, who then prepares an audit report (監査報告).
The convocation notice (招集通知) is issued after board approval, the shareholders' meeting (株主総会) is held, and the tax return (決算申告) is filed afterward.

The illustrated example places document completion around 20 May, board approval and notice decision around 21 May, notice issuance around 22 May, the meeting around 30 May, and tax filing immediately thereafter for the tighter (private-company) timeline.
株主総会 (shareholders' general meeting) is a once-a-year major event for the legal (法務) department of a company; thorough advance preparation is required.
For listed companies (上場会社), a large number of shareholders may attend, so a large venue is often reserved nearly half a year in advance.
A script/scenario (台本シナリオ) is prepared for the chairperson (議長) to read aloud on the day of the shareholders' meeting.
An anticipated Q&A collection (想定問答集) is created for expected questions from shareholders; answers are solicited from multiple functions including accounting/finance (経理), HR (人事), and legal (法務).
A full run-through rehearsal (リハーサル) is conducted before the meeting.
After both the board of directors meeting (取締役会) and the shareholders' meeting, minutes (議事録) must be prepared.
Required items in board of directors minutes (取締役会議事録) include at least the date and time of the meeting (開催日時).

Japanese Companies Act (会社法) requires specific statutory items in 取締役会議事録 (board of directors meeting minutes): venue; names and total number of attending directors (取締役) and company auditors (監査役); names of attending accounting advisors (会計参与), executive officers (執行役), accounting auditors (会計監査人), and shareholders; names of any directors with a conflict of interest (利害関係) in the agenda; name of the chairperson (議長); a statement if the meeting was a board of special directors (特別取締役による取締役会); and a statement if it was a specially convened board meeting (特別の招集にあたる取締役会).

Statutory items for 株主総会議事録 (shareholders’ meeting minutes) include: date, time, and place of the meeting; outline of the course of proceedings and their results; a summary of any opinions or statements that the Companies Act requires to be made at the meeting; names or titles of attending directors, executive officers, accounting advisors, company auditors, or accounting auditors; the chairperson’s name if one exists; and the name of the director who performed the duties of preparing the minutes.
In addition to statutory recording items, Japanese corporate practice allows optional (任意的) items in shareholders’ meeting minutes beyond what the Companies Act mandates.

Minutes must record not only who attended but also special meeting types (special-director boards and specially convened boards) and conflict-of-interest directors, so the record can show legal validity of the meeting and of resolutions.
登記簿謄本 is a document issued by the Legal Affairs Bureau (法務局) that certifies the registered matters of a corporation. Typical contents include the trade name (商号) and head office address (本店住所).

The names 登記簿謄本, 登記事項証明書, and 履歴事項全部証明書 are often used interchangeably by counterparties and financial institutions when they request proof of company registration; they refer to the same type of official document.
In practice it is sufficient to obtain a 履歴事項全部証明書 from the Legal Affairs Bureau.
登記簿謄本 specifically means a paper photocopy of the registered matters.
登記事項証明書 specifically means a certificate whose registered-matter data are stored electronically.
履歴事項全部証明書 is the certificate that also records historical changes to the registered matters going back three years.
A 履歴事項全部証明書 (Certificate of All Historical Matters) is an official Japanese corporate registry document used in back-office legal work to show a company’s registered information.

Typical fields on a 履歴事項全部証明書 include 会社法人等番号 (corporate/legal entity number), 商号 (trade name), 本店 (head office), 公告をする方法 (method of public notice), 会社成立の年月日 (date of incorporation), 目的 (business purpose), and 発行可能株式総数 (total number of authorized shares).
The certificate is issued with the company’s registered address (example shown: 東京都世田谷区) and is a core document for confirming corporate identity, history, and legal status.

When registered company matters (登記事項) change—such as officer (役員) changes or other items decided at a shareholders’ meeting (株主総会)—a registration change (登記変更) must be filed with the Legal Affairs Bureau (法務局).
The statutory deadline for filing a registration change is generally two weeks from the date the change occurred.

To apply, prepare a registration change application form (登記変更申請書), attach supporting documents including shareholders’ meeting minutes (株主総会議事録) and a shareholder list (株主リスト), and submit them to the Legal Affairs Bureau. Forms are downloadable from the Legal Affairs Bureau website.
Registration changes require payment of registration and license tax (登録免許税) and revenue stamps (収入印紙).
For an increase in capital, the registration and license tax is calculated as the amount of the capital increase × 7/1,000.
A tax amount of 60,000 yen is indicated for matters outside the competent jurisdiction (管轄外).
After the application is submitted, processing typically completes in about 1–2 weeks, depending on congestion at the Legal Affairs Bureau.
Once registration is complete, a new certificate of registered matters (登記事項証明書 / 登記簿謄本) is issued.

与信管理 (credit management) is the practice of managing whether receivables from business partners can be collected, because selling goods or services is often done on 掛売り (credit sales), which delays payment (e.g. to the following month) and is equivalent in business terms to making a loan.

Granting credit sales is a 与信行為 (credit-granting act): the company is extending credit (trust) to the counterparty. If the counterparty’s cash flow deteriorates and it goes bankrupt, the outstanding 掛売り債権 (trade receivables) may never be collected and become 貸倒れ (bad debt).
Concretely, 与信管理 consists of setting a 与信限度額 (credit limit) for each business partner. The credit limit is the maximum amount that may be sold on credit to that partner.

The credit limit is set by comprehensive judgment that takes into account: maximum transaction amount and maximum receivable amount; the partner’s financial creditworthiness and bankruptcy probability; the sales side’s risk tolerance; and the company’s strategic policy.
Credit investigation (信用調査) of counterparties is performed as part of the process of establishing these credit limits.
When a trading partner with unrecovered credit-sale receivables (掛売り債権) goes bankrupt, several methods exist for recovering the claims (債権回収対応).

Offset (相殺処理): If mutual transactions exist so that a debt to the partner is also present, consider set-off of the claim against the debt. The claim’s due date must have arrived. If the contract contains an acceleration clause (期限の利益喪失条項) that causes the payment deadline to fall due upon bankruptcy, set-off against the debt owed to the partner becomes possible.

Goods repossession (商品の引き上げ): Taking back goods that were sold cancels the occurrence of the receivable itself. However, once legal reorganization (法的整理) is under way, an asset-preservation order (資産の保全処分) may already have been issued, making repossession difficult.
Relevant factors in such situations include the company’s own financial strength and fundraising capacity, as well as the presence or absence of collateral.
知的財産権 (intellectual property rights) are exclusive monopoly rights granted to protect ideas, creations, and similar outputs produced by human intellectual creative activity.
Main types of Japanese IP rights (definitions excerpted from the Japan Patent Office / 特許庁): patents, utility models, design rights (意匠権), trademarks, and copyright (著作権).
Patents protect inventions that utilize natural laws and are novel and highly advanced. Example: inventions relating to speeding up communications or mobile-phone communication methods.
Utility-model rights protect the shape, structure, or combination of an article. Example: the shape of a smartphone cover that can be attached to a belt to improve portability.
Design rights (意匠権) protect original, aesthetically pleasing designs of articles (shape, pattern, color, etc.). Example: a smartphone design featuring beautiful, easy-to-grip curved surfaces.

Trademark rights protect marks (letters, figures, etc.) used to distinguish goods or services. Example: a mark a telephone manufacturer displays on its products to distinguish them from other companies’ products.
Copyright (著作権) protects copyrighted works—creative expressions of thoughts or feelings. Examples: novels, music, paintings, maps, anime, manga, movies, and photographs.
Intellectual property rights (知的財産権) are frequently positioned as a source of competitive advantage in corporate activities and constitute one of the important rights a company holds.
In manufacturing and licensing businesses, a specialized intellectual-property department is often established and operated separately from the back-office functions.
Back-office personnel are not ordinarily expected to master every detail of IP law, but they should understand the typical IP issues that arise in day-to-day operations.
Joint research and development with other companies is increasing because it shortens R&D schedules and makes more efficient use of research resources.
When companies collaborate on R&D, ownership (帰属) of the resulting intellectual property frequently becomes a point of contention.
Results of joint development are generally treated as joint inventions (共同発明).

Under Japanese law a co-owner of a joint invention may not exploit the invention independently without the consent of the other co-owners; this restriction can be severe if a party later wishes to use the technology in a different business.
The legal treatment of licenses and exploitation rights for jointly owned inventions differs from country to country, so extra care is required in cross-border collaborations.
Ideally, the allocation of IP rights should reflect each party’s contribution, share of research-cost burden, degree of risk-taking, and the value of any background patents already held.
In practice it is often extremely difficult, both operationally and in negotiations, to determine such allocations objectively.
Therefore a company should, in advance, consider the ultimate commercial exit for the technology and decide the rights-attribution outcome it can accept.
Any company engaged in development activity should actively obtain and manage patent rights.
Patent applications are typically prepared and prosecuted with the assistance of a patent attorney (弁理士), yet back-office staff still need a working knowledge of the basic rules of patent law.
Not every invention is eligible for patent protection. For patent rights to be recognized as an 'invention' (発明), four requirements must be satisfied.
Requirement: the subject must be a creation (創作であること). Mere discoveries of natural objects or natural phenomena (天然物や自然現象の発見) are not recognized as inventions.
Requirement: the subject must be of a high/advanced level (高度のものであること). Simple contrivances (考案) that fall under utility model rights (実用新案権) are not treated as patentable inventions.
