Human-made arrangements such as sports rules (e.g. football rules) are not patentable inventions.
A patentable invention must have novelty (新規性): it must be new, i.e. an invention that is not publicly known. The principle is that an invention already released to the world cannot obtain a patent.
Novelty is lost (新規性が喪失) in cases such as: the invention is already being sold on the market, or it is being viewed by an unspecified large number of people.
Novelty of an invention is lost if it has already been disclosed, including publication in lectures or academic conferences and publication on the internet.

Japan has an exception provision called 新規性喪失の例外 (exception to loss of novelty): if procedures to apply the exception are completed within one year from the date novelty was lost due to disclosure, patent rights can still be obtained.
The novelty-loss exception is useful when a product or service is launched to market first and the patent application is delayed.
A patent application requires submitting a 明細書 (specification) to the 特許庁 (Japan Patent Office).
If a company lacks in-house intellectual-property know-how, drafting the specification is commonly outsourced to a 弁理士 (patent attorney).

Even when outsourcing, the applicant is interviewed on points such as the effect of the invention, the problem to be solved, and industrial applicability, so the overall structure of a specification should be understood.
The structure of a Japanese patent specification is set out in Patent Law Enforcement Regulations Articles 24–25 and can be compared to a research report.

Specification sections (with research-report analogues): 発明の名称 (title of the invention) ≈ research title; 技術分野 (technical field); 背景技術 (background art); 発明が解決しようとする課題 (problem to be solved) ≈ research theme; 課題を解決するための手段 (means for solving the problem); 発明の効果 (effects of the invention); 図面の簡単な説明 (brief description of drawings); 発明を実施するための形態 (mode for carrying out the invention) ≈ experimental data; 産業上の利用可能性 (industrial applicability); 特許請求の範囲 (claims); 要約書 (abstract).
職務発明 (employee invention) is an invention created by officers and employees (役職員) in the course of their work duties.
Default legal rule: if there is no prior agreement, rights to a 職務発明 belong to the natural person (the officer/employee inventor), not automatically to the company.
If invention rights vest in the individual, the company cannot freely use them for business, so companies normally include assignment of employee inventions in work rules or contracts.

The agreement document differs by status: officers (役員) — conclude a memorandum (覚書) on assignment of employee inventions; employees (従業員) — specify 職務発明規程 (employee invention regulations) in the 就業規則 (work rules); contractors (業務委託) — specify intellectual-property-rights assignment provisions.

Assigning rights to the company is not enough: the company must also pay reasonable 発明報酬 (invention compensation) as consideration, and both assignment and compensation should be set out in the 職務発明規程.
Compliance (コンプライアンス) has become a widely recognized term in corporate management; it was previously translated mainly as 'observance of laws and regulations' (法令等の遵守).
In the modern view, companies are expected not only to comply with laws but also to fulfill Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) as social entities.

Compliance management (コンプライアンス経営) means operating with high ethics and morals, building proper internal organizational systems, maintaining a self-cleansing function (自浄作用), and contributing to a sustainable society represented by ESG and SDGs.
In a broader sense, compliance encompasses legal observance plus the development of internal control systems and social contribution activities.
This discussion appears in the legal-affairs (法務) section covering compliance and harassment countermeasures, reflecting the rising importance of compliance-oriented management.
Compliance (コンプライアンス) is a broader concept than mere legal compliance (法令遵守).
Legal compliance covers laws, government ordinances, and similar statutes (法律・政令など).
Internal company norms (社内規範) form part of compliance and include items such as employment regulations (就業規則).
Social norms (社会規範) form part of compliance and include social common sense (社会常識など).
CSR (corporate social responsibility) and related expectations also fall within the concept of compliance.

The diagram on the page layers or relates these elements (legal rules, internal rules, social norms, CSR) as components of a unified compliance concept in back-office and corporate management contexts.
Compliance begins with the prevention of scandals and misconduct (不祥事). Understanding misconduct starts from examining the mechanism of why fraud (不正) occurs.

Donald Cressey's Fraud Triangle Theory (不正のトライアングル理論) states that fraud occurs when three elements are present together: (1) Motivation/Pressure (動機・プレッシャー) — a psychological trigger such as excessive quotas or financial need; (2) Opportunity (機会) — an environment in which fraud can be committed, such as the absence of internal checks; (3) Attitude/Rationalization (姿勢・正当化) — a lack of ethics that would otherwise restrain the person, e.g. 'someone else is doing it, so I can too.'

Among the three fraud-triangle elements, Motivation/Pressure and Attitude/Rationalization are influenced by individual human qualities, whereas Opportunity is influenced by the internal control system (内部統制).

Internal control (内部統制) is defined as 'a mechanism for management to operate the company efficiently and soundly' (経営者が会社を効率的かつ健全に運営するための仕組み). From a fraud-prevention standpoint, its construction was made mandatory after 2006.
Building internal control requires a system and processes that incorporate six basic elements. The first of these basic elements is the Control Environment (統制環境).

Internal control frameworks commonly include these elements: (2) risk assessment and response, (3) control activities, (4) information and communication, (5) monitoring (surveillance activities), and (6) response to IT (information technology). Building a new internal-control system is typically a company-wide project.

Internal control has inherent limitations. It may fail in cases such as management override (経営者自らによる内部統制の無視), collusion among multiple staff (複数担当者による共謀), and cost-effectiveness constraints on control functions (費用対効果による統制機能の限界). In those situations, fraud risk remains.

Controls alone are insufficient. Officers and employees must raise their own ethics and integrity, and the organization must use self-cleansing mechanisms so that the fraud-triangle factors of motive/pressure (動機・プレッシャー) and attitude/rationalization (姿勢・正当化) are not created.

An internal whistleblowing (hotline) system (内部通報制度) is a compliance, fraud-prevention, and risk-management measure. It strengthens the company’s self-purification function and can contribute to higher corporate value.
A Deloitte Tohmatsu Financial Advisory survey, 「企業の不正リスク実態調査」(2016), found that the most common route by which fraud was discovered was internal reporting (25%), higher than internal audit (20%).
Because internal control cannot reliably stop management fraud, running a whistleblowing system in parallel makes risk management more effective.
From June 2022, the amended Whistleblower Protection Act (公益通報者保護法) requires businesses with more than 300 employees to establish the systems needed to respond appropriately to internal reports.
Harassment countermeasures are legally mandated for companies under various statutes that define the required measures.

Japanese workplace harassment types and governing laws: power harassment (パワーハラスメント / パワハラ) under the Power Harassment Prevention Law (パワハラ防止法); sexual harassment (セクシャルハラスメント / セクハラ) under the Equal Employment Opportunity Act (男女雇用機会均等法); maternity harassment (マタニティハラスメント / マタハラ) related to pregnancy, childbirth, and childcare leave under both the Equal Employment Opportunity Act and the Childcare and Family Care Leave Act (育児・介護休業法).
For all harassment types the basic company policy is the same: companies must design and operate rules and regulations (ルール・規程) as required harassment countermeasures.
Required company measures include establishing a consultation window (相談窓口の設置) and a system with assigned staff and responsible persons (担当者および責任者の設置).
When harassment occurs, fact-finding requires hearings from related parties (関係者への事情聴取) to grasp the facts.

Rapid response obligations include privacy protection (プライバシーの保護), disciplinary action against the perpetrator (行為者の処分), and measures to improve the victim’s working conditions and workplace environment (被害者の労働条件・職場環境の改善).
Possible disciplinary responses include disciplinary dismissal (懲戒解雇), recommended resignation (諭旨解雇), demotion (降格), work suspension (出勤停止), pay cut (減給), and reprimand (けん責).
Recurrence prevention requires analysis of the cause of occurrence (発生原因の分析), re-thorough communication of prevention regulations (防止規程の周知再徹底), and implementation of training (研修などの実施).
Companies must also define the types of power harassment, sexual harassment, and harassment concerning pregnancy, childbirth, and childcare leave.
具体的なハラスメント防止規程については、厚生労働省によるひな型が公開されているので、それを参考にする。

総務 (soumu / general affairs) literally means performing a company's comprehensive, general operations; it is often called a '何でも屋' (jack-of-all-trades) because its scope is broad, yet formally defining the job of 総務 is actually difficult.

Typical core duties that 総務 handles proactively include: 社内備品・資産管理 (internal supplies and asset management), 固定資産管理 (fixed-asset management), 情報システムツール・アカウント管理 (IT tools and account management), オフィス美化・環境づくり (office beautification and workplace-environment creation), 保険管理 (insurance administration), 社内イベント企画 (internal event planning), 来客・電話・メール対応 (visitor, phone and email handling), オフィス管理 (office administration), 労働組合対応 (labor-union liaison), お歳暮・暑中見舞い・贈答品 (seasonal gifts and courtesy items), 社宅管理 (company housing management), and 会社パンフレット・ホームページ作成 (company brochure and website production).
This material appears in a Japanese practical handbook covering the full range of back-office functions (経理, 人事, 法務, 総務, 経営企画 and DX).
総務（general affairs）業務は多岐に見えるが、集約すると2つの役割に分けられる：(1) コミュニケーションセンターとしてカルチャー醸成、(2) メンバーが安全・安心に仕事ができる環境づくり。
総務の仕事の一つは社内外にわたるコミュニケーションである。対外的には来客対応、電話対応、贈答品対応などで取引先とのコミュニケーションを円滑化する。対内的には納会・忘年会などの社内イベントにより社内コミュニケーション活性化を目指す。
総務はコミュニケーションセンターとして機能する業務が求められる。納会などの社内イベントは「たかが納会、されど納会」であり、参加前は面倒に感じても実際に参加すると楽しかったという経験が多い。
組織のカルチャーや働くモチベーションは、何でもない活動から徐々に醸成されていく。一つひとつの地道なコミュニケーション活動から、会社・組織・チームで働くことの楽しさや意義を感じ、モチベーションにつながる。
コロナ禍を経てリモートワークなど出社が必須ではない業務環境が整備されつつある今日こそ、コミュニケーションの重要性が一層増している。
リモートワーク推進により業務効率化は可能だが、一方で孤独感によるうつ病などのリスクが高まることが指摘されている。またITツールに不慣れなため取り残される社員が出てしまうこともある。
このような時代背景において、総務はオンラインとオフラインのコミュニケーション環境を設計することで、社員のモチベーションに影響を与える重要な役割を担っている。

Creating a workplace environment is one of the core duties of the General Affairs (総務) department. Various workplace stresses undermine productivity, including messy and unorganized offices, interruptions from visitors and phone calls, missing loaned items, and accidents or disasters.

Negative productivity factors that are manageable by individuals in a small company become large company-wide inefficiencies as the organization scales to dozens or hundreds of people. General Affairs must therefore match office, equipment, supplies, and IT environments to the organization’s size and growth phase, systematize operations, and pursue overall optimization with a sense of balance.

General Affairs (総務) is characterized as “the back office of the back office” (バックオフィスのなかのバックオフィス). While functions such as accounting/finance and HR/labor handle company-wide common tasks that front-line departments do not, General Affairs typically covers the remaining gaps and the common tasks of the entire back-office function.

The most appropriate image for General Affairs is “the company’s mom and dad” (会社のお母さん・お父さん): an existence that fills in what is missing when needed and watches over the organization. This is presented as the ideal vision for the function.
For performing 総務業務 (general affairs / administrative work), three key skills and growth points are emphasized, starting with negotiation and communication ability.
Skill ①: 交渉力・コミュニケーション力 (negotiation and communication skills). People who thrive in 総務 typically have strong communication, and among those skills negotiation is especially outstanding.
Negotiation in this context is not about defeating the other party. It is the ability to work so that both sides can operate under more Win-win conditions and feel comfortable doing their work.

総務 involves frequent internal and external negotiation: ordering supplies and equipment with agents and manufacturers; coordinating with real estate companies and interior contractors during office relocations. Communication and negotiation arise in many everyday situations.
「お母さん力・お父さん力」 (mother power / father power) refers to a disposition of wanting to take care of others. People with this quality may be well suited to 総務 work.

Tendencies associated with お母さん力・お父さん力 that fit 総務: approaching someone who is in trouble; thinking “is there something I can do?” and acting; preferring to see others shine rather than oneself; being willing to spend time without reservation if it helps someone; being a behind-the-scenes supporter (縁の下の力持ち) type.

General affairs (総務) work supports the entire company and is a source of pride, but it is behind-the-scenes work that does not make the individual shine. Adopting the mindset of a professional who supports the company from the background leads to better performance.

Compared with other back-office functions, general affairs does not typically demand high specialization or deep knowledge; the core career-planning challenge is therefore how to acquire deep expertise.
A practical path to expertise is to become strong in one high-specialization back-office domain: accounting power (経理力 / money / カネ), HR power (人事力 / people / ヒト), or legal power (法務力 / law / 法律).
General-affairs careers are usually built by rotating through other back-office functions rather than remaining solely in general affairs, producing a broad generalist profile.

Money, people, and law are all essential specializations for management control; combining the generalist breadth of general affairs with depth in any one of these areas produces a recommended T-shaped (T字型) career.
T-shaped skill development for general affairs consists of a horizontal bar of broad back-office generalist skills plus a vertical bar of specialized skill in accounting, HR, or legal.
総務 (soumu / general affairs) acts as the company's window (窓口) for responding to various external organizations and agencies.
When advancing interior design for a new office contract, 総務 works with design companies as part of office setup.
The book covers all back-office operations (バックオフィス業務): accounting (経理), HR (人事), legal (法務), and general affairs (総務), including the evolution of 総務 into management planning and DX.

External parties involved with 総務 include vendors and agents that handle office supplies, consumables, and office fixed assets; when product lines are diverse, Amazon, Rakuten, and similar EC sites are used for direct purchasing alongside supplier management.

Lease and rental companies provide high-value fixed assets such as company cars, multifunction printers, and PCs; for expensive procurement, leasing or rental is considered instead of purchase from cash-flow and maintenance (保守メンテ) perspectives, and the main bank may introduce a group lease company.
Insurance agencies are used for fire insurance and third-party liability insurance; communication is almost never direct with insurers and is instead negotiated through the agency.
Real estate management companies are counterparties for new office/lease contracts and for ongoing office management after the contract.
Shareholders are counterparties for shareholder meetings and IR activities; communication style differs substantially depending on whether the company is listed or unlisted.
Business partners (取引先) are involved in seasonal gifts, year-end/New Year greetings, and New Year cards.
Inquiry content and the type of external institution determine the appropriate response method.
Facility management (ファシリティマネジメント) is the first step in creating a comfortable working environment (働きやすい環境づくり).

Office environment creation is called facility management; its scope is broad and includes office selection, office design, furniture and fixtures, OA equipment, energy management, reception, mail, and related functions.
Everything related to the office is basically treated as general-affairs (総務) work, so the goal is to keep improving the environment.

OA equipment and rental equipment are core facility-management items. Multifunction printers from makers such as Xerox or Canon are typically introduced under lease contracts; monthly cost is the unit lease fee plus usage-based counter charges for printed volume.
A choice must be made between rental and purchase. Rental usually requires sufficient volume to qualify for a corporate contract.
Required PC specifications differ by department and type of work, and models change yearly, so models should be selected in coordination with front-line departments.
For desk-work-centered roles, equipment must be prepared according to job type because it directly affects work efficiency.
Other OA items under facility management include telephones, FAX machines, shredders, and network equipment.
Office facilities for employees commonly include water dispensers that provide both cold water and hot water; refill bottles can be requested from the vendor at any time.
Vending machines may also be installed and restocked by vendors.
Companies should provide a space where employees can eat lunch on-site. Offering a company cafeteria (社食) requires a contract with an external vendor.
Consumables that are used regularly in the office should be managed through periodic inventory (棚卸) followed by ordering.
Consumable orders can be placed via EC sites such as Amazon or Rakuten Ichiba, or in bulk from specialized vendors.
There is no fixed rule for inventory and ordering frequency, but roughly once a week is a practical guideline.
When performing inventory and placing orders, create a consumables management list (消耗品の管理リスト) and fill it in completely without omissions so that details remain clear.
Book title: バックオフィス業務のすべてがわかる本 (A book that explains everything about back-office operations), covering accounting (経理), HR (人事), legal (法務), general affairs (総務), management planning (経営企画), and DX.
Example provided of an office consumables management list (オフィス消耗品の管理リストの例) used to track supplies.
The list tracks items such as A4 paper (A4用紙), copy paper (コピー用紙), B5 paper (B5用紙), and tissues (ティッシュ, 5-box packs) across weekly periods (e.g., April week 1 and week 2).
Columns typically include current inventory (在庫) and order quantity (発注数) to support restocking decisions.
Sample entries shown: A4 paper inventory of 10 with order quantity 5 (and a later figure of 12); tissues with inventory 3, order 2, and another 2.
Office relocation (オフィス移転) is treated as a major, department-wide event for General Affairs (総務), requiring coordinated effort across the team.
Growing companies must periodically search for new offices because headcount growth steadily makes existing space too cramped.

The traditional (previously mainstream) relocation method was: restore the current office to original condition (原状回復) and vacate it, then lease a new office and perform interior construction from scratch, with another move expected after several years.
Multiple alternatives to that traditional full-restore-and-rebuild cycle now exist when choosing and moving to a new office.
Candidate-site selection (オフィス候補地の考え方) is a distinct planning step in the relocation process.
When relocating an office, four main options are compared: shared office (シェアオフィス), rental office (レンタルオフィス), furnished/used property taken over as-is (居抜き物件), and a standard leased property (通常の物件).

Shared office: use an open space or individual desk whenever desired; low initial cost (no interior, fixtures, or deposit); high mobility and flexibility; cost can rise if many people are registered; low interior freedom; fewer communication opportunities; relatively few properties.

Rental office: use a rental space with shared interior and fixtures; low initial cost (no interior, fixtures, or deposit); basic fixtures and equipment already installed; higher per-tsubo unit cost; restoration to original condition required on exit; reduced interior freedom; relatively few properties.

Furnished/used (居抜き) property: occupy with the previous tenant’s interior left in place; interior construction costs can be reduced; a good interior can be reused if conditions match; properties are relatively scarce.

Standard leased property: sign a lease and carry out interior construction before occupying; full freedom to decide interior and design; abundant property candidates; both move-in and move-out costs tend to be high.

Office relocation (オフィス移転) generates large medium- to long-term costs including rent, so accurately estimating the budget is essential when considering a move. Understand the thinking behind office budgets before proceeding with office selection.
Brokerage fees (仲介手数料) are budgeted as rent × number of months; the usual market rate is 1 month of rent.
Deposits/security (often 敷金 or 保証金) are typically budgeted as rent × months, with 10 months being a common market rate.

B工事 interior construction (防災/防水/空調 and other works affecting the entire building) is budgeted as area (tsubo) × unit price per tsubo, typically several tens of thousands of yen per tsubo. Because these works impact the whole building, the owner specifies the contractor and there is little room for negotiation.
C工事 interior construction costs are budgeted as area × tsubo unit price, with a typical market range of 100,000–300,000 yen per tsubo.
Furniture, fixtures, and related equipment costs are budgeted as area × tsubo unit price; they vary by the items chosen and by how much of the work is included in the construction contract.

Rent + common-area fees (賃料 + 共益費) are budgeted as area × tsubo unit price. For properties near stations in central Tokyo, roughly 25,000–50,000 yen per tsubo is needed. Because the amount is relatively small compared with rent, it does not require heavy emphasis during budget setting.
Restoration/reinstatement costs (原状回復費) are budgeted as area × tsubo unit price, with a typical market range of 30,000–100,000 yen per tsubo.
When planning an office relocation, set the overall budget framework in advance. Communicate this budget when negotiating with real estate agents and interior design companies.
Office interior construction is classified into A works, B works, and C works (A工事・B工事・C工事). These classifications are specified in the office lease contract and must be confirmed.
A工事 (A construction): The building owner has the right to select and decide the contractor. Typical examples include foundation work (地盤工事) and structural/body work (躯体工事).

B工事 (B construction): The building owner has the right to select and decide the contractor. Typical examples include air conditioning, fire prevention and disaster prevention work (防火防災工事), and distribution board installation (分電盤設置).
C工事 (C construction): The tenant has the right to select and decide the contractor. Typical examples include ceiling work and electrical wiring.
Before searching for candidate office locations, roughly estimate the required space (坪数 / tsubo) in addition to setting the budget.
Required office size can be estimated using: (A) total headcount × (B) required tsubo per person × (C) office utilization rate.
Required office floor area (坪数) is calculated primarily from the number of people who will use the office. Occasional business travelers generally do not need to be included if trip frequency is low.
A typical rule of thumb for office use is 2–3 tsubo per person. Providing 3 tsubo per person yields a comfortably spacious workplace.

Required area differs depending on seating type: fixed desks versus free-address (hot-desking). Organizations with remote work, frequent client-site work, or heavy travel often waste space with assigned desks, so free-address layouts are preferred.

When free-address is chosen, further multiply by expected office utilization (attendance) rate. The ratio of people absent due to remote work or travel is applied to obtain the minimum necessary space.
Worked example: a 40-person organization needing 2.5 tsubo per person with a hybrid attendance rate of about 60 % (three days per week) requires 40 × 2.5 × 60 % = 60 tsubo.
Any extra needs such as event space or additional common areas should be added to the calculated required tsubo.
Once approximate budget and size are decided, real-estate brokers are asked to introduce candidate properties. Multiple listings will appear, so evaluation criteria must be made explicit in advance.
Any property that looks promising must be physically inspected (内見) rather than judged from documents alone.
Key search axes for office locations include the characteristics of the area itself and access factors such as nearest station and rail lines.
When selecting an office property, evaluate walking time from the station, distance to clients and partners, building age and grade, and floor layout.

Internal viewing (内見) checkpoints include: exterior and entrance; common areas; elevator count, performance, and congestion; pillar positions and ceiling height; window position, brightness, and sunlight; toilet location, number, type, and cleanliness; shared break spaces; garbage storage; parking (surface vs. multi-story); neighboring tenants; and building security systems.
Once a property is chosen, consult interior contractors to decide the design. Office design embodies company culture, so it should reflect management’s priorities and the firm’s mission and vision.
Internally list desired design elements and share them with contractors; they typically respond with several perspective (パース) proposals.

BIM (Building Information Modeling) is a method of representing an actual building as a data model. Increasingly used for 3D office design, it enables digital walkthroughs and 360-degree review of interiors.
Interior construction is one of the largest costs in an office move; design proposals arrive with estimates that should be reviewed carefully and without undue compromise.
Office design can be deliberately linked to company culture so that physical spaces reinforce identity, values, and the nature of the business.

Freee Corporation (an accounting-software company) gives each conference room a concept and names rooms with accounting- and labor-related terms such as Kintaikanri (勤怠管理, attendance management) and Taishakutaishohyo (貸借対照表, balance sheet).
Using domain-specific vocabulary as room names is presented as a concrete way to embed the company’s professional culture into everyday office environments.

When signing a lease (賃貸借契約) with a real estate management company or owner, review these contract check items: whether a joint/surety guarantor (連帯保証人) is required; the rent payment schedule; the prior-notice period for mid-term cancellation (中途解約) and whether it is unnaturally long; whether a cancellation penalty (違約金) exists and its amount; whether prohibited-matter clauses are reasonable; whether interior-construction work divisions (内装工事の工事区分) are reasonable; and whether restoration-to-original-condition work divisions (原状回復の工事区分) are reasonable.

After an office relocation, many administrative procedures still arise (government filings and notices to counterparties). General affairs (総務) cannot handle them alone; coordinate with accounting/finance (経理財務), HR/labor (人事労務), legal (法務), sales (営業), and other departments.

Relocation procedures and contacts include: registration change at the Legal Affairs Bureau (法務局での登記変更); tax notifications to the tax office (税務署), prefectural tax office (都道府県税事務所), and municipalities (市区町村); labor notifications to the Labor Standards Inspection Office (労働基準監督署), Hello Work (ハローワーク), Pension Office (年金事務所), and health-insurance association (健康保険組合); notices to clients and partners (取引先や協業先); and account-information changes with financial institutions (金融機関への口座情報変更).

Companies face various risks depending on their business content, and insurance enrollment is important so employees and related parties can work with peace of mind and the company does not bear excessive risk.

In manufacturing or construction, an employee performing high-place work who falls and suffers lifelong residual disability can lead to the company being held liable for management responsibility, potentially resulting in damages of tens of millions of yen.
A fire at an operating store can damage not only the company's own equipment and fixtures but also the landlord under a lease contract.
A service business operating sports facilities may experience accidents such as injuring a customer due to incorrect guidance during customer service.
Such risks can cause significant harm to related parties and can also affect the company's business activities and even its continued existence.
Representative types of insurance should be considered for these operational risks (specific types listed as following on the page).
Main types of insurance that companies typically join include third-party liability insurance (第三者賠償責任保険), property/fire insurance (損害保険・火災保険), and work-related accident insurance (業務災害保険).
Third-party liability insurance covers compensation claims from general consumers and corporate customers arising from operations in personal-service industries, construction sites, and factory work.

Property and fire insurance covers the company's own real estate and equipment; when premises are leased (tenant contracts), it also covers the owner's property. Coverage commonly extends beyond fire to water damage, typhoons, lightning, and similar perils.

Work-related accident insurance (業務災害保険) compensates employees for on-the-job injuries, hospitalization, death, and disability; it functions as a supplement (上乗せ) to statutory workers' compensation insurance (労災保険).

Instead of separate policies, companies may purchase a comprehensive insurance package (総合保険) that covers overall business-activity risks in a single contract. Premiums under this arrangement typically vary in proportion to business scale (e.g., sales revenue).
Because insurance exists to cover unforeseen risks, the possible scope of coverage is theoretically unlimited. Unnecessarily expanding the coverage range simply increases premium costs.
A primary factor that determines insurance premiums is the breadth of the coverage (保障範囲) that is selected.

Corporate insurance premiums and coverage should be evaluated using insurance payout amount, total value of assets under coverage, and accident occurrence probability, which also varies with business size (sales or headcount).
Premiums change according to sales and asset scale, and are revised every year based on nationwide disaster occurrence rates and insurers' claims-payout experience.
When selecting insurance, match the scope of cover to company size and the relative importance of the risks the business faces.
Prioritize cover for risks that could harm third parties over purely internal losses (e.g., fire insurance on own facilities may be optional, but cover for owner-owned property should be mandatory).
Prioritize policies for non-monetary risks such as reputation risk that cannot be resolved with money alone.
Review and adjust contract terms every year with the agency so coverage stays aligned with current business conditions.
Company-wide events (全社イベント) handled by General Affairs (総務) are not mere social gatherings; they are opportunities to strengthen employee unity and raise motivation by embedding purposeful programs.

Employee award ceremonies at company events can recognize special results or contributions separately from bonuses, raises, or promotions, allowing flexible praise of people who embody company values rather than only daily performance metrics.

When a company newly creates or revises its Mission, Vision, and Values (ミッション・ビジョン・バリュー), sharing them—including the creation process—at an all-hands gathering accelerates permeation as the company’s most important guiding principles.
New Year, year-end, and other company milestones are effective times to re-announce business plans and clarify goals so that the entire organization’s business vector is aligned.
Personnel-system revisions or organizational changes can be explained carefully at company-wide events to aid understanding and acceptance.

When the company faces many issues, company events can include workshops in which every employee proposes internal improvements; the operating principle is never to deny any individual’s opinion and to cultivate a free, open atmosphere.
General Affairs typically serves as organizer (幹事) for regularly held company-wide events such as all-hands meetings and year-end parties (納会).
When advancing a company-wide event, do not start acting immediately; first drop at least the key items into a written plan (企画書).
Always decide the purpose of the event before proceeding.
For company-wide events, begin coordination at least one month in advance.
Decide the venue: rent an external conference room, use an internal large conference room, or rent a hotel party venue. Venue choice is important because it determines the event atmosphere.
Decide the duration: full day, half day, or several hours.
Incorporate content from prior charts/diagrams into the plan. Always decide after consulting management. It is recommended to prepare a social gathering (懇親の場) at the end of the event.
Involve general affairs (総務) and other departments; create a schedule and task list and clearly assign a responsible person for each task.
Avoid collecting money from individuals as much as possible; budget the event as a company expense under welfare costs (福利厚生費). Decide a per-person budget and allocate the total amount.

Phone and reception handling in offices is increasingly done by whoever notices rather than designated staff, but general affairs (総務) staff still handle it most often; treat it as core work, not extra, and stay faithful to basics with polite, careful execution.
Poor basic professional communication during phone or reception contact can damage the company image; staff must at least know the minimum customer-facing rules.

Phone handling basics: answer within 3 rings; if it rang longer, add “お待たせいたしました” (sorry to have kept you waiting); state company name and your own name; note the caller’s company name and personal name; listen to the matter and take notes; transfer to the internal person in charge when appropriate; if that person is absent, say you will check and call back.
Reception handling basics: at the entrance confirm the visitor’s company name, personal name, and appointment purpose; if the visit is for a meeting, escort them to the meeting room.
These practices come from a comprehensive Japanese guide to back-office operations covering accounting, HR, legal, general affairs, management planning, and DX.
When interacting with people outside the company, staff must maintain awareness of themselves as the 'face of the company' (会社の顔).
Always respond with a smile and polite, courteous language (丁寧な言葉遣い).
Greet and welcome visitors in a clean, neat appearance (清潔な格好).
Look up, make eye contact, and speak clearly and distinctly.
When informing customers of the names of internal personnel, do not attach honorifics (敬称) even if the person is a superior.
Telephone answering and reception, traditionally representative tasks of general affairs (総務), can now be handled via cloud services due to technology, so dedicated staff are not always required.

Although some may criticize digital handling as lacking warmth, it provides an opportunity to communicate DX (digital transformation) efforts to customers and frees time for other work; active consideration of such tools is recommended.
Cloud PBX services offer inexpensive telephone systems that include all necessary functions such as call forwarding and directories.
Unlike older IP telephony limited to 050 numbers, current cloud PBX can obtain standard area-code numbers (e.g., 03 for Tokyo 23 wards) with the same usability as conventional phones.
Calls can ring simultaneously on office handsets and personal smartphones.

Introduction and operating costs of cloud PBX are comparable to existing landline systems; IVR (automated interactive voice response) functionality is included and can also support consumer call-center operations.

Reception can likewise be IT-enabled using terminals such as iPads so that staff need not sit at a physical window; cloud services that lend customer-operated terminals are available and should be actively considered.
Cloud PBX (クラウドPBX) is a telephony service that lets an organization share internal extensions (内線) and external lines (外線) over the Internet, including from locations outside the physical office.

Typical endpoints that can join a Cloud PBX include office smartphones, fixed landline phones (固定電話), and tablets; all of them connect through the Internet rather than traditional on-premises PBX hardware.
The same Cloud PBX can also interconnect multiple offices so that staff at a different site use the same shared extension and external-line pool.
Because the service is Internet-based, users can place and receive both internal and external calls even when they are not physically in the office.
Japanese corporate general-affairs (総務) practice includes seasonal gift-giving (ochugen in summer and oseibo at year-end) because it strongly smooths business and interpersonal relationships.
Robert B. Cialdini’s principle of reciprocity (返報性の原理) underpins this custom: people instinctively try to repay a received favor or gift with something of greater value.
Whether the recipient actually wanted the item is irrelevant; the obligation to reciprocate still arises.
Even if the giver previously made a negative or neutral impression, receiving a gift typically converts that impression into a positive one.
Because gifts can indirectly influence sales and profit margins, they can be used as a deliberate business strategy rather than mere custom.

Effective gift operations require a maintained list of counterparties that includes addresses plus transaction importance, nature of the relationship, and preferences, so gifts can be budgeted and ranked accordingly.
Once ranks and budgets are set, items are selected at department stores or gift shops and shipping is processed; the gift list itself must be kept current.
Ochugen (お中元) mid-year gifts in Japanese business/general-affairs practice should arrive by July 15; gifts are typically selected in June and shipped in early July.
Oseibo (お歳暮) year-end gifts should arrive by December 20; gifts are typically selected in November and shipped in early December.
These timing rules distinguish お中元 from お歳暮 as a practical back-office (総務) task in Japanese corporate gift-giving.

In modern companies, many business-tool accounts exist across the organization (including front-line/field operations) because IT tools have become widespread and cloud services have lowered the barrier to initial adoption.
Shadow IT is a real risk: tools may be in use that the general-affairs (総務) function does not even know about.
When account and password management rules are not established, the risk of information leakage increases significantly.
A serious control failure occurs when people who have left a role (through resignation or internal transfer) can still log in to the related business tools.
Access to accounting and HR information must be strictly limited; login privileges for accounting systems and payroll systems (and similar tools) must be designed and assigned per IT system.

Key points for creating account/password management rules: (1) define rules for which tools may be used, (2) decide approval/decision-making authority, (3) set account and password management rules for each individual tool, and (4) perform periodic inventory and review of all accounts.

Dedicated account-management tools that can centrally store and manage IDs and passwords across many applications have become common; they are especially worth considering when the organization grows or employee turnover rises and account administration becomes complex.
アカウント管理ツールは、組織内の複数システム・デバイスにわたるアカウントを横断的に管理するための仕組みである。
接続・管理対象の例として、貸与PCの情報、メール・チャットなどの全社共通システム、人事系システム、スマートフォン・タブレット等の貸与デバイス情報、営業系システムが挙げられる。
管理主体として、総務・情報システムの管理者と、現場責任者側の管理者が関与する構成が示されている。
バックオフィス業務（経理・人事・法務・総務から経営企画・DXまで）の文脈で、アカウント管理はIT資産・ID・権限の統合管理の一部として位置づけられる。
経営企画 (management/corporate planning) is a core back-office function whose typical work can be summarized as a mix of strategy, finance, operations, and transformation tasks.

Typical 経営企画 jobs include: 事業計画 (business planning), M&A, KGI/KPI setting and management, 予算編成 (budget formulation), コスト合理化プロジェクト (cost-rationalization projects), ファイナンス戦略 (finance strategy), 設備投資決定 (capital-investment decisions), 事業ポートフォリオ管理 (business-portfolio management), コーポレート・ガバナンス (corporate governance), 業務フロー改善 (business-process improvement), ERP導入 (ERP implementation), DX, 特命プロジェクト (special-mission projects), CV運営, and 新規事業推進 (new-business promotion).
The source book frames 経営企画 as part of a complete back-office picture that also covers 経理 (accounting), 人事 (HR), 法務 (legal), 総務 (general affairs), and DX.
経営企画 (corporate/management planning) handles a wide variety of important themes whose content and scope are extremely broad.
The most important perspective when thinking about 経営企画 work is to deliberately not clearly define the domain of its operations (「業務の領域をあえて明確に定めない」).
For ordinary departments, clearly defined duty allocation makes work more effective and efficient; 経営企画 is the exception to this rule.

This characteristic exists because 経営企画 essentially has two connecting roles: (1) linking the various internal departments to one another, and (2) maintaining a direct connection with top management/executives.
A conceptual diagram shows 経営企画 as the hub that ties together 経理財務, 生産管理, 人事労務, 開発, 総務法務, 営業 and マーケティング, with a direct pipeline (直接的パイプ) to executives.
Work possessing two specific characteristics (those of supporting and taking on parts of executive-level work) all falls under the scope of management planning (経営企画).
The role of management planning can be restated as work that carves out a portion of the executive’s job and provides support for it.
An executive’s job cannot be clearly defined in a fixed way, because it changes according to factors such as business model, growth phase, and organizational condition.

Because the executive role itself is inherently undefined and shifting, management planning that supports executives should likewise not try to rigidly define its own work; not defining it is actually the correct approach.
As a result, people working in management planning share some common points, but the concrete content of their jobs can differ greatly from company to company (千差万別).
Because the business scope of management planning is hard to pin down, companies position the function in various ways; it can nonetheless be broadly classified into four types.
A high-level classification of management planning contrasts drive-oriented (ドライブ志向) approaches with management-oriented (管理志向) approaches, and includes a management-type (管理型) category.
Corporate planning (経営企画) roles can be classified along two axes: drive-oriented vs. management-oriented, and omnidirectional vs. limited business scope.

Drive-oriented (ドライブ志向) corporate planning proactively takes the lead, issues instructions to executives and various departments, and promotes overall management. Although final decisions rest with executives, this type advances work to a near-decision-making state and sets the stage.

Management-oriented (管理志向) corporate planning stays behind the scenes in coordination and support. It prepares materials, assists with tedious clerical work and analysis/research, and facilitates communication between departments rather than actively driving the whole organization.

When the business scope is omnidirectional (全方位型), corporate planning constantly handles company-wide themes from a broad perspective. It must understand mid- to long-term strategy, organizational design, and Mission-Vision-Values, and may even revise those company-wide guidelines as the business evolves, requiring execution in unison with executives.

When the scope is limited (限定的), corporate planning focuses narrowly and deeply on domains that tend to become company issues or debate points. It often supplements missing viewpoints or resources of departments or business units and is expected to serve as a helper or super-sub when needed.

Corporate planning (経営企画) departments can be classified into several types with distinct roles and capabilities, including an all-purpose type, a growth-phase intervention type, an analysis/staff type, and a secretariat type (事務局型).

万能型 (all-purpose/versatile type): Functions as the right-hand of top management. Members must be capable of discussing at the same level as the executive team. This type often owns mid- to long-term company strategy, including business strategy formulation, M&A execution, and investment/financing decisions.

Growth-phase / special-mission type: Provides leverage (テコ入れ) against major issues that arise in sales, marketing, manufacturing, development, and other functions at different growth stages. This role frequently involves special-mission projects and new-business work.

Analysis / fact-based staff type: Excels at numerical analysis and collecting factual information so that executives can make decisions more easily. It often demonstrates value in budgeting, mid-term management plans, KPI management, and group-company management.

事務局型 (secretariat type): Does not itself drive initiatives or necessarily hold a company-wide perspective, so it is a weak ‘right-hand of management.’ It functions instead as a secretariat that can address specific needs when required (‘scratch the itchy spots’). This pattern is common in companies that assign secretary-like duties to corporate planning.
There is no single correct or incorrect form (正解・不正解はない) for the types and involvement of management planning (経営企画) in an organization.
Management planning should be shaped around the company’s desired/ideal business model (あるべきビジネスモデル).
経営企画 should complement and fill gaps in the strengths and weaknesses (強み・弱み) of executives (経営者) and other departments (各部署).
The type of 経営企画 function and the degree of its involvement must therefore be aligned with that business model and those organizational gaps.
When deciding which operations (業務) 経営企画 should handle, a clear grasp of the company’s own strategy (自社の戦略) and organizational structure (組織把握) is indispensable.

Management accounting (管理会計) is accounting and numerical management for decision-making. It is completely different in content from the financial accounting and tax accounting mainly handled by accounting and finance departments.
Management accounting covers everything related to business decision-making and therefore has a very wide scope.

For management planning (経営企画) roles, it is highly useful to master these management accounting areas: break-even point analysis (損益分岐点分析), KPI management, budget formulation (予算編成), performance analysis (業績分析), and capital investment decision-making (設備投資意思決定).

Finance is not merely fundraising. It means considering how to raise funds, how to invest those funds, procurement methods and investment balance—i.e., designing investment fields and investment recovery, and designing the business’s value-creation cycle.
In corporate management, finance is the theory of designing both procurement and investment in order to maximize the company’s corporate value.

Finance encompasses various domains such as securities investment theory, corporate finance, and venture finance. For management planning, the recommended focus is the corporate value evaluation (企業価値評価) portion.
When considering business schemes, legal review must always be performed.

Basic items of important laws such as the Companies Act (会社法), Antimonopoly Act (独占禁止法), and Intellectual Property Law (知的財産法) should be acquired; detailed statutory text and fine rules are understood with support from the legal department.

When designing advantageous business contracts and structures, the ability to translate them into contracts while balancing return and risk is required; this is built by accumulating business sense one step at a time.
Mid-level and above management planning staff need comprehensive soft skills in addition to basic hard skills in order to earn trust from other departments and from management.
Communication-related skills for advancing decision-making are especially important; these skills are rarely acquired instantly and are often cultivated through accumulated experience.

Logical thinking (ロジカルシンキング) is the ability to correctly organize existing information and to connect given information with logic so that a coherent line of reasoning can be formed. It is a fundamental skill for collecting and analyzing information from multiple sources, selecting what is needed, and organizing it.

Important management decisions always combine dynamic choice (which only executives can make) and logic. Management planning’s minimum role is therefore to organize the logical path so that it can support management decision-making.

Project management is the ability to hold an entire project together and keep it progressing smoothly. It covers goal setting, budget management, progress management, To-Do design, organizational structure and role assignment—the factors that determine project success. The skill is essential whenever work involves departments beyond management planning itself.

Facilitation skill (ファシリテーションスキル) is the ability to activate a meeting or discussion so that it actually achieves its purpose. A meeting that does not move forward or reach decisions is a failed facilitation.

Because management planning frequently acts as secretariat or coordinator, the success of meetings is directly linked to the success of the project. During meetings the facilitator must perform fact-finding, listening, questioning, negotiation, deadline-setting, summarizing and similar actions in order to keep the discussion advancing.

経営企画 (corporate/management planning) work is driven by several key stakeholders with distinct roles: 経営陣 (executive management), 各事業部・フロントメンバー (business units and front-line staff), other back-office departments, and 株主 (shareholders).

経営陣: 経営企画業務 basically reflects the executives' 経営方針 (management policy) in decision-making. For planning members they function as de facto superiors. Work is frequently advanced in close integration with the CEO, CFO, and COO.

各事業部・フロントメンバー: They are the main actors who execute actual field operations and constantly work alongside 経営企画. Planning supports them from a company-wide, mid-to-long-term perspective that is hard to see from daily operations. Collaboration is indispensable especially when promoting 部署横断プロジェクト (cross-departmental projects).

その他バックオフィス部門 (経理財務, 人事労務, 法務, 総務): These functions support 経営企画 by supplying detailed information matched to the analysis needed—e.g., 業績数値 (performance figures) from accounting/finance, and organizational/HR performance from 人事労務.

株主: A core purpose of company management (and thus of 経営企画) is 「企業価値の最大化」 (maximizing corporate value). Growing the business and obtaining shareholder evaluation is the key to this, so understanding the needs shareholders seek is an indispensable viewpoint for planning work.
Shareholders are important stakeholders (alongside others) for maximizing corporate value and determining optimal capital structure.
In M&A situations, financial institutions and investment banks frequently introduce deals and serve as advisors, playing a key role in investment and financing strategy.

Consulting firms include strategy, general, IT, and think-tank types; they are engaged according to project characteristics, typically for know-how and resources on a per-project basis rather than continuously. Large companies may retain firms with consultants stationed similarly to internal staff.

The management planning (経営企画) function acts as the liaison/window for group company management, exchanging information and needing to grasp issues around group companies’ performance, organization, and business development.

For joint ventures, capital/business alliances, or other multi-company projects, each company’s management planning department serves as the window for collaboration and is expected to act as the company’s representative.

In M&A promotion, parties may act as advisors or investors. Funds that introduce deals or participate in investment schemes can also provide management support. When a company launches CVC (Corporate Venture Capital: a venture capital arm established by an operating company), horizontal collaboration with funds/VCs via LP (Limited Partnership) investments and deal introductions is important.

Specialists in legal, financial accounting, tax, and labor fields (lawyers, certified public accountants, etc.) are used for expert investigation and advice when verifying the feasibility of business expansion.
経営企画の本丸業務の一つは事業計画（中期経営計画）の策定である。会社によって呼び方や定義は異なるが、事業計画と中期経営計画は基本的に同じものと理解してよい。
事業計画は会社全体の中長期戦略や数値計画をまとめたものであり、会社がこれから進んでいく方針そのものである。
事業計画の最終責任は経営者にあるが、広範囲かつ大量の全社経営情報を収集する必要があるため、経営企画がサポートしながら作成していく。
事業計画の主な目的は次の4つである：(1) 経営者自身の目標の言語化・経営スキル向上、(2) 従業員に対する社内目標の明確化、(3) 融資や資金調達、(4) 株主へのIR。
経営企画としては、主に②（従業員に対する社内目標の明確化）をトリガーにして事業計画を立てることが多い。年度が始まる前や会社の重要な節目の際に作成する。

A business plan is created to clearly define goals for employees and align everyone's direction (vectors) toward the same objectives. Mid-term management plans are typically prepared on a fixed cycle of 3 or 5 years.

In practice, a business plan consists of two main parts that should not be confused: (1) a strategy-and-organization perspective that describes future plans qualitatively, and (2) a numerical/financial perspective that describes future plans quantitatively.

The strategy and organization component covers: mission and vision; market environment analysis; target market; the company's strengths and weaknesses; entry barriers and competitive advantages; sales expansion strategy; investment and financing plans; organization chart; and measures to strengthen the organization.

The financial (numerical) component typically presents a 3-to-5-year forward-looking plan using the three financial statements—Balance Sheet (B/S), Profit and Loss (P/L), and Cash Flow (C/F)—and ultimately expresses the target corporate value / enterprise valuation.

Terminology, who is responsible for creating each part, and the emphasis of each section can differ by industry and by stakeholder; therefore the two components of a business plan must not be mixed up.
A business plan (事業計画) expresses an organization's future direction and policy in both qualitative (定性面) and quantitative (定量面) terms.
Qualitative and quantitative parts of a plan must be linked and consistent; avoid mismatches in which the qualitative story is not reflected in the numbers.

「事業計画」 / 「中長期経営計画」 (business plan / mid-to-long-term management plan) is typically owned by the CEO and the head of the management planning office (経営企画室長), emphasizing a coherent story, strategy, and vision.
「予算計画」 / 「収支計画」 (budget plan / P&L plan) is typically owned by the CFO and the head of management planning, emphasizing flexible scenario-making and case splits.
Pitch slides and presentation materials (ピッチスライド / プレゼン資料) sit in a related but distinct category from formal mid-to-long-term business plans.
Vision and mission (ビジョン・ミッション) sit at the top of the planning stack that corporate / management functions must keep aligned with both qualitative narrative and quantitative plans.
Business plan creation schedules and processes differ by company size and other factors, but proceed by successively deciding a set of core elements.

Core elements of business plan creation include: setting final profit and corporate-value targets; deciding mission and vision; external-environment analysis; market analysis and market-size assessment; competitive-environment analysis; benchmark (competitor) analysis; target-market segmentation; identification of Key Success Factors (KSF); identification of strengths, weaknesses and issues; and business-portfolio analysis.
Top-down targets are set as an overarching constraint on the rest of the plan.
Internal (self) analysis covers function-by-function and business-unit analysis, organizational-capability analysis, and formulation of basic strategies by function and by business.
Plans are typically split into a one-year horizon and a three-to-five-year horizon.

Investment allocation is directed toward priority “boost” (teko-ire) areas; the investment plan is built mainly around CAPEX (capital expenditure / 設備投資) together with a corresponding funding/procurement plan.
Hiring plans are derived by working backwards from each function’s and business unit’s basic strategies and action plans; evaluation, development and talent-strengthening plans are also woven in.
P/L statements are prepared for each unit; after detailed P/Ls are completed they are linked to the company-wide B/S and C/F statements.
The resulting bottom-up figures are compared with the original top-down targets and a final adjustment is made.
Back-office work (accounting, HR, legal, general affairs, management planning, and DX) creation/scheduling timelines scale with organization size.
Organizations of several dozen people can typically complete the relevant process/document within 1 month.
Organizations of around 100 people require a minimum of 1–2 months.
Large companies of about 1,000 people or listed companies should treat it as a process requiring at least 3 months.
Schedule the work with these size-dependent durations in mind rather than assuming a uniform short timeline.
MVV (Mission, Vision, Value) is the core raison d'être of a company and the direction it should pursue; it is also relevant to personnel evaluation systems.
Mission (M): the mission the company should fulfill in society.
Vision (V): the future state or desired appearance the company aims to achieve.
Value (V): the value standards and action guidelines that the company considers important.
The three MVV elements are interrelated (typically shown as a diagram of how they connect).
MVV (Mission, Vision, Values) is connected to both the organization side and the business-strategy side of a company.
HR and organizational systems are used to set KPI targets that align with strategy.
When designing management accounting (管理会計), it is essential to first understand purposes and strategies at the management level, then build the accounting design around them.
In company management, Mission and Vision are the highest-level concepts. Companies may instead call them 経営理念 (management philosophy), 社是 (company motto), or パーパス (purpose).

Mission (ミッション) is the company's mission to society (社会に果たす使命), viewed from outside the company. Vision (ビジョン) is the desired future state (ありたい姿), viewed from inside the company. They differ mainly in viewpoint and share much in substance, so they are sometimes combined for clearer messaging to employees.

Values (バリュー) sit below Mission/Vision. They strongly express the organization's perspective: value standards and behavioral standards that show how people inside the organization should act and what they should prioritize.
人事ポリシー (HR policy) is a nearly identical concept to Values.
Values have a very strong influence on culture formation and therefore determine an organization's strength and direction.

A 事業計画 (business plan) expresses management policy on the business and strategy side. Mission/Vision state long-term ideals and goals (e.g. 5–10 years). A business plan translates those into a nearer time horizon, reflecting the actual business and competitive environment, down to concrete plans and numbers.

MVV (Mission, Vision, Values) and the business plan are referenced throughout company management and back-office work. Understanding how they relate improves ease, accuracy, and resolution of each function.

Example — Conduct Group Mission: 「コーポレートを彩り、奏でる」 (“Color and play/perform corporate”). コーポレート is a collective term for administrative/back-office departments. The mission is to realize a society in which people in these functions thrive and their value is felt across companies.

Example — Conduct Group Vision: 「いつも変革の先で待つ存在へ」 (“Become an existence that always waits ahead of transformation”). Accounting/finance, management planning, and HR/labor tend to become follow-up, after-the-fact departments; the desired state is to lie in wait ahead of growth and change and be able to propose, not merely process.

The company's Values deliberately include behaviors that back-office people tend to be weak at. Acting on Values is meant to recast work often dismissed as mere 事務作業 (clerical work) and to build a team and culture that approach the Mission/Vision.

From Values, HR and organizational systems follow: org charts and job descriptions define roles such as Client Service / Accounting Professional / HR Professional, aiming beyond a typical specialist firm that only does client work.

The author's company (Conduct Group) presents its MVV (Mission, Vision, Values) alongside its business plan as an organizational example, splitting content into an organization side and a business/strategy side.
Mission: コーポレートを、彩り、奏でる (to color and play/harmonize corporate functions).
Vision: いつも変革の先で待つ存在へ (to become an existence that always waits ahead of transformation).
Values: 1. 楽しさの追求 (pursuit of enjoyment/fun); 2. ゼロベース思考 (zero-based thinking); 3. プロフェッショナリズム (professionalism).
Client-facing roles are given broader authority, and this practice is presented as a reflection of the company's values.
Business plan / service lines are centered on management support, accounting, and HR, with a focus on latest industries and startups.
HR and organizational system covers roles and division of duties (分掌), distinguishing accounting professionals and HR professionals.
KPI targets are framed as multi-year goals such as reaching a specified number of advisory/consulting clients and a specified profit level after a given number of years.

A mission that frames the entire corporate (コーポレート全体) supports keeping service lines broad from founding rather than narrowing them, with a motto of comprehensive one-stop service rather than specialization.

Unlike the majority of small firms that expand only in a narrow domain such as accounting or HR, a group can build a service line (product strategy) covering the wide areas of accounting, HR, and management.

Targeting latest industries, startups, and ventures fits this model because those customers especially value a function that coordinates the entire corporate, creating a match with the provider’s services.
Future expansion of the service line into additional back-office areas such as legal and general affairs remains consistent and highly compatible with a “corporate” mission.
Mission and vision are fundamental concepts that even determine product lineup = competitive domain = business domain.

MVV (Mission, Vision, Values) is ultimately decided by the top manager through repeated, thorough dialogue with themselves and the management team, while also taking stakeholder expectations into account.
Corporate planning’s basic involvement in MVV is to set up opportunities for the manager to think, rather than to decide the content itself.
In an MVV creation process, corporate planning should act in a secretariat/facilitation role while involving the manager and management team throughout.

Mission, Vision, and Values (MVV) are created by combining business/organization analysis with the founder's or management's genuine intent (Why), then formalizing them into statements that may use impactful catch copy (optionally written by a copywriter).
MV must be goals that management can fully accept from the heart and that will not change for 10 years.
Start by grasping the industry's challenges, pain points, and trends, then forecast how the industry will evolve.
Identify the company's own challenges in running its business, its brand image, and its current culture (via employee interviews and daily communication).
Thoroughly extract why the leader wants to run the business (the Why).
After analysis, verbalize Mission and Vision by combining findings with the manager's thoughts.

For Values: define the talent profile of people who can thrive in the business (personality and skill requirements); also define the opposite profile of people who cannot thrive or are not valued, because contrast makes language and listing easier.
Group common traits into behavioral standards and distill them into about 3–7 items; organize them MECE (no gaps, no overlaps).
Formalize the result as an official Values statement (copywriter optional for polish).
Management accounting (管理会計) is defined as accounting and numerical management conducted for the purpose of decision-making, in contrast to the accounting work of the finance/accounting department.

The accounting used by the finance and accounting function is mainly called financial accounting (財務会計). Although both are forms of accounting, their content is entirely different; management accounting is primarily the domain of management planning (経営企画).

Financial accounting is, in principle, accounting whose rules are set by accounting standards and tax law. Management accounting, by contrast, has a very unclear domain and outline; it is no exaggeration to say that ‘if you handle numbers, everything is management accounting.’
Both management accounting and financial accounting deal with accounting figures, but they differ in many characteristics (purpose, rules, time horizon, responsible department, and required skills).

Typical contrast: financial accounting is used for settlement reporting and tax filing, has strict established rules and a clear boundary, focuses on past figures, is performed by accounting/finance, and requires accounting theory, bookkeeping, and tax knowledge.

Typical contrast: management accounting is used for business decision-making, has flexible or unclear rules, is future-oriented, is performed by management planning or business planning, and requires broad knowledge, thinking ability, and skills such as KPI/KGI design.
Related management-accounting activities include KPI management, KGI design, and other forms of numerical control that support management decisions rather than external reporting.

Management accounting (管理会計) covers multiple domains; the minimum set to know includes management indicators, budgeting, performance analysis, departmental/project visibility, cost-structure analysis, and product costing.
Create management indicators (管理指標) that matter for management control, using both a business-unit perspective and an organizational perspective.
Set budget targets (予算目標) on an annual, semi-annual, or quarterly cycle so that management PDCA can be run.
Compare actual results with budget, plan, and history; quantify the drivers of performance and turn the findings into improvement actions.
Move from company-wide-only performance views to visibility by department or project so that analysis and improvement actions can be more detailed.
Decompose cost structure into variable costs (変動費) and fixed costs (固定費) in order to analyze the relationship between sales and profit/loss (CVP-style analysis).
Calculate the costs required to manufacture products according to defined rules and policies, then aggregate those costs (原価計算 / cost accounting).

KPI (Key Performance Indicator), also called 重要業績指標 (jūyō gyōseki shihyō / important performance indicator), is a core element of management accounting that every company's management planning function must master, regardless of industry.
KPIs are target numerical values set for executives and frontline staff; they are used to embed goals throughout the organization and to drive the management PDCA cycle (Plan-Do-Check-Action).
KPI is explicitly described as a tool for turning the PDCA cycle.

PDCA example (sales closing KPI): Plan — set a monthly target of 10 closed deals and define the concrete actions needed to reach it. Do — execute those actions. Check — actual result was 8 deals (2 short); root-cause analysis showed the number of sales meetings was insufficient. Action — add new measures specifically aimed at increasing the number of sales meetings.
KPI setting proceeds in steps: first decompose management figures with a logic tree (STEP 1), then assign those figures to each domain/area (STEP 2).
A logic tree (ロジックツリー) is a method for setting KPIs by logically breaking large overall numbers such as sales or profit down one by one into constituent parts.

Example of logic-tree decomposition of sales (売上高): sales = units sold (販売台数) × selling price (販売価格); units sold can be further split by region (e.g., Area A vs Area B). Each resulting number can become a KPI.
The key point of a logic tree is '漏れなくダブりなく' (no omissions, no overlaps), which equals MECE (Mutually Exclusive and Collectively Exhaustive).
MECE application example: if sales areas include A and B plus an additional C area, C's sales volume must be added without omission so that the sum of sales volumes matches the company-wide total.

Profit is calculated by subtracting costs (manufacturing costs and SG&A/selling, general and administrative expenses) from sales revenue, so the cost side must similarly be decomposed using the same logic-tree approach.
KPI setting STEP 2 is assignment of KPIs to organizations: after decomposing numbers into KPIs, those KPIs (which are on-site target figures) must be allocated to specific departments or teams.
Organizational assignment example: area A sales-volume KPI is assigned to the corresponding area A team inside the sales department, which then owns PDCA cycles for that target.

Price-related KPI example: selling price is assigned to the product-planning department (inside planning headquarters) rather than the sales department, because product price is determined at the product-planning stage and that department therefore bears responsibility.

Typical organizational mapping for KPI assignment: sales HQ (area teams), factory (manufacturing and production-control sections), and planning HQ (marketing, product planning, engineering) receive the KPIs defined in STEP 1.
Sales (売上高) should be decomposed into units sold (販売台数) and selling price (販売価格), with responsibility assigned to different departments, so that field staff accept the resulting targets.

Assigning entire sales responsibility to the sales department without understanding KPIs causes problems: sales cannot control price and becomes dissatisfied, while product planning stops taking price design seriously, producing irrationality and demotivation across the organization.

KPIs appear throughout management-planning work: business plans / mid-term management plans, budget formulation, capital-investment decisions, personnel evaluation systems, and cost rationalization. It is almost true that 'where there are numbers, there are KPIs' (数字あるところにKPIあり).
A KPI is a numerical value broken down so that people in the field can easily understand it.

Every industry and department has core numerical concepts used in operations. Manufacturing examples: yield (歩留り), operating rate (稼働率), lead time. SaaS examples: Life Time Value (LTV), Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC), churn rate. Consulting examples: man-month unit price (人月単価), Availability.
All field-management information can ultimately be restated as numerical KPI indicators.

KPI is a powerful tool even when the field currently works with vague language. Example: everyone says 'we must raise productivity,' but productivity can mean (a) capacity one machine produces per hour at full operation, (b) output quantity of the whole factory/line per hour, or (c) marginal profit generated per hour. People in the same manufacturing section often interpret it differently.

The essence of KPI management is to decompose and define such terms clearly so that field and management share the same goal perspective. KPI then becomes the tool that links every field action to the goal.
KPI thinking can be practiced in daily life: while waiting at a checkout, measure the purchase amounts of people ahead, the number of people waiting, and the elapsed time.

A supermarket's approximate daily sales can be estimated with: average purchase amount per person × [operating hours related to the time until your turn at checkout (= number of people waiting ahead of you)] × number of registers. Each term in this formula is itself a KPI.
While waiting in a checkout line, the figures needed for this estimate can be grasped immediately if one thinks a little, so the situation itself can be used as training in KPI management.
KPI is described as the royal road of management control (経営管理の王道).
People who want to build experience in management planning (経営企画) are advised to train daily at connecting numbers with the actual field/operations (数字と現場をつなげる).

Investment decision-making (投資意思決定) is the process of deciding on investment projects that have two defining features: (1) a large-scale cash outlay and (2) an intended recovery period of several years or more (medium- to long-term).

Typical cases of investment decision-making include: purchasing equipment to introduce a new production line; planning a new product and launching it in the market; using project finance to construct a power plant; and forming a new business division to expand into a new business.
In the management-planning (経営企画) function, staff are expected to estimate economic viability, evaluate, and judge such large-scale projects.
Investment decision-making must begin with an understanding of finance theory; several pieces of basic finance knowledge are required as prerequisites.
To understand the finance theory used in investment decisions, it is recommended to read at least one book that focuses on corporate valuation (企業価値評価).
Finance theory for investment decisions rests on a set of basic prerequisite knowledge items (typically numbered ①–⑤) that should be mastered before applying the methods.
When making medium- to long-term decisions, one must understand the concept that time has value (時間価値の概念 / time value of money).
Receiving 1 million yen now is more valuable than receiving the same 1 million yen one year later.
Paying 1 million yen now is more costly (has higher present value/cost) than paying 1 million yen one year later.

If the expected return (期待リターン) is 5%, 1 million yen today can be invested (e.g., in stocks) and will grow on average to 1.05 million yen in one year; thus 1 million yen now equals 1.05 million yen in one year.
The same equivalence applies to payments: paying 1 million yen now forgoes the opportunity to invest it, so it is equivalent to paying 1.05 million yen one year later.

Key related concepts listed for decision-making: hurdle rate = WACC (Weighted Average Cost of Capital); Cash is King; incremental/differential thinking (増分・差額の考え方); NPV (Net Present Value) and IRR (Internal Rate of Return).
Time value of money at a 5% expected return: 1,000,000 yen today is equivalent in value to 1,050,000 yen one year later (whether receiving or paying).
Compound interest (two-year horizon): 1,050,000 yen after one year grows to 1,102,500 yen after two years, calculated as 1,050,000 × (1 + 5%) = 1,102,500 yen.

Investment decision-making rule: When cash flows occur over many future years, each year’s cash flow is discounted back to present value using the expected return (time value of money); the project is then evaluated by the sum of those present-value cash flows.
DCF (Discounted Cash Flow) is the name for cash flows that have been discounted back to present value.
The next concept introduced is that the hurdle rate equals WACC (Weighted Average Cost of Capital).

From the perspective of shareholders or banks providing capital to a company, investment of funds (e.g., 1 million yen) comes with the expectation of a return exceeding the original amount, reflecting the time value of money.
On the Balance Sheet (B/S), funds procured from shareholders or banks appear on the credit (right) side as liabilities and equity.
The debit (left) side of the B/S records how those procured funds have been converted into investments/assets.
A typical conversion example is purchasing large equipment, which is capitalized as a fixed asset.
After investment, the company deploys the invested capital in operations so that the new business generates additional cash greater than the originally procured cash.
The excess cash is then returned to capital providers as dividends (to shareholders) or interest (to banks).

Capital cycle on the B/S: (1) procure funds from shareholders/banks (right side increases); (2) invest those funds in the business (flow from right side to left side); (3) operate the business so cash grows (left side expands and cash flows back toward the right); (4) return the return to providers (right side decreases).
The balance sheet (貸借対照表 / Balance Sheet) shows how investment circulates in a company through funding sources and uses of capital.
Liabilities (負債 / Debt) represent funds procured from banks, which finance equipment investment (設備投資) and human-capital/talent investment (人材投資).
Equity / net assets (純資産 / Equity) represent funds procured from shareholders (株主).
Together, bank debt and shareholder equity form the right-hand side of the balance sheet that funds productive investments, creating a circulating investment cycle.
Shareholders and banks expect additional returns on their capital; from the company's perspective this additional return is an additional cost, and the expected level differs by industry.
Cost of equity (株主資本コスト) = risk-free rate + risk premium × β (beta).
Cost of debt (負債コスト) = the bank interest rate.
Cost of equity is calculated using the CAPM (Capital Asset Pricing Model / 資本資産価格モデル).
Risk-free rate (リスクフリーレート): the interest rate on a safe asset; typically the yield on 10-year government bonds is used.
Risk premium (リスクプレミアム): the expected return from a diversified investment across the entire stock market.
β (beta) value: the company-specific risk coefficient.
From the company's viewpoint, the expected return demanded by capital providers is the weighted average of the amounts of equity and debt funding and their respective expected returns.
This weighted-average expected return (cost) is called WACC (Weighted Average Cost of Capital / 加重平均資本コスト).

WACC (Weighted Average Cost of Capital) is the return demanded by capital providers (equity holders and holders of interest-bearing debt). Equivalently, it is the hurdle rate: the minimum return a company must earn on business investments.
Investment decisions should be made by checking whether the expected return exceeds WACC (the hurdle rate).
