WACC is computed as the weighted average of the cost of equity and the after-tax cost of interest-bearing debt, using the proportions of equity and interest-bearing debt in the capital structure: WACC = (E/V)*Re + (D/V)*Rd*(1-tax rate), where V = E + D.
"Cash is King" is the finance principle that medium- to long-term investment decisions must be judged on cash generation, not on accounting profit.
Accounting profit (shown on the P/L) is obtained by adjusting cash-basis receipts and payments according to the accrual basis and the matching principle of expenses and revenues.
Finance therefore strips away those accounting conventions and asks whether a project can purely generate cash over the medium to long term.
Depreciation is ignored in investment analysis because it produces no cash outflow; it is only an accounting allocation of a prior cash expenditure.
Consequently, all medium- to long-term investment decisions should be evaluated on a cash-flow basis rather than a profit basis.
In investment decision-making, always think in terms of increments or differences (増分や差額で常に考える). When judging one investment, evaluate only the portions that changed before versus after the decision.

Example of incremental analysis when adding a new production line to an existing factory: total investment 3 million yen before vs 4.5 million yen after (increment +1.5 million yen); revenue 1 million vs 1.5 million yen (+0.5 million); costs/cash outflows 0.7 million vs 1.1 million yen (+0.4 million); total cash flow 0.3 million vs 0.4 million yen (+0.1 million yen).

The new investment must be judged solely on the incremental cash flows: a 1.5 million yen outlay that produces an additional 100,000 yen of cash flow each year. Using the post-investment totals (1.5 million yen revenue minus 1.1 million yen costs = 400,000 yen cash flow) overstates the project and must be avoided.
Final investment evaluation uses NPV (Net Present Value) or IRR (Internal Rate of Return) as the decision criteria.
NPV (Net Present Value / 現在価値の合計額) is the sum of discounted cash flows over the entire investment period, including the initial investment. If NPV is positive, the investment decision is Go.
IRR (Internal Rate of Return / 内部収益率) is the rate of return that makes NPV equal to zero. If IRR exceeds WACC (the hurdle rate), the investment decision is Go.

Economic feasibility calculations for actual decision-making follow this sequence: (1) grasp condition information such as sales, costs, and investment amounts through discussion with the field; (2) calculate NPV/IRR using a simulation sheet; (3) judge whether NPV is positive or IRR exceeds WACC.

A simulation sheet typically has time on the horizontal axis and cash flows on the vertical axis. There is no fixed format, but a spreadsheet should be prepared with functions that automatically compute DCF, NPV, and IRR once cash flows and WACC are entered.

The evaluation period for an investment depends on the company and the nature of the investment. In principle, the period should be the one during which the investment can normally generate cash flows.

Companies often calculate investment evaluation periods over a span of around 10 years, but the period can be set longer or shorter depending on the specific investment. If an investment is judged to generate perpetual cash flows, terminal (perpetual) value after the evaluation period may also be included.

Investment decision-making notes: Management planning primarily supports the economic (numerical) portion of evaluations, but correct decisions cannot be made from numbers alone. Much qualitative business information is hard to express numerically, and calculated figures themselves can change greatly depending on optimistic versus pessimistic assumptions. Economic calculation results are only one judgment criterion and are not absolute.
Investment decision-making shows its true value when combined with business plans and budget management.

Investment evaluation methods can feel unfamiliar to those accustomed to financial accounting. Accounting/finance typically judges profitability via profit = P/L. Accounting is fundamentally a period-divided evaluation model: assuming the company is a going concern, it intentionally introduces periods (fiscal years) and checks profit annually.

By contrast, investment decisions evaluate by project or business unit with no period concept; they assess the total return the project or business generates overall. Because there is no period division, evaluation uses cash flow rather than profit = P/L.

The two approaches form a grid of corporate activity: with time on the horizontal axis and projects/businesses on the vertical axis, horizontal (time-based) evaluation is profit = P/L while vertical (project-based) evaluation is investment decision-making. Neither method is inherently superior; evaluating from both perspectives enables more accurate and precise assessment.
Management planning is a function that requires the ability to flexibly change viewpoints in order to see matters correctly.

Investment decision-making (投資意思決定) is closely related to accounting profit (会計上の利益 / P/L); a company's reported profit in any given year is the aggregated outcome of multiple overlapping investment projects rather than a single isolated result.
Example: A company's year-3 P/L is expressed as the sum of the results of three investment projects A, B, and C that started at different times and whose effects overlap in that accounting period.
If investment projects are correctly evaluated and decided upon before they start (入口時点 / entry-point evaluation), the overall P/L will naturally become favorable.
P/L at the moment an investment is started is especially important because later-period accounting results are largely determined by those initial decisions.
Profit is evaluated along a time axis (横軸 = 時間) by accounting period, so each year's P/L reflects the concurrent effects of projects begun in prior years.
M&A promotion is a prestigious (star) task for corporate/management planning departments, but it is also a rare type of work that one may seldom encounter.

M&A (Mergers and Acquisitions) is the act of completely restructuring an entire company as a whole. It generates many complex issues, requires advanced knowledge and expertise, and involves a large number of related parties and specialists.
Main parties in M&A: Buyer/acquiring company (譲受企業) — the company on the buying side; Seller/transferring company (譲渡企業) — the company on the selling side.
M&A intermediaries introduce and match cases and advance transaction negotiations from a neutral position.

FA (Financial Advisor) is the advisor for the transfer/acquisition. The FA becomes the ally of the contracted company, serving as overall coordinator and contact window to drive the entire M&A. M&A can sometimes proceed without an FA.
Lawyers provide legal advice and/or perform legal due diligence.
Certified public accountants and tax accountants provide accounting/tax advice and/or perform accounting and tax due diligence.
Social insurance and labor consultants (社労士) provide labor-related advice and/or perform labor due diligence.
Consulting firms conduct business due diligence and/or support post-M&A integration work (PMI).
Banks provide financing support at the time of M&A.
Funds and similar parties provide capital in exchange for shares.
In M&A work, corporate planning (経営企画) mainly serves as the internal contact window and the driver that advances decision-making inside the company.

Corporate planning has functions similar to those of M&A intermediaries and financial advisors (FA / ファイナンシャルアドバイザー), but the core mission of intermediaries and FAs is counterpart-company contact and coordination plus provision of M&A know-how and information about the other party.

When corporate planning itself is highly proficient in M&A know-how, the company may run the deal with corporate planning at the center; in that case intermediaries and FAs perform only the minimum necessary contact work with the counterpart and its FA.
A distinctive feature of M&A is that the process is long.

Typical M&A process stages include: current-state analysis and issue identification; examination of M&A effects and synergies; execution of a non-disclosure agreement (秘密保持契約書); review of initial disclosure information; initial valuation and deal-structure consideration; identification of other important issues; execution of a basic agreement (基本合意書); formation of a due-diligence team; execution of due diligence; management interviews and site visits; organization of findings and assessment of their impact on contract terms and negotiation policy; negotiation and agreement on the share-purchase agreement (株式売買契約書) and ancillary contracts; signing of those contracts; closing procedures including transfer of share ownership and payment of consideration; price adjustment; and start of the post-acquisition integration (PMI) process aimed at realizing synergies.
In M&A, the first thing that must be understood is the method of determining the acquisition (purchase) price.

Acquisition price is determined mainly by three factors: (1) stand-alone valuation based on the seller's business plan, (2) valuation adjustments arising from due diligence, and (3) synergies expected from post-deal integration.
Stand-alone valuation treats the target as an independent ongoing business using the seller's own business plan as the starting point for value.
Due diligence (DD) findings are used to modify that stand-alone value (up or down) before a final price is set.
Expected synergies from combining the businesses can support a higher acquisition price; the upper bound of the model is the price that would apply if those synergies were fully realized.
The buyer's acquisition-price range sits between the stand-alone (independent-business) value and the fully synergized value, after DD adjustments have been reflected.
The model therefore contrasts (a) value implied solely by the seller's business plan with (b) the price the buyer is actually willing to pay once DD and synergy considerations are included.
Company and business valuation (standalone valuation) uses three main approaches: (A) the income approach (インカムアプローチ), (B) the market approach (マーケットアプローチ), and (C) the cost approach (コストアプローチ).

In practice, the income approach and market approach are considered more theoretically superior. The cost approach is used only in limited cases, such as small unlisted companies or owner-managed companies, where the income and market approaches cannot be applied.

Income approach (DCF method / DCF法): Valuation is based on cash flows the business generates. Merits: it is the most theoretically sound method and can reflect future excess earning power. Demerits: results can vary, subjectivity easily enters the calculation, and objectivity is weaker.

Market approach (multiples method / マルチプル法): Valuation uses indicators from comparable companies in the same industry. Merits: high objectivity and easier reflection of market valuations. Demerit: comparable companies or industries may not exist.

Cost approach (net asset method / 純資産法): Valuation is based on the net asset amount on the balance sheet (B/S). Merits: it can capture current liquidation value and is easy to calculate. Demerits: future earning power is not reflected, and valuations tend to come out low.
Income-approach and market-approach results are often combined in actual valuations.
Due Diligence (DD) is a procedure in which the buyer conducts a detailed investigation of the seller from multiple perspectives after a basic agreement has been signed.
The two main purposes of DD are: (1) revising corporate value (i.e., the acquisition price) and (2) identifying material risks associated with the M&A.
DD typically lasts from about two weeks to one month and is performed by specialists covering business, legal, financial, HR, and IT perspectives.

DD generates a large volume of documents and communications. Corporate planning (経営企画) is responsible for submitting materials requested by DD experts and M&A intermediaries/FA, attending interviews with the seller, receiving DD reports, and handling extensive practical and coordination work during the DD period.
Speed is critical in DD; if corporate-planning work becomes a bottleneck, the entire M&A transaction can be delayed.
Closing an M&A deal is not the goal but the starting point. After closing, Post Merger Integration (PMI: 買収後の経営統合) begins and is a major responsibility of corporate planning.

M&A success rates are said to be only around 30 percent; many deals fail to realize expected synergies. PMI is the key process for ensuring those synergies are actually achieved after the acquisition.

PMI involves entering the seller’s operating environment and transforming management across group-governance transition, culture integration, organizational change, and monitoring/realization of business synergies.

Because the companies typically have completely different cultures and histories, group management does not succeed overnight; it requires facing the raw operating reality and steadily, hands-on reform work.
In PMI a “100-day plan” is prepared: a comprehensive schedule of integration tasks to be executed in the 100 days following the acquisition.
PMI (Post-Merger Integration) after M&A includes current-situation analysis and grasping of the status quo (現状分析・現状把握).
A PMI task team should be formed (PMIタスクチームの組成) to drive integration work.
Post-integration vision and the direction of transformation must be formulated and shared (統合後ビジョンの変革方向性の策定と共有).
Job-duty allocation (職務分掌), organizational structure, and reporting lines (レポートライン) should be improved as part of PMI.
Human-resource strengthening (人的リソース強化), system/policy review (制度見直し), and motivation-improvement measures (モチベーション向上施策) are key PMI actions.
Execution of sales synergy (売上シナジー) and cost synergy (コストシナジー) should be started.
Quick hits—defined as measures from which effects can be obtained easily and immediately (すぐに効果が得られやすい施策)—should be realized early in PMI.

In management planning (経営企画) departments, repetitive routine work is scarce; the majority of work consists of projects, frequently including company-wide cross-functional projects or special assignments under the president.
Projects cannot be executed merely by repeating past similar work; each project's theme and content is unique, so project management must be a reflexive basic competency for any such assignment.
Project management begins from an initial hypothesis.
The first step in advancing any project is to clearly define its purpose and key issues (論点).

Every project shares an unchanging structure: it is formed because a problem/challenge exists; there is a desired outcome to achieve by solving it (the purpose = 論点); and the problem cannot be solved by simply extending ordinary daily operations.

Typical reasons a project cannot be handled as daily work include the need to involve multiple stakeholders and leverage team capability, the need to invest budget, and the need to proceed according to a planned schedule.
Create the overall project plan before the project starts; this pre-start planning is strongly recommended for project success.

Expert project managers (seasoned management consultants) can largely complete issue identification from only a simple initial hearing, with about 60–70% of the problem-solving hypothesis already formed.

Inability to form an initial hypothesis on solution direction often signals unsolvable issues, insufficient budget, or insufficient schedule, raising failure probability; consider abandoning that project and quickly shifting resources to another.
Prior preparation and hypothesis-building are critical to project success.
Project success depends heavily on who participates and whether their commitment can be secured.

Design project structure and communication at the outset: all-participant meetings and frequency; team subcommittee meetings and frequency; steering committee (final-decision-maker review) meetings and frequency.
Provide a shared IT environment so members use common tools for communication and progress management.
Small projects can manage detailed tasks and progress with spreadsheets using WBS (Work Breakdown Structure) and Gantt charts.
For large cross-functional projects with many stakeholders, shared visibility of communication, progress, and discussion outcomes from a common viewpoint is essential.
DX (Digital Transformation / デジタルトランスフォーメーション) has been treated as a buzzword for over 10 years.
The COVID-19 pandemic from 2020 forced remote work (リモートワーク), which became a trigger for many companies to forcibly advance digitalization.
Many companies still find realizing digitalization and DX difficult despite this push.
Japan's Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications (総務省) conducted a 2023 Telework Security Reality Survey (テレワークセキュリティに係る実態調査), treating remote work progress as one indicator of DX.

Companies frequently cite these barriers to telework (and thus DX): necessary terminal/equipment setup (必要な端末等の整備), security assurance (セキュリティ確保), employment regulations setup (就業規則の整備), labor time management (労働時間の管理), and document digitization (文書の電子化).
Back-office DX refers to digital transformation of functions such as accounting, HR, legal, general affairs, and management planning.

A March 2023 survey by Japan's Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications (総務省「テレワークセキュリティに係る実態調査」) with n=5811 identified the main challenges companies face when introducing telework (テレワーク導入にあたっての課題).
The most cited challenge was preparation of terminals and equipment needed for telework (テレワークに必要な端末等の整備) at 37.4%.
Ensuring security (セキュリティの確保) was the second-highest challenge at 32.6%.
Handling responses to business partners and customers (取引先や顧客への対応) was cited by 28.3%.
Establishing employment rules/work regulations related to telework duties (テレワーク業務に関する就業規則の整備) was reported by 27.7%.
Improving the communications environment, including insufficient speed or lines (通信環境の整備（通信速度や回線の不足等）), was a challenge for 25.7%.
Managing working hours of teleworking employees (テレワークをする社員の労働時間の管理) was cited by 25.6%.
Providing instructions, guidance, and evaluations to teleworking employees (テレワークをする社員への指示・指導・評価) was a challenge for 24.5%.

Additional challenges listed (without top-line percentages in the visible data) include: work disruption from incomplete document digitization (文書の電子化が進んでいないことによる業務への支障); individual employees' progress management of their own work (個々の従業員による業務の進捗管理); shortage of personnel who can introduce and maintain telework (テレワーク導入・維持に対応できる人材の不足); selecting which tasks and which employees to convert to telework (テレワーク化する業務や対象となる社員の選定); insufficient internal communication and difficulty sharing information (社内コミュニケーションの不足、情報共有の困難); work disruption because documents cannot be signed or stamped (書類へのサインや捺印ができないことによる業務への支障); securing a suitable place for telework (テレワークに必要な場所の確保); other issues; and some respondents reporting no particular challenges (特になし).
This survey data appears in a Japanese practical handbook covering all back-office functions from accounting, HR, legal, and general affairs through management planning and DX.

Most corporate challenges (especially those related to DX) are strongly influenced by back-office departments, and the majority can be resolved if each back-office function proactively addresses them as part of its original duties rather than treating them as extra work.
Progress in back-office DX is equivalent to the back office possessing DX know-how, which in turn drives DX across the entire company; this relationship is not an exaggeration.
Barriers (walls) that block DX promotion can be resolved by the back office.

Typical DX challenges mapped to responsible back-office functions include: terminal/device provisioning and securing security personnel (General Affairs and Legal); management of devices and telework support; talent acquisition; documentation; and internal communication plus information sharing (Labor, General Affairs, HR/Labor, and back office overall).

For people working in the back office to strongly promote DX themselves, they must first correctly understand DX: why the company is doing DX (purpose), the walls and challenges that must be overcome, and the concrete initiative measures to take.

Back-office DX is often demanded vaguely by executives as a magic phrase ('this era IT is important, reform back office with DX') without concrete content; first understand specific back-office DX initiatives.
Priority ranking and how to proceed with each DX initiative should be considered when planning back-office digital transformation.

Paperless / digitization of Ho-Ren-So (reporting, contacting, consulting): eliminate paper-based ringi applications, stamp approvals, document creation and all related paper materials by converting them to digital.
Cloud migration: move from on-premise servers to cloud so that tools can be used from anywhere as long as an internet connection exists, enabling remote work.
Electronic government applications: use e-Tax, eLTAX, e-Gov and GビズID (G Biz ID) to perform electronic filings instead of paper submissions to government offices.
RPA (Robotics Process Automation): teach robots the procedures of standardized/routine tasks so those tasks can be automated.
AI-OCR: scan receipts and invoices, let AI process them; auto-learning functions improve reading and judgment accuracy over time.
AI chat (e.g. ChatGPT-style services): apply to inquiry handling, email drafting, Excel formula help, answering questions from other departments, and bouncing ideas for planning documents.

Workflow / application-flow digitization and unification: create a single electronic system covering expense claims, invoice approvals, paid-leave and overtime applications so that application and approval can be done digitally with designed flows.
Make systems accessible to anyone (not just specialists) and prepare remote/telework environments; expected effects include work-style reform, operational efficiency and stronger recruiting power.

In 2014, Oxford University's Dr. Michael A. Osborne published the paper "The Future of Employment," identifying jobs likely to disappear within 10 years, including data entry (99% probability), payroll clerk (97%), and general clerical work (96%). Many of these high-risk jobs are back-office related, reinforcing the public impression that advancing IT technology will eliminate such work.
As of 2024 (10 years after the paper), not all back-office employment has disappeared, but the displacement of such work is gradually progressing.

The World Economic Forum's "Future of Jobs Report 2023" (published May 2023) predicts that over the next 5 years, technology advances and digitalization will cause the loss of 14 million jobs worldwide, equivalent to 2% of global employment. The top three occupations facing the greatest job losses are accounting/payroll, general affairs/secretarial work, and data entry, each projected to lose over 25% of employment.
Back-office-related work is at the forefront of tasks that digitalization will render unnecessary for humans; structural change in these functions cannot be avoided.
Rather than merely being pessimistic about digitalization, the key is how organizations ride this inevitable wave and respond to it.
The essence of back-office operations consists of two complementary dynamics: "standardization" (標準化) and "complexification" (複雑化).

Back-office work contains a mix of two types of tasks: (1) simple, easily rule-based, high-volume work that should be standardized, and (2) work requiring human skills plus an understanding of company strategy that should be complexified in order to generate added value.
Back-office work can be classified into four types by considering two axes (the page introduces this two-axis classification framework).

Back-office work can be classified using two axes: (1) whether the work is single-domain or must be considered across departments/functions (single vs. multiple domains), and (2) whether it exists for management decision-making or for operational execution (経営判断 vs. オペレーション).
Those two axes produce four natures of back-office work: 標準化業務 (standardized), 専門化業務 (specialized), 汎用化業務 (generalized/versatile), and 複雑化業務 (deliberately complexified).

Practitioners already perform all four types of work, often unconsciously; conflicting advice such as “standardization is the greatest mission,” “keep high expertise,” or “work with the same eye as management” arises because back office contains several different natures of work.
標準化業務: repetitive work inside a single back-office domain that is easy to make efficient. Examples: data entry, simple bookkeeping, hire/leave processing, application procedures, phone reception.

専門化業務: high-expertise judgment that requires advanced knowledge and long-cultivated experience within one domain. Examples: setting accounting standards, internal-control governance, designing evaluation systems, due diligence.
汎用化業務: cross-departmental communication and system-building that demand personal, flexible, generalist responses. Examples: business-process design, company-wide events, recruitment PR.

複雑化業務: work that affects the whole company and is decided together with management; it is deliberately not standardized so that added value and decision quality rise. Examples: business plans, HR policy, M&A, new-business schemes.

Back-office work can be classified into specialized operations (専門化業務), standardized operations (標準化業務), generalized operations (汎用化業務), spanning/cross-cutting operations (またがる業務), and operations (オペレーション).
In the classification diagram, the relative area sizes indicate that standardized operations (標準化業務) occupy a considerable majority of back-office work.
Standardized operations are typical 'defensive work' (守りの業務) and account for roughly 70–80% of total work hours (工数).
'Offensive work' (攻めの業務) consists of everything other than standardized operations and accounts for roughly 20–30% of total work.
Complex operations (複雑化業務) that involve company-wide management decisions are estimated to be less than 5% of total work.
Work that is expected to disappear in the future is, unsurprisingly, standardized operations (標準化業務).

The essence of back-office DX is to automate the 70–80% of work hours that are standardized operations using IT, thereby shifting the organization toward complex operations that only humans can perform.
The book covers all back-office operations from accounting (経理), HR (人事), legal (法務), and general affairs (総務) through to management planning (経営企画) and DX.
Ideal back-office direction (あるべきバックオフィスの方向性) is framed around three axes: specialization (専門化), generalization/universalization (汎用化), and complexification (複雑化).
Specialization: use DX so that operations are entrusted to IT (DX を用いて、IT に業務を任せていく).
Generalization: build deep expertise and know-how across the entire team (深い専門性・ノウハウをチーム全体で構築する).
Link the back office with other departments so that work is connected effectively and efficiently (バックオフィスと他部署を絡めて、業務を効果的・効率的につなげる).
Develop talent capable of making complex management judgments (複雑な経営判断ができる人材を育成する).
DX improves back-office efficiency but is a difficult, labor-intensive project to implement in back-office functions due to the inherent nature of those operations and departments.
Back-office staff already think constantly about operational efficiency and productivity gains; almost no one views DX itself as a meaningless or unwelcome initiative.
A fundamental, often subconscious barrier to DX is evaluating “productivity” at the individual-person level rather than at the business-process or task-unit level.
Person-dependent work systems (人依存の業務体制) are a primary cause that stalls back-office DX.

Workplace remarks such as “A-san’s processing is always accurate and error-free” or “A-san knows everything; just ask and you’ll generally get the answer” signal over-reliance on a trusted veteran and constitute a warning sign that must be addressed before DX can advance.
A healthier state for DX readiness is one in which conversations and knowledge are not centered on irreplaceable individuals.

In back-office operations, a critical distinction exists between processes whose logical subject is a person versus those whose subject is the work itself or an organizational mechanism/system. Person-as-subject language (e.g., following a specific individual’s method) signals 属人業務 (person-dependent operations), while work- or system-as-subject language indicates more transferable, institutionalized processes.

Example of person-as-subject: 「Aさんがつくったやり方に従えば、処理が正確で間違えない」 (“If you follow the method A-san created, processing is accurate and you will not make mistakes”). The subject remains the individual, tying accuracy to personal knowledge rather than a documented system.

Example that can shift toward work/system-as-subject: 「Aさんがつくった〇〇を見れば、大体のことがわかる」 (“If you look at the XX that A-san created, you can understand most things”). Here the artifact or mechanism, rather than the person, becomes the primary reference.

From the individual’s perspective, A-san typically acts with good intentions: researching internal operations, devising personal efficiency improvements, gradually earning high internal evaluation, and becoming a relied-upon person. This path is locally rational but organizationally risky.

The more this pattern accelerates, the more the ‘person-as-subject’ state is locked in. Individually optimized, person-unit 属人業務 is thereby strengthened, reducing scalability, knowledge transfer, and resilience across functions such as accounting, HR, legal, general affairs, management planning, and DX.
The implied organizational goal is to convert personal ingenuity into mechanisms and documented work so that the subject of operations becomes the process or system rather than any single employee.
For successful DX (digital transformation) of back-office work, change the grammatical/logical subject from 'people' to 'work' (仕事).
People-as-subject state: assign work to people. Work-as-subject (DX-ready) state: assign people to work; it also becomes possible to assign tools to work.
When processes follow a system created by a person (A-san), processing is accurate and error-free, versus relying on asking that person for knowledge.
A DX-hindering cause is the principle of consistency (一貫性の原理) plus risk-avoidance judgment: people doing the same routine work repeatedly try to preserve/express how they have always done it.
Another DX-hindering cause is rejection of business-process change combined with risk judgment.
Back-office operations consist of high-volume, highly routine tasks processed at fixed timings.

People instinctively dislike taking actions that differ from what they have actually been doing or from the roles they have been given; resisting this requires strong will or a compelling reason. Related sayings include that sticking to original intent is beautiful, while frequent changes of orders or retracting previous statements inconvenience others.

This consistency instinct is often combined with 'risk avoidance' as a convenient justification, for example arguing that digitalization should be stopped because it poses high security risks. Such reasons can actually originate from the back-office side's true feeling that changing existing methods is bothersome and unpleasant, so a pretext is attached.

The back-office characteristic of handling confidential information, and therefore judging introductions cautiously, is a rational and correct risk-avoidance perspective. At the same time, one must calmly and objectively judge whether 'risk avoidance' is being used as a shield to deny DX or change itself.
If a genuine decision is made not to pursue DX on risk-avoidance grounds, thorough comparative examination must still be performed to determine whether returns exceed the risks.
Causes that obstruct DX readily reflect the inherent characteristics of back-office work, so special attention is required.

DX is neither a denial of human capability nor a denial of the past. Promoting DX requires the awareness that one is fighting human instinct, and that changing people's mindsets is the key to success.

Key DX viewpoints such as 'eliminating personalization (属人性の排除)' and 'reform / break from the past' do not mean ignoring human power or rejecting history. Adopting that mindset or denying the existing back office itself causes DX to fail immediately.
Even in a world where DX advances, human capability remains important. People who have performed many standardized tasks by hand must move toward newer, more complex work or they will not survive.

The first step of change is not DX consultants or external advisors arriving uninvited, denying the company's previous back office, and rebuilding from zero. Reform cannot succeed without the cooperation of the back-office people who already understand the existing operations.

Common mistaken view of back-office DX: DX is a process that excludes human power. Correct view: DX is not about denying people themselves, but about eliminating situations where one person is struggling alone and then improving. Sharing useful mechanisms across the whole team and standardizing them requires the power of people who can use IT.

Common mistaken view of back-office DX: DX starts from denying the past. Correct view: DX is a process of changing in response to newly changing IT technologies and business environments. Even if operations are refreshed through DX this time, if new technology is developed, the parts changed this time will naturally be updated as well.

In the author’s company, recent business-improvement projects almost always include digital elements or DX-context improvements. A key perspective is understanding the meaning of the work (業務の意味を理解する).
Typical sequence for a back-office DX / improvement project: organize current processes and understand background → organize issues → set the ideal (あるべき姿) state → create methods to solve the issues.

When organizing processes and understanding background, detailed hearings (ヒアリング) are conducted with each individual in the back-office field about their work content, followed by process organization and visualization (見える化).

Back-office DX projects highlight the strength of people: human capability to use IT is essential for team-wide sharing of useful mechanisms and for standardization, rather than treating DX as a way to remove people.

When asked why a given back-office process is performed in its current form, 70–80% of people reply that they do not know why, that it has always been the rule, or that it has been that way since they inherited the work from a predecessor.

A common waste in improvement efforts is focusing on people rather than on the work itself. The absolute rule for business-process improvement (including but not limited to DX) is to focus on the process, not the person.
Focusing on people tends to produce other-blame thinking in which individuals conclude that they themselves are not at fault.

In the initial hearings of a business-improvement project it is useful to check whether participants can shift their mindset from judging whether a person is ‘good or bad’ to judging whether the process is optimal and can be improved.

Involving key persons who can make this mindset shift in a DX project substantially raises the probability of success. Observation of successful versus unsuccessful back-office DX cases underscores the importance of this change in perspective.

The impact of back-office DX is very large. Precisely because it is not straightforward, it can serve as a competitive differentiator and can generate company-wide DX starting from the back office—a revolutionary initiative.
Effect 1 of back-office DX: large reduction in man-hours for standardized work and reallocation of the freed resources to value-added work.
The most direct expected benefit of DX is man-hour reduction for standardized tasks. Simple work previously performed by hand can be automated by IT and thereby eliminated.

Merely substituting IT for existing tasks is insufficient. True DX value appears only when the released capacity is shifted to work that requires human hands or brains (complex work, specialized work, and general-purpose work).

DX is therefore not merely a head-count or task-reduction exercise; it is an effort to redefine the overall mission, added value, and very nature of the work that the back-office function has been responsible for.

Using IT tools in back-office work equals standardization: it requires (1) deepening one's understanding of IT, (2) handing work to something other than oneself (the IT tool), and (3) designing and splitting the work so it can be transferred. This process is essentially the work of middle management.
Middle managers do not raise results as individual players; they manage subordinates and staff to maximize team performance. Promoting DX therefore instills a spirit of team play.

When team-play capability rises in the back office, people who can perform middle management and systematization grow internally. DX project experience enlarges the 'capacity of the back-office organization' itself, producing growth of both individuals and the organization as a whole.

DX reduces the need for excessive hiring. Deeply skilled, experienced talent in accounting, HR and similar domains is extremely scarce; people who can only perform replaceable, standardized clerical work do not constitute true back-office talent.
DX clarifies the definition of the talent actually required for back-office work, enabling selection and concentration in recruiting and thereby making hiring more efficient.

DX itself has a recruiting-promotion effect: because DX is a major challenge that everyone in the back office must overcome, companies that undertake it attract ambitious candidates. Publicizing DX initiatives in recruitment PR or job postings raises the probability that high-aspiration back-office talent will apply.

Back-office DX can serve as the entry point for company-wide DX. Tools that involve every employee (accounting/payment rules, payroll systems, chat systems, etc.) are led and managed by the back office; once they are digitized, they create a company-wide flow and trigger for DX.
As DX know-how accumulates inside the back office, that organization can also function as the PMO (Project Management Office) for DX/IT projects that arise throughout the company.

The essence of DX is the fostering of a transformation culture and mindset that matches the management environment. A back office that can itself drive the drive for change is a highly valuable existence.

Cloud-type tools (クラウド型ツール) are contrasted with on-premise-type tools (オンプレミス型ツール). On-premise means: (1) the software must be installed on a PC to be used, and (2) the company either owns a dedicated server or rents a server from another company.

Two main advantages of cloud-type tools: they can be used anywhere as long as there is an internet connection plus a PC or smartphone, which prevents drops in work productivity caused by location constraints.

Accessing internal on-premise tools traditionally often relies on VPN (Virtual Private Network) to reach the company's local network. That extra network-construction step is not easy for small and medium-sized enterprises that lack an information-systems department.

Because servers and data reside in the cloud, information that one person inputs and saves can be viewed immediately in real time by others over the internet. This 'anyone / real-time sharing' characteristic is indispensable when multiple people or teams work simultaneously.
The defining combination of cloud-type tools is summarized as 'anywhere' × 'anyone' × 'real-time'.
On-premise tools run in a company's own office environment on dedicated terminals, while cloud tools are accessed over the internet without requiring users to be physically in the office.
Cloud computing should not be viewed as overly complex: everyday smartphones already rely on cloud mechanisms to deliver many services.
A natural question follows: if personal devices already use the cloud, why should business work still require coming to the office and using dedicated terminals?
In business, alternatives to a purely on-premise environment have become a normal, expected option.
Digital transformation (DX) makes it possible to use cloud tools 'anywhere,' 'by anyone,' and 'in real time'; this capability should be treated as a shared, common understanding.
Cloud tools are often described from the service-provider side as SaaS (Software as a Service), pronounced 'saas' or 'saz' in Japanese.
The phrase 'SaaS-type tools' carries a slightly different nuance, but it is essentially the same as 'cloud tools'.
The book presents a categorized list of major cloud-type IT tools used in Japanese back-office operations (accounting, HR/labor, legal, general affairs, and related DX functions).
Accounting systems (会計システム): マネーフォワード会計, freee会計.
Invoice issuance systems (請求書発行システム): マネーフォワード請求書, freee会計, ラク請求書発行, Misoca, board, BtoBプラットフォーム.
Accounts payable / invoice receipt: マネーフォワード債務支払, freee会計, バクラク請求書受取, BtoBプラットフォーム.
Expense management: マネーフォワード経費, freee会計, バクラク, SAP Concur, 楽々精算.
Payroll calculation systems (給与計算システム): マネーフォワード給与, ジョブカン, freee.
Attendance systems: KING OF TIME, Touch On Time, マネーフォワード勤怠, freee人事労務.
HR systems: カオナビ, HARMOS, jinjer人事, タレントパレット, SmartHR.
Labor application systems (労務申請システム): SmartHR, マネーフォワード社会保険, オフィスステーション.
Year-end adjustment systems (年末調整システム): マネーフォワード年末調整, freee人事労務, SmartHR.
Contract management: クラウドサイン, DocuSign, マネーフォワード契約, freeeサイン.
Contract review/check tools: LegalForce, GVA assist, LeCHECK.
Trademark acquisition systems: Toreru, Cotobox.
Data storage: Google Drive, Microsoft Teams, Dropbox, Box.
Chat tools: Microsoft Teams, Slack, Chatwork, LINE WORKS, Google Chat.
Wiki / knowledge sharing: Confluence, Notion, Kibela, esa, NotePM.
Workflow tools: バクラク, サイボウズ, チームスピリット, ジョブカン.

Back-office cloud tools vary in the breadth of their service domains depending on the development company. Some have expanded from a core function into broader suites, while others remain specialized in a single domain, and some are industry-specific (vertical SaaS).

Examples of expansion: freee and Money Forward (マネーフォワード) originally centered on accounting systems but have become closer to comprehensive package-type offerings, now also covering areas such as HR/labor (人事労務) and electronic contracts (電子契約).

Vertical SaaS tools (バーティカル SaaS ツール) are cloud tools specialized for a particular industry or business type; users should keep in mind that they are surrounded by a very large number of such cloud tools.

SaaS-type (cloud-type) tools are constantly evolving. From the vendor side, a defining characteristic is that updates and feature additions can be performed easily even after the service has launched, because the vendor manages the cloud servers and can change data after go-live.

This contrasts with on-premise software, in which the user downloads and installs the product (historically via CD-ROM). Any vendor update then required redistributing media and reinstalling on each PC; cloud delivery eliminates that process.

Users must remember that SaaS tools will continue to receive updates and new features over time. Features described by a salesperson are only the current snapshot; selection should also consider likely future additions and take a medium- to long-term view.

When SaaS features are updated, integration methods between tools from different vendors and different functional domains are also typically updated, which increases convenience. Cross-domain integration is a critical issue for back-office tools.

Concrete integration examples that can substantially improve operational efficiency: (1) converting payroll-calculation results into journal-entry (仕訳) data and posting them into the accounting system; (2) feeding attendance-system totals into the payroll system for labor-hour aggregation and overtime-pay calculation.

The book covers the full range of back-office operations, spanning accounting (経理), human resources (人事), legal (法務), general affairs (総務), management planning (経営企画), and digital transformation (DX).
Example of inter-system data flow: contents of invoices issued by a billing/invoice system are entered as journal-entry (仕訳) data in the accounting system.
Example of inter-system data flow: results produced by a personnel-evaluation system are output as condition-change notification documents in a contract-management system.

Back-office cloud tools exist across many functional domains; some vendors offer multi-domain platforms while others specialize in a single area, which makes selection difficult especially for beginners.

A recommended four-step process for introducing cloud tools: (1) Clearly verbalize and summarize the company's current problems and the reasons for wanting cloud tools; (2) Collect service materials from as many vendors as possible via inquiry pages, without preconceptions; (3) Build an in-house comparison table of features, merits, and demerits because vendor feature lists do not use a common baseline; (4) Map the comparison table against the company's own priority functions/goals derived from step 1 and select the system that can actually achieve those goals.

Creating a comparison table alone is insufficient for decision-making; the organization must first define the functions that matter most (tied to the original problems) and then choose the tool that fulfills those purposes.

When gathering and comparing cloud services (steps 2 and 3 of a selection process), compare points such as pricing structure, company-prioritized core functions, UI/UX, optional features, and the vendor’s development maturity and future update potential.

Cloud-tool pricing is often composed of a basic fee plus usage-based (pay-as-you-go) charges. A typical advantage is low initial implementation cost, so expenses are usually not large at contract start. However, as headcount or sales scale grows, costs can increase exponentially. When considering adoption, simulate approximate 3- to 5-year cost projections in advance.
For main required functions: do not simply list every feature each service has. The key is to rank functions that are important to your own company in order of priority.

Operability, design quality, and ease of use are collectively called UI/UX (User Interface / User Experience). Evaluate whether operations are intuitively easy to understand, whether use causes little stress, whether overall system and individual page design is good, whether page loading and navigation are not sluggish, and whether the overall user experience is positive.

Optional functions are those that are not most important but would be convenient if available. They serve as useful reference information when core functions alone do not clearly differentiate services.

Understand whether a service currently offers only assembled core functions or is already well developed. Investigate or inquire about: how long the company has existed, whether the product is a company focus, development-team size, time since initial release, and capital strength. This indicates the likely richness and speed of later feature additions and updates.
When introducing and using cloud-type IT tools, fully utilize each tool's fundamental philosophy and core basic functions; otherwise the advantages of the cloud tool cannot be realized.
Cloud tools offer many features, but each product is built around a basic underlying philosophy (central core functions) that must be used first.

Representative Japanese cloud accounting systems (freee and Money Forward) both emphasize three core capabilities: linking bank-account and credit-card data, automatic journal-entry input, and AI-OCR checking.

A practical anti-pattern: recording transactions in a paper passbook and then manually keying them into the cloud accounting software instead of using bank-account linkage turns the cloud tool into unused treasure (宝の持ち腐れ).
Additional features beyond the core should still be used, but they are secondary to fully exploiting the tool's central design.
Rules for lowering the adoption barrier: first simply pick the tool up and try it; actually starting to use it is especially important for cloud tools.

The essence of DX (digital transformation) is fostering a culture and mindset of change that matches the business/management environment. Cloud tools have functions that change daily, so immersing yourself in a system-using environment necessarily exposes you to ongoing change; avoiding that environment reduces opportunities to notice change.
It is important to first try using cloud tools. Many cloud tools offer free trial periods and introductory campaigns to lower adoption hurdles; actually touching and testing usability is recommended.
Rule 3 for cloud tool adoption: introduce them while considering the optimal business flow, rather than simply overlaying them on existing methods.

Starting to use cloud tools often reveals that current ways of working will not allow the tools to be used well. Introduction creates opportunities to rethink processes differently from prior flows, for example through IT automation and omitting double-checks.
Cloud tools should be used as an opportunity to revise and change business flows (further detail on business flows is covered in the following section).
When introducing cloud-based IT tools, simply installing them is insufficient; business process (workflow) design must be performed first.
New or changed IT tools always exist because there is a specific business process one wants to change; the desired change must be examined concretely while using the new tool.
Designers must understand the entire process including upstream and downstream steps, identify all people involved, and determine how the process should be altered.
Cloud-tool introduction therefore requires 'business-flow design capability' (業務フロー設計力).
Business-flow design means decomposing and designing work according to the 5W1H framework.
Key design questions: Why (purpose / issue to be achieved), What (content of the work), Where (location: remote, office, etc.), Who (role allocation), When (schedule and deadlines).
Back-office operations cover accounting (経理), HR (人事), legal (法務), general affairs (総務), management planning (経営企画), and DX.
Process design should address How: methods via communication, tools, and documents.

A payment-process (支払業務) flow-design example maps four operational challenges: difficulty detecting fraudulent processing (不正処理の検知が困難); location constraints caused by original-document handling (原本処理により場所の制約が発生); extra rework cost from human error (人的ミスによる手戻り対応コスト増); and busy-period delays plus missed payments (繁忙期の処理遅延・支払漏れ).

Illustrated payment flow steps include application/invoice sending (申請・請求書送付), original receipt and input confirmation (原本受取・入力確認), exception handling/confirmation (例外対応・確認), journal-entry posting (仕訳計上), master-data matching (マスター突合), and payment execution (支払).
Roles shown in the flow are Accounting Staff 1, Accounting Staff 2, and Accounting Manager (経理担当者・経理責任者).

When improving business processes (業務フロー), follow these steps: (1) Decide fundamental goals and plans—set both quantitative and qualitative targets to achieve through improvement, then plan the organizational structure and schedule. (2) Organize the current business flow by interviewing other departments as well, visualizing it from an overall company-wide perspective rather than only one's own department. (3) Identify issues and problems in the organized flow; the ECRS framework (called イクルス) can be used for problem discovery. (4) Design solutions for each issue, often by introducing new tools to increase efficiency; if many solutions exist, assign priorities rather than attempting all at once.

ECRS (イクルス) is a business-improvement framework with four principles: Eliminate (排除)—remove the work itself to gain efficiency; Combine (結合)—merge the work with other tasks; Rearrange (再配置)—gain efficiency by changing sequence, reassigning people, etc.; Simplify (簡素化)—switch to a simpler method.
Process visualization should include other departments through hearings so that the flow is seen from an end-to-end, cross-functional viewpoint rather than a siloed one.

When multiple countermeasures exist, it is better to prioritize them than to try to implement every possible solution at once; introducing new tools is a typical way to redesign the flow for greater efficiency.

When implementing operational changes, announce and explain the specific change contents to affected stakeholders and departments; important feedback from departments should be treated as improvement points and reflected in the business design.

In actual practice, changes often do not proceed according to plan. Quickly analyze the causes of failure, thoroughly investigate them, and revise the plan. This correction cycle is not something that ends immediately; repeating it continuously is how the new operations become established.

Business flow design is the entry point on the 'user' side of IT systems. A business flow considers all related operations, including those outside the system. Because the IT system is treated as only one part of the business flow, the relationship is 'business flow design > IT tool introduction.' The ability to design business flows is therefore one level above the ability to merely introduce IT systems.

Business flow design goes beyond standardized back-office work and becomes 'generalized operations.' Designing a flow requires going beyond one's own department or domain, considering business impact across other departments, and creating the ideal operations with an overall-optimization philosophy and purpose.
Business flow design is needed not only in the back office but in every department.

Introducing cloud tools is a first step into business flow design, which is one of the value-added functions of the back office. When introducing tools, take a higher vantage point and approach the challenge positively.

For SMEs whose back-office functions are not yet mature, using the accounting or HR systems that a tax accountant (税理士) or labor and social security attorney (社労士) runs in their own office, instead of owning in-house systems, has major disadvantages from a management-control perspective and is not recommended.

A concrete disadvantage of relying on external professionals' systems is that internal company data cannot be extracted immediately when needed for counterparty credit checks, financing, subsidies, investigations, and similar situations.
Not maintaining back-office systems in-house lowers management awareness (経営管理意識), which makes it harder for the company and its managers to grow.
If a company later changes its tax accountant (税理士) or labor and social security attorney (社労士), handover mistakes to the new specialist can cause large management losses.
Cloud-type tools counteract those disadvantages through the characteristics of being usable anywhere (どこでも), by anyone (誰でも), and in real time (リアルタイムに).
When outsourcing accounting or HR work to specialists, apply the same check used for internal back-office staff: confirm whether they can actually use cloud-type systems.

DX (digital transformation) and remote work are inextricably linked: DX includes paperless operations and digitization, and the ultimate goal is an environment in which work is possible regardless of location.
When DX advances, a remote-work environment becomes a powerful tool; offering employees a choice between commuting and remote work also meets diversifying work-style needs.
Remote work supports building a location-independent environment and accepting/utilizing diversity.

Japan’s social context driving work-style change includes population decline, the ‘lost 30 years,’ collapse of lifetime employment, pension-system strain and the ‘20 million yen for retirement’ problem, women’s increased labor-force participation, the freelance era, and COVID-related social change.
Labor-force decline and fewer full-time employees create a shortage of people who can deliver results; capable talent is in high demand across companies.
Traditional ‘excellent talent’ was the internal career-track generalist who rotated through departments in one firm and was promoted from within.

The current definition of excellent talent has shifted to people who can think and act independently in changing environments, accumulate new experience and skills, and produce results; the relevant pool of such people is broader than traditional career-track employees.
リスキリング（reskilling）は「環境変化による学び直し」と定義される。
内閣府が2023年10月に公表した「新しい資本主義実現会議（第23回）」では、リスキリングを積極的に行う人ほど年収が高いという結果が報告されている。
同会議の基礎資料に基づく調査（n=7,539）では、年収別の割合として「学び直しをしている」「趣味の学習だけしている」「自ら学び直す意欲はあるが実際に学習はしていない」「自ら学び直す意欲はなく実際に学習もしていない」の各層の分布が示されている。
出典は内閣府「新しい資本主義実現会議（第23回）基礎資料」である。

People who can deliver results through experience and learning amid changing environments are those who retain work motivation (勤労意欲) and learning motivation (学習意欲) despite various personal purposes, circumstances, and surrounding environmental changes.

Examples of such people include: those who thrived full-time at a company but shifted working styles due to life events such as marriage, childbirth, childcare, or caregiving; those who achieved results in the past and became independent freelancers based on that experience; those who resolve to start a new business and take on new challenges; those forced to resign and relocate overseas due to family circumstances; and highly motivated students who intern at companies from their student days to accumulate business experience.
A key common trait among these individuals is continued desire to work and learn even while their personal environments change.
Remote work environments are one important means that allows such people to stay active and contribute.
A common tendency is to treat promotion of remote work primarily as a visible operational-efficiency measure; this view misses the true nature of remote work.
The essence of remote work is acceptance of a culture of diversity (多様性というカルチャーの受容).
Remote work should therefore be pursued with awareness that it strengthens hiring power and employer branding, raises motivation, and thereby improves the speed and stability of business growth.

Remote work implementation is almost always discussed together with paperless operations and digitization, because physical paper and files remaining in the office force commuting for tasks such as stamping/sealing (押印).

Back-office processes that should be made paperless and digitized include banking transfers, petty-cash payments, accounting voucher entry and approval, invoice issuance, invoice receipt and payment approval, and expense reimbursement applications.
Banking: contract and use internet banking; shift from over-the-counter, convenience-store, and invoice-based transfers to account transfers (口座振替).
Petty cash: replace cash payments with employee reimbursement processing (including temporary advances/仮払), plus credit cards and corporate cards (コーポレートカード).
Accounting: abolish printed-paper voucher approvals; perform voucher creation (起票) and approval entirely inside the system.
Invoice issuance: introduce an invoicing system, send invoices by bulk email to counterparties, or outsource mailing.

Invoice receipt and payment: introduce an accounts-payable system, upload evidence (証憑) for in-system approval, generate Zengin-format CSV transfer data from the system, import it into internet banking, and execute batch transfers.
Expense reimbursement: introduce an expense system with in-system approval workflow and replace paper receipts with camera photos or scanned data as evidence.
Back-office DX replaces paper tax filings (税務申告書類・決算書の届出) with e-Tax, eLTAX, or tax-declaration systems that are data-linked to those services.
Paper time cards used at offices or business sites can be replaced by attendance-management systems that support clock-in via PC or smartphone, plus chat-based attendance and work reporting.
Payroll withholding income tax (給与天引きの所得税) processing likewise moves to e-Tax, eLTAX, or data-linked tax systems.
Social-insurance and labor-insurance declarations can be handled by dedicated labor-application systems or by e-Gov.
Employee joining and leaving paperwork can be submitted digitally rather than on paper.
Internal and external communication can be digitized through chat systems, virtual offices, and voice-chat systems.
Paper-based ringi / approval applications (稟議申請) are replaced by workflow systems.
Physical evidence and documents are stored via data-storage solutions or kept inside the various back-office systems once those systems are introduced.

To advance paperless operations and digitization (ペーパーレス化・電子化) in the back office, system introductions and business-process changes are required across many back-office domains; attempting to change everything in parallel is time-consuming and high in difficulty.
Prioritize paperless/digitization initiatives using two conditions and introduce them in descending order of priority.

High-priority items for paperless/digitization: (1) operations that output a large volume of paper or that require a large amount of in-office processing; (2) operations that involve not only the back office but also other departments.
The greatest caveat of remote work is that it tends to depend on individual abilities, making it difficult for the organization to grow and become stronger.
Reduced face-to-face communication is the main root cause of remote-work problems; less interaction in communication produces harms in many places.
An organization's learning process decreases under remote work.
When organizational members learn and grow, face-to-face communication is sometimes necessary.
Mehrabian's law: the impression given to others comes only 7% from the content of speech itself; the remainder comes from nonverbal auditory and visual information.
メラビアンの法則 (Mehrabian's Law / 7-38-55 rule) describes the relative weights of how people are influenced during communication, with spoken verbal content accounting for only 7%.
This finding applies only to limited first-impression situations and must not be overgeneralized or misinterpreted as applying to all communication.
When conveying a message effectively, verbal content alone is insufficient; nonverbal (non-verbal) information that can only be transmitted in face-to-face interaction is also important.
Excessive remote work reduces opportunities for effective face-to-face input learning, which can hinder organizational growth.

Text communication skills are essential in remote work because chat tools and electronic documents become the primary channels; this includes organizing information clearly and using exaggerated emojis or phrasing so that emotions come through.
Face-to-face communication conveniently combines verbal and non-verbal cues, so much of that rich information is lost in text and misunderstandings become common.
People who are weak at text communication (often including sales staff accustomed to in-person negotiations) can be disadvantaged, experience stress, and suffer drops in motivation.
Remote work makes qualitative evaluation difficult because managers cannot observe detailed work processes, thinking, or behavior, forcing a greater reliance on results-based evaluation.

Results-oriented evaluation is a poor fit for back-office functions whose outcomes are inherently hard to see, so employees’ true capabilities may not be assessed accurately and dissatisfaction can arise.

Remote work raises mental-health risks (depression and other psychiatric issues) because of harder performance evaluation, the extra cognitive load of text communication, a tendency toward overwork, and loneliness from reduced face-to-face contact.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, increased remote work was associated with a rise in workers developing mental illnesses such as depression.

Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働省) 'Guidelines for Appropriate Labor Management in Telework' (テレワークにおける適切な労務管理のためのガイドライン) require companies to implement health-assurance measures, including countermeasures against overwork (過重労働対策) and mental health measures (メンタルヘルス対策).
Employee health management is now treated as a natural/obligatory duty of the company, not an optional welfare extra.
Drawbacks of remote work such as isolation and mental-health risk can be mitigated by activating communication in remote environments; those methods are covered in section 7-14 of the source.

Back office functions are a key player in promoting remote work; a promotion structure and clear role assignments are essential, and back-office departments (general affairs, management planning, etc.) often lead because they must drive paperless operations, system introductions, and DX.

Japan’s Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications “Survey on Telework Security” (published March 2023, n=2,946 telework-implementing companies) found that 40.7% of firms said management-planning or general-affairs departments handle information-security issues arising from remote-work promotion—the most common answer.

Having a dedicated IT or information-systems department is ideal, yet back-office involvement in security and DX is a natural consequence of their responsibility for paperless processes and system adoption.

Survey results on organizational arrangements for information-security measures among telework companies include: IT executive (CIO) present 10.4%; security executive (CISO) present 9.8%; information-systems department present; separate security department present; management-planning/general-affairs departments handle the work when no specialist unit exists; knowledgeable individuals handle it ad hoc; system-management work outsourced; security-countermeasure work outsourced; telework introduction/operation department clearly designated; telework-promotion executive clearly designated (multiple answers allowed).

In organizations without an information systems department or CIO (IT executive), form a project team to promote remote work. Staff the secretariat and project management roles with back-office personnel who have a company-wide perspective.
Newly introducing remote work requires more than paperless operations and communication measures: organizations must also establish institutional rules/systems and implement security measures.

Create a Telework Regulation (テレワーク規程) covering basic remote-work rules: purpose, eligible persons, work discipline (服務規律), working hours, contact/communication structure, equipment lending, information management, and cost burden/allowances.

Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (厚生労働省) publishes model employment rules for telework that can serve as a reference. Because telework regulations form part of the employment rules (就業規則), they must be filed with the Labor Standards Inspection Office (労働基準監督署).

Establish rules addressing remote-work-specific health risks and long working hours. Use MHLW’s “Guidelines for the Appropriate Introduction and Implementation of Telework.” Example measures include suppressing email sending and restricting system access, procedures for overtime/holiday/night work, a health-consultation system, and activating communication.

Remote work raises information-leakage risk because company data leaves the office or is accessed from external environments. Example countermeasures: ICT architecture choices, terminal login authentication, single sign-on (SSO) password management, HDD encryption, antivirus software, and privacy/peek-prevention filters (覗き見防止フィルター).

Deemed working hours (みなし労働時間) for work outside the workplace apply only when the worker is not in a communicable state and cannot receive specific instructions. If internet chat is possible, the deemed working hours system cannot be used for remote work; actual hours must be managed.

Telework regulations should specify company cost burden for items such as internet fees, pocket WiFi, and home monitors. Living expenses such as utilities (水道光熱費) are generally not borne by the employer.

Commuting allowance after a shift to remote work depends on the work rules (就業規則). If a commuting-pass equivalent is paid every 3 or 6 months, change the rules to actual-expense reimbursement. Some companies replace commuting allowance with a remote-work allowance.

Mid-work absences (中抜け時間) during remote work count as break time and must be deducted from reported working hours. Use an attendance system that allows multiple break entries per day. Start time may also be delayed to account for breaks.

Workers' compensation (労災保険) applies to remote work for accidents or disasters that occur under the employer's control, i.e., during working hours. Accidents arising from purely private acts, even during work hours, are not covered.
In back-office DX, after introducing IT tools and promoting remote work, the final issue to solve is know-how-ization (ノウハウ化) and the related activation of communication (コミュニケーション活性化).
One answer to 'what is a strong company' (depending on business model, growth phase, and organizational model) is accumulation of know-how and branding that results from continuing that accumulation.
Back-office DX must focus on the work itself and on mechanisms so the organization can escape a people-dependent work culture.
Organizations must move beyond a state centered on standardized work: they need to create mechanisms, design operations as a whole, and develop talent who can master IT—especially cloud tools.

What follows standardized work is: (1) specialized work that exercises expertise, (2) generalized work that builds cross-departmental mechanisms, and (3) complex work that involves management decisions.
Remote work as part of DX creates opportunities to hire talent who already have those abilities and who can change.
Remote work also creates communication challenges that must be addressed from the standpoints of organizational growth, personnel evaluation, and health management.

The two resulting priorities are therefore: (1) know-how-ization / knowledge-ization of operations, mechanisms, specialized knowledge, and cross-departmental management support; and (2) communication activation that promotes that knowledge work.
The two final important measures for back-office DX (digital transformation) are know-how-ization (ノウハウ化) and communication activation (コミュニケーション活性化).
The purpose of back-office DX is a shift of people toward value-added work (人による付加価値業務へのシフト), rather than merely automating tasks.
Even if standardized work is replaced by IT and spare capacity is created in back-office man-hours, the true purpose of DX is not achieved unless a foundation exists for performing complex work.

Know-how-ization (ノウハウ化) is the act of creating systematized and verbalized know-how at the organizational (not individual) level so that everyone can continuously grow; this know-how itself constitutes the organization's brand.
Communication activation functions as a mechanism that enables people to act autonomously and enjoyably for themselves and for the team, thereby supporting construction of that organizational brand.
ノウハウ化 (know-how-ization) is a very methodical, painstaking process of documenting a company's accumulated experience so it can be transferred and reused.
Know-how is the complete accumulation of a company's past activities and results; it constitutes the company's strength itself.
Know-how has both visible (explicit) and invisible (tacit) components.

Franchise restaurant chains illustrate know-how-ization: headquarters packages accumulated know-how into manuals given to franchise owners together with the chain's signage and brand name, enabling business expansion.

Typical contents of a restaurant-chain operations manual include: ingredient procurement routes and methods; developed menus; store design; customer-service manuals; staff recruitment and training methods; income/expenditure and goal-management methods; location analysis covering customer-attraction power and competitor research; and documented success/failure cases from past store openings.

In franchise business models, headquarters companies systematize and verbalize know-how cultivated over years of operations, treating that documented know-how as a source of revenue and competitive advantage.

Know-how-ization itself is ultra-high-value-added work that becomes the ultimate foundation supporting management; documentation (typically written manuals provided to franchisees) is a critical element of that process.

Build internal know-how documentation using cloud wiki tools such as Confluence, Notion, Kibela, esa, or NotePM so that documents created by anyone are stored in the cloud, freely searchable and viewable, and shareable internally or externally.

Accumulate as internal know-how: project records (purpose, progress, issues, analysis) for future project reference; laws, business-environment, and market-environment information, updated whenever there are amendments; required knowledge and skills for each task, presented as explanations, FAQs, or case studies; company regulations (work rules, approval procedures, HR rules, accounting rules); departmental task lists together with implementation methods and manuals; and meeting minutes from internal and external meetings, shared within the team.
Documenting work processes helps new organizational members imagine the work, select necessary information, and raises the overall capability of the team.
The most important element for promoting know-how (ノウハウ化) is habituation (習慣化)—making documentation and verbalization a culture and habit rather than a one-off effort.

Verbalization (言語化) is a difficult task that includes: logically explaining in words content that was previously conveyed only orally; leaving work as words or documents rather than just finishing the task; and holding a contribution mindset toward the whole team, not only oneself.

Almost no one can naturally perform verbalization and documentation; therefore organizations should create a habit in which all members document and verbalize knowledge, which also supports brand building.

Tips for know-how creation: start by writing small pieces of information rather than attempting large things at once; create a system in which continuing the practice itself leads to evaluation and rewards; repeatedly communicate the importance of know-how and brand building; appoint a person in charge who continuously cares for the process.
Alongside converting tacit knowledge into know-how (ノウハウ化), communication activation is a second core DX countermeasure that forms the foundation for resolving challenges of DX and remote work.

Communication activation helps people feel the value created through human interaction, dissolving the prejudice that DX makes people unnecessary and helping individuals recognize the added value they themselves should provide.
Deeper interpersonal understanding reduces perceived unfairness in personnel evaluations and gives a sense of security to people who struggle with text-based communication.
A sense of working as a team and being useful to others supports mental health (countering depression) and sustains motivation.
Understanding the team and finding value and fulfillment in contributing to others and the organization fosters team spirit, which in turn advances know-how-ization.
The essential design principle for communication-activation mechanisms is 「メリハリとバランス」 (rhythm/contrast and balance).

Remote work / DX and face-to-face communication have somewhat contradictory effects: increasing mandatory office days to boost face-to-face contact reduces the “choices within diversity” that is a key benefit of remote work.
The goal is therefore to enjoy the merits of both modes through deliberate rhythm and balance; DX itself can be used to create the mechanisms that achieve this balance.

When designing such mechanisms, adopt the mindsets of slightly departing from conventional work common sense, not treating communication too strictly as a work task, and enjoying an entertainment-like quality.

Remote-environment communication measures should be planned deliberately; examples include virtual office tools, internal clubs/circles, monthly offline events, cross-department shuffle lunches, 1on1s on a shorter cycle than formal evaluations, casual chat rooms, open/shared work reports, and expanded member-introduction opportunities.
A virtual office tool recreates a company’s physical workplace as an internet virtual space so people can meet and chat as if they were in a real office; examples include Gather and oVice.
Virtual office spaces can be freely customized; some services also allow avatar customization, giving an RPG-like sense of being at work.

Simply introducing a virtual office does not make people start chatting; key influencers must be involved so that casual talk is seen as normal and valuable, and everyone understands that culture—this takes time.
Internal club or circle activities create gatherings outside work hours; through those activities people learn one another’s personalities, which supports cross-department communication.

Club and circle activities must have regular actual activity so they do not become groups in name only; companies can budget activity costs as welfare (benefit) expenses and share results via internal newsletters or open chat so activity is visible, which raises effectiveness.

Monthly offline events are one of the simplest remedies for communication shortage in remote-work environments; design them around interaction (group discussion on themes different from daily work, mixers, etc.) to increase mutual communication.

Cross-department shuffle lunches create lunch settings that cross departmental and supervisor–subordinate barriers in order to promote communication and give work stimulation; hearing other departments and ranks yields new encounters, deeper mutual understanding, a renewed sense of why one works at the company, better grasp of one’s own work and other units’ roles, voluntary improvement awareness, and higher motivation.
When running shuffle lunches, balance departments and ranks so each session yields different stimulation, and have the company bear costs so everyone can participate equally.

1-on-1 meetings are the densest supervisor–subordinate communication; in remote-centered organizations raise their frequency above the evaluation-cycle cadence, and shift the agenda toward subordinate-to-supervisor consultation rather than only evaluation/feedback from the supervisor.
Creating a dedicated chat room for casual conversation is another listed measure for communication.

Chat is the central communication method in remote work. Text-based chat tends to create an atmosphere in which only work-related topics may be discussed, so creating a casual/miscellaneous talk room (雑談ルーム) lets people freely post current status, daily feelings, troubles, and private activities and get to know one another.

Setting formal rules for a casual talk room is somewhat contradictory, but example topics include: sudden personal questions about work; important memos to leave; low-priority information not directly related to work; weekend plans; information learned from work or outside study; and small troubles that do not warrant calling for help.
