Sharing information in daily-report (日報) form at the end of the workday can activate communication. In remote work even same-department colleagues cannot easily see what others did that day, so reports give a chance to learn what nearby people and other departments did.

Daily reports should remain a communication tool: spending too much time producing them is counterproductive, so keep volume reasonable. Including a free space for personal impressions and opinions of the day, not only work content, is effective.
In large companies with frequent transfers, hires, and departures, expanding member-introduction opportunities can strengthen intra- and inter-department communication.
If the company produces an internal newsletter (社内報), increasing the volume and number of employee-introduction pages creates richer content that helps people understand colleagues as individuals.
Employee directories or self-introduction pages should go beyond name and department to include experience by job type, previous-job information, and qualifications related to work.
When creating pages people would want to read, include private/personal aspects such as personality.
Incorporate Q&A-format content to increase engagement and readability.
Focusing on hobbies and how holidays are spent can make the material more appealing.
Mixing in varied information (personal details plus structured Q&A) supports attractive, readable page design.
The book covers all back-office operations, spanning accounting (経理), HR (人事), legal (法務), general affairs (総務), management planning (経営企画), and DX.
Back offices face structural challenges, including a 'wall' (壁) between the back office and management (経営者).
Chapter 8 (the final chapter) presents transformation toward a 'strategic back office' (戦略型バックオフィス) as the direction back offices should take in a turbulent management environment.
Some executives and front-office departments hold negative images of the back office, though such views may include somewhat cynical or exaggerated perspectives.
Back-office functions (accounting, HR, legal, general affairs, management planning, and DX) are frequently viewed by executives and front-line departments through a set of negative stereotypes.

Typical stereotypes portray back office as: performing only detailed/menial work; existing mainly to follow laws and rules; a cost center that generates no revenue; nitpicking small issues; having unclear actual activities; lacking understanding of frontline operations; and focusing primarily on document checking.
Such negative images are commonly held even by people with long back-office experience and can produce company-wide harm.

Prejudice against back office tends to produce a vicious cycle: simple or low-value-added work is assigned to it; compensation and salary levels for back-office staff decline; communication from operations and management becomes after-the-fact, overwhelming staff with reactive processing; staffing becomes thinner, further degrading response speed and quality; and organization members cannot obtain the performance and HR information that back office should disseminate, leading to poor decisions.

Back-office work covers a large volume of both large and small tasks: daily routine operations, continuous knowledge input, responses to legal amendments and rule changes, ad-hoc/spot project work, and digital (DX) correspondence.
Despite this heavy workload, back office is often not highly evaluated because it fails to meet expectations.
In business generally (not only back office), the way to raise added value and service satisfaction is to provide service that exceeds the other party’s expected value.
Organizational problems include decline in members’ governance awareness and self-cleansing function, which can lead to legal violations and compliance violations.
Such problems can be distinguished as issues of internal members (e.g., front-line departments) versus problems inherent to the back office itself.
Back-office functions are frequently undervalued in companies, with low organizational expectations, yet this view is questionable given their actual contribution to management.
Essential back-office roles: accounting/finance visualizes performance and numbers, supplies funds, and keeps cash flow circulating.
Essential back-office roles: HR/labor enables continuous hiring of good talent and growth of organization members.
Essential back-office roles: legal solidifies contracts, deal structures, and schemes with counterparties while protecting governance and compliance.
Essential back-office roles: general affairs (総務) enables members to work safely, securely, and with high motivation.
Essential back-office roles: management planning advances business-strategy formulation and M&A and makes dynamic management action possible.
There is no valid reason for these back-office functions and missions to be slighted in company management.

Top back-office positions such as CFO (最高財務責任者), CHRO (最高人事責任者), CLO (最高法務責任者), CAO (最高総務責任者), and CSO (最高戦略責任者) are not typically neglected; the author knows of no organizations that treat those roles as unimportant.
Despite respect for those C-level roles, the back office as a whole still tends to be undervalued; the mechanism producing that gap needs to be clarified.

One structural reason back offices are undervalued is 'career plan discontinuity' (キャリアプランの断絶). In traditional Japanese company organizations, a sharp split existed between the 'career-track / general positions' (キャリア組・総合職) aiming for back-office CXO roles such as CFO or CHRO, and the 'clerical positions' (事務職) that performed routine administrative processing. Career-track staff were typically only 20–30% of the function; the remaining 70–80% were concentrated and managed as a 'routine-work force.' This structure is called the 'old-fashioned / previous-era back office' (前時代型バックオフィス).

People who fell off the career track often gave up on growth and spent the rest of their employee lives as clerical workers. Because those clerical workers constituted the large majority, their image became the default image that other departments held of the entire back office.

A second major issue is the positioning of the back office as a cost center (コストセンター)—defined as a department that generates only costs and no revenue. The critical fork between a cost center and a profit center (プロフィットセンター, a revenue-generating department) is how goals are set and where motivation originates.

Profit centers (e.g., sales or marketing) set revenue-side performance and KPI targets. Achieving those targets produces evaluation and rising motivation. Because revenue generation is the priority, they must increase activity volume so that income exceeds costs.

Cost centers set cost-side KPI targets; activities that reduce cost are what get evaluated. Because personnel expense is typically the largest cost item, the incentive that arises is to reduce activity volume itself in order to hit the cost target. This difference in the treatment of activity volume is a key point of the analysis.
Traditional 'old-era type back office organizations' have reached their limits as clerical work is transformed.
Back office DX is a key transformation that drastically lowers the value of personnel who only perform routine administrative/clerical tasks.
Minimum talent requirements after DX: either deep specialization skills, or generalization skills (ability to design systematization and standardization mechanisms).
The cost-center mindset (focused only on cost optimization of standardized work) is no longer sufficient for specialized work, generalized work, or the further stage of complex work.
After DX, remaining value-added work (beyond leftover standardized tasks) must be judged and evaluated by different criteria than simple cost reduction.
A 'strategic back office' is proposed as a solution that moves beyond treating the function purely as a cost center.
Required back-office functions and evaluation methods are changing: specialized work and complex work sit on a different axis from standardized work and generalized work that DX will eliminate.
The old sole objective of merely reducing operations is insufficient; new evaluation approaches aligned with management decision-making are needed.

A 'strategic back office' (戦略型バックオフィス) is positioned as the unique partner that can stay close to executives and help them realize strategy, because strategy cannot be discussed without the executive.

Executives growing a business repeatedly encounter common walls, worries, and challenges that the author identified through combined experience as a manager, management consultant, certified public accountant, tax accountant, labor and social security attorney, and practitioner in startups and listed companies.
Challenge ①: Executives are lonely. They typically have no one they can truly consult with.
Even when an executive appoints an external mentor, there is still no partner who fully understands the company’s own business, feels the same level of responsibility, and thinks together with them.
In an owner-operated company the executive is simultaneously representative director and shareholder; no other person holds that combination of rights and responsibilities.

In a large or listed company the executive bears responsibility toward stakeholders such as shareholders and financial institutions, yet no one else can stand on an equal footing and share that responsibility.
When something goes wrong or fails, an executive cannot shift blame onto anyone else; that is inherent to the position.

Matters involving personal emotions (e.g., hiring), sensitive personal information (e.g., compensation), or company cash, finance, and legal issues leave the executive with even fewer possible consultation partners.

A company's capacity (器) cannot become larger than the manager's (経営者) capacity; this is also expressed as 'manager's vessel = company's vessel.' If the manager does not grow, the company will never become large and will remain small. The phrase also describes the process of the manager growing as the company's stage rises.

Main reasons a manager's vessel does not grow: lack of an attitude of keeping a broad field of view and always learning; little interest in people, so people around them leave; poor money sense and a haphazard approach; no internal vision, or a weak one that cannot attract people; looking at the past or the immediate present rather than the future; insufficient resolve to take full personal responsibility at the end.

These factors amount to a lack of leadership. Leadership is the power to foresee the future and guide members. If a leader cannot correctly foresee the future, they cannot guide members in the right direction.
For a company to grow, the manager is constantly tested on two abilities: the power to foresee the future, and the power to guide everyone.
Managers are always tormented by these two challenges; the pressure can crush the manager and halt organizational growth. Back office can become the manager's problem-solver.

Back-office functions (HR information, performance figures, legal schemes, organizational activation, mid- to long-term management plans, etc.) govern the structure of the entire company. Designing the company's overall framework is the work of determining the company's vessel.
Aggressive hiring that enlarges the organization forces the manager to enlarge their own vessel. Pulling in more capital requires increasing the credit (与信) of both the company and the manager.
Back-office actions have a large influence on the ‘vessel’ (capacity) that managers must grow into.
Because it holds important confidential information, the back office is uniquely able to approach a manager’s real worries.

In small owner-managed companies, accounting staff often act as bantō (chief clerk): they manage key information and serve as the president’s right hand, typically covering other back-office functions as well.

In business, ‘strategy’ is often used for industry/market/competitive analysis or STP (segmentation, targeting, positioning), but those are only frameworks or actions. Strategy in essence is: taking a medium-to-long-term view; deciding what to take and what to discard; and changing existing structures to match change.
A ‘strategic back office’ (戦略型バックオフィス) is a back office that accomplishes those three essential aspects of strategy.

Three characteristics of a strategic back office: (1) a viewpoint equal to or exceeding the manager’s; (2) decision-making actions that change the structure of the front line; (3) changing the structure of the back-office organization itself in response to change.

Managers operate from the viewpoint of contributing to stakeholders—employees, shareholders, financial institutions, and business partners—who provide management resources; the manager’s responsibility is to return both monetary and non-monetary value to them.

A key professional maxim is to work with a viewpoint two levels above one’s own position: understand not only the direct supervisor’s thinking but also that of the supervisor above them, because the direct supervisor is themselves trying to contribute to their own boss.

Back-office functions support managers; therefore they should adopt the perspective of the stakeholders to whom managers themselves are trying to contribute, rather than stopping at the manager’s viewpoint.

Standing in stakeholders’ shoes enables back-office staff to understand and empathize with managers’ concerns; this understanding is uniquely available to back office because it is surrounded by a large number of internal and external stakeholders.

The book systematically introduces each back-office function together with its related stakeholders so that readers can cultivate a medium- to long-term perspective that goes beyond day-to-day operations.

Front-office departments mainly work with customers and business partners, whereas back office deals with nearly all stakeholders: government/administration, counterparties, shareholders, employees, and financial institutions. Correct understanding of those stakeholders is therefore essential.

Knowing each stakeholder’s perspective is equivalent to standing at the same viewpoint as management, who is trying to deliver value to those parties. The only function that can realistically share that viewpoint is the back office, because it converses with many stakeholders.

Stakeholder demands are highly diverse. Employees alone may seek salary levels, working hours, motivation, workplace happiness, and growth opportunities. The many demands of all stakeholders converge on the CEO/management; back office is expected to share that pressure, understand it, and co-create countermeasures.

Complex operations that back office should solve together with management include: concretizing and verbalizing mission, vision, and policies for banks, investors, and employees, then converting them into both quantitative and qualitative plans. Required capabilities include understanding actual company operations while involving all departments, and correctly interpreting numbers and strategy.

Preparing B/S, P/L, and C/F that create a favorable impression on stakeholders requires understanding the thinking and needs of financial institutions and investors, plus the ability to involve the business front line and converge financial-statement figures toward target numbers in advance.

Building evaluation methods that each contributing employee can accept requires understanding of corporate values, HR policy, and business strategy, together with sound knowledge of evaluation systems and motivation theory.
Mechanisms that raise employee motivation and activate mutual communication include office and facility selection; back office must also negotiate with vendors to obtain favorable terms.

In new business expansion, legal risk must be considered when designing structures and dealings with business partners. Needed capabilities include correct understanding of the legal regime of the target industry, understanding of partners’ needs, and negotiation skill.
These items belong to the category of “complex operations” that management and back office should think through jointly, as opposed to routine processing work.

High-value back-office work (経理・人事・法務・総務から経営企画・DXまで) requires fusing accumulated know-how with the business side rather than remaining purely administrative; complex tasks become ones the back office can address proactively only when it fully deploys its expertise.

These operations significantly step into business-side work. For example, producing a convincing business plan (事業計画書) is impossible without information linkage with frontline staff, a correct understanding of the business and its structure, and joint formulation in which back office and business become integrally mixed (渾然一体).

Pursued to its limit, back-office work exhibits two defining features: (1) it approaches the mindset of executives (経営者の発想に近くなっていく) and (2) it fuses with the business itself (ビジネスと渾然一体化していく). This fusion is the essence of high-value-added back-office functions.

A practical first step for the back office to adopt an executive perspective (経営者の視座) and deliver original value is to add “plus-alpha” (プラスアルファ) to one’s existing duties rather than remaining within traditional boundaries.
Plus-alpha actions (プラスアルファのアクション) are proactive, value-added activities beyond routine back-office work; they do not develop if one only passively performs regular duties.
Plus-alpha actions become possible only when one consciously considers them before starting work or after finishing it.
Example plus-alpha action: personally analyze performance results, form hypotheses, and act on them rather than only closing the monthly books.
Example plus-alpha action: after monthly closing, reconsider the company’s HR policy and propose changes to a supervisor.
Example plus-alpha action: create a dormant-asset management table and share it with accounting so it can be used in monthly closing.
Example plus-alpha action: prepare pattern-based contract formats so the sales department can decide and use them without checking with legal each time.
Example plus-alpha action: review sales contracts (e.g., purchase-and-sale agreements) and return comments to the sales team.

Three useful starting points (切り口) for plus-alpha actions: (1) provide something useful to executives/management; (2) provide something useful to the front-line/field departments; (3) provide something useful across back-office functions (horizontal collaboration).
Most of an executive's (経営者) job consists of making decisions (意思決定).
Day-to-day practical work in front of you can be performed by other members of the company, but decisions that determine the direction of management (経営の方向性) can only be made by the executive.

Decisions have inherent properties (性質) that are composed of two axes: (1) the degree of importance they give to / impact on the company (会社に与える重要度), and (2) the degree of urgency of the situation (事態の緊急度).

A decision-handling framework/matrix uses these axes together with the number of related departments (関連部署の多さ) to determine response type: whether department heads should change organizational structure (構造を変えていく), whether the organization should respond as a whole, whether field staff (担当現場) should handle it (or sometimes not respond), and whether the matter is medium-to-long-term (中長期的な).
Executives should jointly advance decisions aimed at changing organizational structure (構造を変えるための意思決定をともに進める) and pursue structural decision-making.

The most troublesome decisions are those of high importance but low urgency. Low urgency means they do not require immediate resolution, yet high importance means that inaction causes the business or organization to deteriorate gradually.

Humans gain a sense of security from handling immediate responses and firefighting. Being somewhat busy supports a sense of purpose and health, while prolonged idleness can lead to mental and physical decline.

Acting for the future goes against instinct and consumes extra energy. Even when told it will be useful later, people postpone it (like childhood summer homework). Prioritizing what is immediately in front of you is human instinct; countering it requires effort, so such decisions are difficult.

High-importance, low-urgency decisions have large impact, so they become company-wide work and require medium- to long-term thinking about solutions that are truly necessary for the company. Awareness alone does not enable execution.
Therefore the back office must have the resolve to jointly advance these decisions that a CEO working alone tends to avoid.

Such decisions often proceed as project-type work: not as the regular organization, but by temporarily assembling team members from across the company for that project's achievement, with role division.
If the back office can launch project-type work throughout the company, it can help the CEO proceed with energy-consuming, easily avoided troublesome decisions.
Some back-office staff find project-type work difficult because 70-80% of back-office work is regular/periodic, so they are unused to irregular work whose start and end are not defined.

Among back-office functions, management planning (経営企画) is most accustomed to project-type work; concrete methods are covered in the cross-departmental projects section of the management-planning chapter.
Back-office functions (accounting, HR, legal, general affairs, management planning, and DX) can take the lead on company-wide projects rather than only supporting front-office work.
Example project led by back office: DX promotion — systematize and IT-enable all internal operations to raise operational efficiency and productivity.

Example project led by back office: performance-management and evaluation-method improvement — establish business KPIs and performance indicators while redefining evaluation metrics for every department.

Example project led by back office: company-wide communication activation — increase both the frequency and the cross-functional span of communication (casual and official) in order to build a strong internal culture.

Example project led by back office: internal-control construction — strengthen corporate governance by improving management structure, the control environment, IT utilization, and business-process flows.

Example project led by back office: group-company management — optimize management resources across the entire group in sales, tax, legal, performance, and HR domains, and set rules for inter-group transactions, consideration, and secondments.
To realize a "strategic back office" (戦略型バックオフィス), a strong team is essential.
The core idea is to design the back-office organization according to the management environment, growth phase, and overall organizational strategy, rather than using a one-size-fits-all structure.
When a company is still small and the back-office organization is first being formed, specialization and versatility of the team are generally low.
A very small number of back-office members typically handle many different tasks concurrently, combining IT systems and human effort to solve operational problems.
In the early stage, workload is concentrated in accounting/finance (経理財務), HR/labor (人事労務), and general affairs (総務); complex work done jointly with management is limited to a few areas.
In the founding phase with funding shortages, fundraising such as financing becomes a priority, which creates some complex tasks specifically in the accounting/finance domain.

Immediately after a back office is formed, organization design can be illustrated by classifying work into standardized operations (標準化業務), specialized operations (専門化業務), and generalized operations (汎用化業務).
Different functions (accounting/finance 経理財務, HR/labor 人事労務, legal 法務, general affairs 総務) are assigned different intensities of those operation types, often shown as high/medium/low (高/中/低).
As the business and organization grow, the form of the back office does not stay fixed; it branches in many directions according to strategy.

Nintendo’s core competence is IP (intellectual property). Consequently its legal department is a highly specialized back-office unit, commonly referred to as “Nintendo’s strongest legal department” (任天堂の最強法務部).
In the stable-growth phase, back-office organization design should be adjusted to strengthen selected functions (legal affairs is given as an example).

Departments (accounting/finance, HR/labor, legal, general affairs, management planning) differ in the mix of standardized versus complex work; typical intensity ratings in the example are low or medium.

In consulting businesses whose revenue depends on high-caliber talent, recruitment branding becomes a high-priority activity and the HR/labor function often operates as an integrated extension of top management.
Two factors must be woven into back-office design: (1) the distinctive features of the firm’s business model and operating environment, and (2) the changes that accompany growth.
Once those two factors are incorporated, the back office must strategically define the critical functions and critical processes it needs.
Talent/HR architecture should then be designed to match the chosen back-office organization design.
Back-office operations each have distinct characteristics, so no single 'superman' exists who can execute every function.
Talent must therefore be allocated dynamically, taking into account each person's growth direction and career plan.
Individuals growing substantially in response to changes in the management environment is the most important way to accumulate back-office know-how that lets the organization adapt to new conditions.
The era in which back-office staff only perform clerical/administrative work has ended.
Organizations must now strategically nurture and build a new back-office organization.
A 10-year financial simulation (simulation sheet) is used to evaluate the economic viability of an investment or project by projecting P/L, cash flow, B/S, and DCF metrics (units: million yen).

Cost structure includes material costs (starting at 65.0, tracking ~65% of sales), packaging, MFR, DAR, repair costs, other variable costs, depreciation (MGRDR = 20.0 for years 0–4 then 0), and common/indirect costs that grow with sales.
Operating profit (EBIT) is sales minus total costs; it is negative in early years (-2.8, -1.1) then turns positive and grows.
A constant tax rate of 30.6% is applied to compute after-tax operating profit (NOPAT).

Free cash flow (FCF) is calculated as: after-tax operating profit + depreciation − capital expenditure − increase in net working capital. Initial capex is −100.0 in year 0; depreciation is 20.0 for five years (straight-line on a 100 investment); NWC increases by 10.0 in year 0 then by 1.0 annually for several years.
Balance-sheet tracking: NWC balance starts at 0, jumps to 10.0, then rises to a plateau of 14.0; net fixed assets decline from 100.0 to 0 over five years; invested capital = NWC + net fixed assets.

ROIC (return on invested capital) = after-tax operating profit / invested capital; it is negative or low early and then rises sharply (e.g., 137.3% in year 5) as invested capital falls after depreciation is complete.
DCF valuation uses WACC (hurdle rate) of 10%. Present-value factors are 1/(1.10)^t. Discounted cash flows are summed to NPV = 19.7 (positive NPV indicates economic viability).
IRR of the project is 13.8%, which exceeds the 10% WACC, confirming economic viability of the investment.
Decision rules illustrated: positive NPV and IRR > WACC both signal that the project has economic merit.
